papers.abstract: Robot-use agents (RUAs) have emerged as a promising approach to general-purpose robot control. However, strong performance has so far been achieved only by frontier proprietary models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.2, whereas open-weight models remain substantially less capable. We show that an open-weight 27B reasoning model can be trained to use real robots natively through reinforcement learning, entirely in simulation and without demonstrations. Like a computer-use agent (CUA), the model observes the environment, reasons in a chain of thought, and generates the next end-effector pose, without any harness. We build a Post-training Engine for Agentic Robotics (PEAR) and use it to train the model on simulated robot tasks at scale with robot-use reinforcement learning (RURL), mirroring how frontier models acquire computer use. We find that the skills acquired in simulation generalize well beyond the training tasks: they transfer to an unseen robot, to the real world, and to novel instructions. After training on LIBERO and RoboDojo in simulation, the model succeeds in 60% of our trials on a real dual-arm robot, whereas the base model succeeds in none. On LIBERO, training raises the success rate from 1.6% to 74.4%, approaching GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol at maximum reasoning effort. Compared with $\pi_{0.5}$, a vision-language-action model fine-tuned on demonstrations, our model is substantially more robust to changes in the task itself. On LIBERO-Pro, $\pi_{0.5}$ succeeds in only 0.75% of episodes when assigned a new task in a familiar scene whereas our model succeeds in 57.4%. Finally, the model retains its general capabilities, with no measurable degradation on nine reasoning, coding and vision benchmarks. These results highlight robot-use reinforcement learning as a promising component of foundation-model post-training.
authors: Jiaming Tang, Zhuoyang Zhang, Junxian Guo, Fangzhou Zhao, Yilong Zhao, Zekai Li, Xingyang Li, Yuyang Zhao, Song Bian, Zhijian Liu, Song Han
bullets: An open-weight 27B model learns robot control without demonstrations or a hand-designed harness.

papers.selection_reason: RL-trained reasoning model for real robot control from simulation; directly fits embodied AI, vision-language-action, and robot learning.
papers.title: Training Reasoning Models in Simulation to Natively Use Real Robots
papers.tldr: Simulation-only reinforcement learning trains an open-weight reasoning model to control real robots natively, with strong transfer to unseen robots, tasks, and the physical world.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in speech neuroprostheses have enabled new communication avenues for people who have lost the ability to speak due to neurological illness or injury. These systems can decode neural activity during attempted speech into text by relying on language priors to achieve high decoding accuracy. This performance currently comes at the cost of using a compute-intensive language modeling stack, presenting a major bottleneck for real-world use. Further, current language models incur highly variable and disruptive inference latencies, limiting communication throughput and preventing users from reliably participating in natural conversation. We introduce FETTUCCINE, an end-to-end brain-to-text framework that leverages the speed and portability of automatic speech recognition (ASR) models to address the aforementioned practical challenges, while achieving usable (<10%) word error rates (WER), efficient adaptation to neural non-stationarities, and reliable performance on mobile devices. When evaluated using publicly available data from an intracortical speech neuroprosthesis user, FETTUCCINE outperforms previous end-to-end methods, achieving as low as 4.39% WER. Most notably, our models successfully run on a commercially-available mobile device with throughput reaching up to 370x real-time, providing the first demonstration of brain-to-text decoding on a mobile device. We also show that our models can be successfully finetuned to extend usable performance to future days. Beyond performance, our approach enables localization of the neural features most relevant for decoding via gradient-based saliency maps, which we show align with well-established physiological priors across different ASR model families. Taken together, our results show that FETTUCCINE overcomes core infrastructural and computational barriers, yielding a new class of portable brain-to-text communication.
authors: Jonathan D. McCart, Pranav I. Deevi, Mehdi Azabou, Nanda H. Krishna, Caleb A. McKinney, Nicholas S. Card, Sergey D. Stavisky, Chethan Pandarinath
bullets: Addresses compute-heavy language modeling and unpredictable latency in speech neuroprostheses.
Uses an end-to-end framework based on portable automatic speech recognition models.
Achieves as low as 4.39% word error rate on public intracortical neuroprosthesis data.
Runs on a commercial mobile device and can be fine-tuned across future recording days.
Provides gradient-based saliency maps that identify neural features consistent with physiological priors.

papers.abstract: Learning semantically meaningful human movement representations from 3D pose sequences is essential for human behavior modeling. Existing self-supervised methods derive supervision from artificial assumptions, e.g., invariance to augmentation within a certain range or recoverability of masked regions at a certain temporal scale, introducing heuristic hyperparameters that make the learned semantics sensitive to their settings. We propose BAL, a self-supervised framework that instead exploits supervision intrinsic to human movement: the natural ordering structure of everyday behavior. BAL autoregressively predicts in a semantically abstract latent space, analogous to how humans anticipate others' actions rather than their precise joint configurations. Bidirectional autoregressive prediction, both forward and backward in time, fully leverages these ordering constraints while enabling representation extraction using both past and future context at inference. To suppress representation collapse, BAL decomposes each prediction target into a global component capturing sequence-level semantics and a local component capturing context-independent movement. We prove that the local targets retain nontrivial angular diversity unless the representations are completely collapsed, preserving a meaningful training signal. Experiments on large-scale datasets demonstrate that BAL's representations are highly effective for motion captioning, forecasting, and interpolation, outperforming baselines on most evaluation metrics.
bullets: Addresses the heuristic assumptions and sensitive hyperparameters used by existing self-supervised movement-representation methods.
Predicts in latent space rather than reconstructing precise joint configurations, aligning with semantic anticipation of actions.
Uses forward and backward autoregressive prediction to exploit temporal ordering and combine past and future context at inference.
Separates prediction targets into global sequence semantics and local context-independent movement to prevent representation collapse.
Performs strongly on motion captioning, forecasting, and interpolation, outperforming baselines on most reported metrics.

papers.abstract: Direct diffusion modeling of high-dimensional raw video data is challenging, and existing pixel-space methods often rely on specialized architectures. We introduce JVT (Just Video Transformer), a simple large-patch DiT-style Transformer for pixel-space video diffusion, without a pretrained autoencoder, auxiliary detailers, cascaded stages, or U-Net-style skip connections. We systematically examine video patch embeddings, register tokens, and adaptive layer normalization to identify design choices that balance generation quality and computational efficiency. The resulting JVT design achieves generation quality competitive with latent diffusion baselines in both class-conditioned and unconditional settings. The pixel-space formulation of JVT also naturally supports joint generation of pixel-aligned modalities. We demonstrate this capability through camera-conditioned RGB-disparity generation, which improves camera following relative to RGB-only baselines and yields explicit scene geometry without an additional reconstruction model at inference. These results highlight the potential of simple DiT-style Transformers for pixel-space video diffusion, and we hope our findings offer useful insights and practical guidance for future research.
authors: Jianjun Zhou, Hua Geng, Haoyu Guo
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of directly diffusing high-dimensional raw video pixels.
Studies video patch embeddings, register tokens, and adaptive layer normalization for quality–efficiency trade-offs.
Achieves quality competitive with latent diffusion baselines in class-conditioned and unconditional generation.
Supports joint pixel-aligned modality generation, demonstrated with camera-conditioned RGB–disparity videos.
RGB–disparity generation improves camera following and provides explicit scene geometry without an inference-time reconstruction model.

papers.abstract: Demonstrations are an effective way to accelerate single-agent reinforcement learning (RL), but extending this idea to multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is non-trivial as it is difficult and often impossible for a single person to teleoperate multiple agents simultaneously. Round-Robin Behavior Cloning (R2BC) addresses this by letting a single demonstrator control one agent at a time while the others execute their current policies. However, the resulting imitation policies are limited by the quality of the demonstrations. We propose Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (IBMARL), a framework that extends Imitation Bootstrapped Reinforcement Learning (IBRL) to cooperative teams and uses R2BC to train the imitation policies. At each time step, every agent receives one action proposal from its imitation policy and one from its RL policy, and an ensemble of centralized critics selects among the per-agent combinations of the two. A gated imitation penalty, a soft Q-filtered behavior cloning loss, regularizes each RL policy toward its imitation policy only where the critics value the imitation action more, so that after training each agent executes its RL policy alone, without the centralized critics. On four cooperative multi-agent RL benchmarks, IBMARL surpasses its imitation policies $2.6$-$4.2\times$ faster than demonstration-based baselines on two tasks, is the only method to surpass it on the other two, and exceeds the demonstrator itself on two of the four. With real human demonstrations IBMARL still surpasses imitation learning alone, and does so more than twice as fast as the best baseline.
authors: Tony H. Zhang, Connor Mattson, Daniel S. Brown
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of collecting demonstrations for multiple agents simultaneously.
Uses Round-Robin Behavior Cloning to train initial per-agent imitation policies.
At each step, centralized critics choose among imitation- and RL-proposed actions for each agent.
A gated, Q-filtered cloning penalty regularizes RL toward imitation only when imitation actions are judged better.

Across four cooperative benchmarks, IBMARL improves beyond imitation faster than demonstration-based baselines and can exceed demonstrator performance; it also outpaces imitation learning with real human demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Screen history can serve as searchable visual memory for people and agents, but unlike an offline corpus, it must be encoded and indexed as each screenshot arrives. OCR-based indexing is fast but loses visual information; visual encoding takes over two seconds. Yet screens change incrementally: most pixels repeat within and across screenshots. This raises a question: do visual encoders need to recompute their representations from scratch for every new screenshot? We present StreamEmbed, a system for incremental visual embedding that exploits this redundancy. Guided solely by pixel differences, it combines spatial token pruning, which skips blocks that repeat a neighbor, with temporal KV reuse, which reuses cached keys and values for blocks unchanged across screenshots. A small learned adapter compensates for pruning and reuse to preserve fidelity to full-screenshot embeddings. On ScreenMemEval, our benchmark of 10,426 questions over 184 hours of screen histories from two humans and a computer-use agent, StreamEmbed sets a new accuracy-latency Pareto frontier on an M2 Pro GPU: it encodes up to 3.7x faster than full-screenshot encoding without sacrificing accuracy and improves accuracy over OCR-based indexing by up to 6.3 Recall@10 points at matched latency. A memory-efficient vector index stores a simulated year of screenshots in 0.13 GB of RAM. Together, these results make real-time indexing of screen history in its native visual form practical, laying a foundation for fully local visual assistants.
authors: Dayoon Ko, Yichuan Wang, Soyeong Jeong, Joseph E. Gonzalez, Gunhee Kim, Sewon Min
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between fast but information-limited OCR indexing and slow full visual encoding for continuously arriving screenshots.
Uses pixel differences to prune redundant spatial tokens and reuse cached temporal key-value representations for unchanged regions.
A learned adapter preserves similarity to full-screenshot embeddings despite pruning and reuse.
On ScreenMemEval, it achieves up to 3.7× faster encoding without accuracy loss and up to 6.3 Recall@10 points over OCR at matched latency.
A memory-efficient index stores a simulated year of screenshots using 0.13 GB of RAM, supporting local visual screen-history assistants.

papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) has made significant progress in explaining the internal computations of Large Language Models (LLMs); however, these advances have yet to demonstrate comparable success in explaining the decision-making processes of LLM-based agents. This paper examines the challenges MI tools face when applied to realistic agentic failures. We focus on one such failure: web agents hallucinating actions that are not available on a website. We apply a series of mechanistic analyzes to Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as it interacts with live websites. We find that a linear probe trained on the last prompt token can predict hallucinations before generation begins (0.80 AUC) and steering along a probe direction corrects 85\% of hallucinations, but disrupts 7\% of valid actions. However, these results only provide a partial explanation of why the agent hallucinates. The probe direction is sensitive to prompt formatting, losing much of its steering effect after a minor change to how actions are represented. Additionally, circuit identification can be difficult as the computation is distributed across multiple components and positions, and the information the agent relies on varies across examples. We discuss how these observations challenge the assumptions underlying standard MI methods for circuit discovery and feature identification, and outline future directions for making these methods better suited to explain failures in LLM-based agents.
authors: Mohamed Aghzal, Mor Geva, Gregory J. Stein, Ziyu Yao
bullets: Studies Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct during interactions with live websites, focusing on hallucinated unavailable actions.
A linear probe on the final prompt token predicts hallucinations before generation, achieving 0.80 AUC.
Steering along the probe direction corrects 85% of hallucinations but disrupts 7% of valid actions.
The steering effect is highly sensitive to prompt formatting, and the relevant computation is distributed across components and token positions.
These findings expose limitations of standard circuit-discovery and feature-identification methods for explaining agent failures.

papers.abstract: Autonomous robots are widely used for persistent monitoring of spatiotemporal environments, where quantities of interest (QoI) change across space and time and require repeated measurements. In practice, robot motion can be affected by external disturbances that vary across the environment. When such external disturbances are not considered in trajectory optimization, it can lead to inaccurate predictions of robot motion and, consequently, the information acquired about the QoI during execution. However, estimating disturbances throughout the environment can be inefficient, as disturbances in regions with little overlap with monitoring trajectories have limited impact on monitoring performance. We therefore propose a two-stage informative planning framework for unknown, spatially varying but time-invariant disturbances, combining informed disturbance sampling with disturbance-aware trajectory optimization. First, we identify where QoI measurements are needed and generate alternative paths to these locations using the environment geometry. We then prioritize disturbance measurements based on their expected reduction of disturbance uncertainty along these paths. Second, rather than optimizing information acquisition based on nominal robot motion, we incorporate the learned disturbance belief into trajectory optimization to account for its effects on robot motion and information acquisition. Across four simulation scenarios, the proposed method reduces disturbance-learning time by 25.0--52.3 percent compared with environment-wide estimation and identifies paths that appear costly under nominal dynamics but become preferable when disturbances are considered.
authors: Kaleb Ben Naveed, Haejoon Lee, Anouck Girard, Dimitra Panagou
bullets: Targets persistent monitoring when spatially varying disturbances can make nominal motion and information predictions inaccurate.
First identifies needed QoI measurements, generates candidate paths, and prioritizes disturbance sampling by expected uncertainty reduction along those paths.
Then incorporates the learned disturbance belief into disturbance-aware trajectory optimization.
Across four simulation scenarios, it reduces disturbance-learning time by 25.0–52.3% versus estimating disturbances across the entire environment.
The approach can favor paths that seem costly under nominal dynamics but are preferable once disturbances are accounted for.

papers.abstract: Small language models are attractive for local, low-cost, and privacy-sensitive deployment, but they remain unreliable on mathematical reasoning tasks that require decomposition, exact computation, tool use, and verification. We introduce \textbf{ARCHER}: \textbf{A}ction-trace \textbf{R}einforcement for \textbf{C}alculator-grounded \textbf{H}ierarchical \textbf{E}xecutable \textbf{R}easoning, a two-stage framework for training small language models (SLMs) to produce executable and auditable reasoning trajectories. In the first stage, ARCHER compiles free-form chain-of-thought rationales into typed action traces containing reasoning steps, calculator calls, deterministic runtime observations, verification actions, and final answers. This shifts the supervision target from imitating explanatory text to learning a tool-grounded reasoning policy. In the second stage, ARCHER refines this policy through asymmetric hierarchical reinforcement learning, using grouped and conditionally gated trajectory rewards for answer correctness, tool grounding, process discipline, and trace alignment. Across five standard sub-10B backbones, ARCHER improves over the strongest tool-augmented baseline by 5.51 percentage points on macro-average across benchmark accuracies, including gains of 8.95 points on MATH-500 and 5.33 and 5.34 points on AIME-2024 and AIME-2025. Evaluations on two additional reasoning-specialized 7B backbones further show that executable grounding remains beneficial after reasoning-focused reinforcement learning or distillation. These results demonstrate that executable supervision and reward-guided behavioral refinement provide a general and effective training paradigm for compact mathematical reasoners.
authors: Dhruv Dixit, Khushi Patel, Congcong Xu, Min Song
bullets: Targets the unreliability of compact models on decomposition, exact computation, tool use, and verification.
Converts free-form rationales into typed traces containing reasoning, calculator calls, runtime observations, verification steps, and answers.
Uses asymmetric hierarchical reinforcement learning with rewards for correctness, tool grounding, process discipline, and trace alignment.
Improves macro-average benchmark accuracy by 5.51 percentage points over the strongest tool-augmented baseline across five sub-10B backbones.
Also benefits reasoning-specialized 7B models, suggesting executable grounding complements prior reinforcement learning or distillation.

papers.abstract: Autonomous trading agents need controls that prevent problematic orders without making legitimate tasks impractical. We study this aspect of agentic compliance with TradeGauntlet, a replayable limit-order-book simulator that separates detection, prevention, and execution cost. In 1,680 simulated sessions with Claude Haiku 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, all conduct alerts were self-matches. Gates eliminated those alerts by rejecting self-crossing orders, while the aggregate-gate condition reduced Sonnet's two-sided fills by about 15%. A conduct reminder reduced Sonnet's alert rate but reduced Haiku's fills without a detectable alert benefit. These results show why zero alerts alone do not establish an agent's compliance. Scripted probes and two search methods test weaknesses beyond those observed in the LLM runs. The searches find split-order schedules that evade the implemented conduct rules; a learned baseline catches all 2,400 tested searched episodes but also flags 15% of a large maker's sessions. Aggregate caps reduce the response-dependent gain unevenly, with smaller reductions when only near-touch depth affects prices. A response fitted to five Nasdaq stocks and a separate ABIDES experiment expose the dependence of these estimates on market assumptions. A distinct adversarial prompt elicited refusals from Sonnet in all 240 rounds, yielding no candidate strategies to evaluate. TradeGauntlet provides reproducible tests of controls around trading agents; the experiments do not establish legal compliance or real-market detection accuracy.
authors: Sandip Nandi, Aishwarya Bose, Apurba Bose, Soovadeep Bakshi
bullets: Evaluates detection, prevention, and execution costs in a replayable limit-order-book simulator across 1,680 LLM-agent sessions.
All observed conduct alerts involved self-matches; gates prevented these alerts but aggregate gating reduced Sonnet’s two-sided fills by about 15%.
A conduct reminder reduced Sonnet’s alerts but harmed Haiku’s fills without a detectable alert benefit.
Search-based probes found split-order schedules that evaded the implemented rules; a learned baseline caught all 2,400 searched episodes but falsely flagged 15% of a large maker’s sessions.
Results varied with market assumptions, and the study does not establish legal compliance or real-market detection accuracy.

papers.abstract: Cooperative self-play can teach a humanoid to receive an object without any human data, but the partner it meets after training is never the one it trained with; we show that a fluent self-play handover policy breaks with unfamiliar partners, identify the main cause, and repair it. In a physics-based parcel handover between a Unitree G1 and a learned giver, both trained by alternating PPO self-play, the receiver completes 95% and 90% of handovers with its own partner (two training seeds) but only 31% with scripted partners it has never met. Paired interventions isolate the cause: under a shared reward the learned giver always starts its offer at once, so the receiver learns a single rendezvous, and delaying its own partner by one second cuts success from 95% to 6% (87% to 34% in the second seed). We introduce hidden start-delay randomisation (HSD), a one-line rule on the learned partner that the receiver never observes. After 300 further updates, success with unseen scripted partners rises from 31% to 80% in both seeds, against 35--41% for a budget-matched control. The gain holds on a fresh scenario seed, on eleven held-out partner conditions and on partners that start later than any training delay; it cuts high-force contact three- to five-fold and needs no retraining of the partner.
authors: Mohammad Khoshnazar, Mike Degany, Deyuan Qu, Qing Yang, Matyas Szanto
bullets: Self-play handover succeeds with the trained partner but fails with unfamiliar scripted partners.
The learned giver always offers immediately, causing the receiver to rely on one fixed rendezvous timing.
A one-second delay sharply reduces success, confirming timing overfitting as the main failure mode.
Hidden start-delay randomisation improves unseen-partner success to 80% in both seeds, versus 35–41% for a matched control.
The improvement generalises to new scenarios and held-out partners, reduces high-force contact, and requires no partner retraining.

papers.abstract: Program induction refers to the process in which a learner aims to recover a program from a few given input-output examples. This paradigm broadens programming access by letting users demonstrate the rule-based behavior they want to apply to unseen data, instead of having to implement it themselves. However, recovering a program from finite input-output examples is fundamentally ambiguous, as a finite set of input-output examples is theoretically consistent with infinitely many programs whose output diverges on unseen inputs. We view this problem from a Bayesian perspective, where, given a prior $p^0$ over programs, identifying the target program means concentrating posterior probability mass on it by observing additional input-output examples. In the interactive program induction setting, the learner chooses maximally informative inputs and queries an oracle, such as the user, for their outputs. We derive a greedy query-selection algorithm and show that it terminates after $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{\gamma}\log 1/p^0(f^\star))$ informative oracle queries, and returns the target program $f^\star$ up to approximate equivalence when no other class outweighs it under the prior. The algorithm uses a language model as the prior under a PAC-style relaxation of program equivalence, where the query-selection objective is estimated using importance sampling. On the CodeARC benchmark, the algorithm improves accuracy over the LM only agent by up to 22 percentage points while observing up to 10.5 fewer input-output examples.
authors: Robin Shing Moon Chan, Ryan Cotterell
bullets: Program induction from finite input-output examples is inherently ambiguous because many programs can fit the same observations.
The Bayesian approach treats a language model as a prior over programs and selects maximally informative inputs to query an oracle.
A greedy query-selection algorithm is proven to recover the target up to approximate equivalence with a logarithmic query bound dependent on the target’s prior probability.
Importance sampling estimates the query objective under a PAC-style relaxation of program equivalence.
On CodeARC, the method improves accuracy by up to 22 percentage points while using up to 10.5 fewer examples than an LM-only agent.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates generation by letting a lightweight drafter propose tokens for parallel verification by a target model. Diffusion drafters such as DFlash propose an entire token block in a single forward pass, but mainly focus on text-only tasks, leaving multimodal drafting underexplored. To study this setting, we first introduce a metric of token-level visual dependence based on the KL divergence between next-token distributions with and without visual input. We find that acceptance rates decrease from 46% in the lowest visual-dependence quartile to 22% in the highest, with this disparity persisting after multimodal training. Motivated by this observation, we propose MMFlash, a simple and effective framework that adaptively upweights visually dependent tokens that the drafter predicts poorly. For long video inputs, MMFlash further employs sparse attention to reduce redundant attention computation and improve drafting quality. Across various multimodal benchmarks, MMFlash achieves lossless decoding speedups of up to $3.58\times$, outperforming EAGLE-3 and DFlash by up to 195.4% and 17.1%, respectively.
authors: Sicheng Feng, Zigeng Chen, Song Wang, Gongfan Fang, Xinchao Wang
bullets: Visual dependence strongly affects draft-token acceptance: acceptance drops from 46% in the lowest-dependence quartile to 22% in the highest.
The framework adaptively upweights visually dependent tokens that the drafter predicts poorly.
For long-video inputs, sparse attention reduces redundant computation and improves drafting quality.
Across multimodal benchmarks, MMFlash achieves lossless speedups of up to 3.58×, outperforming EAGLE-3 and DFlash by up to 195.4% and 17.1%, respectively.

papers.abstract: LLM-based verifiers are increasingly used to evaluate agent executions, but their reliability is typically measured under a single representation of the trajectory. In deployed agent systems, the same execution may be exposed through composed tools, delegation boundaries, or compacted histories, changing what execution evidence is directly observable to the verifier. It therefore remains unclear whether correct verifier judgments persist across such abstraction boundaries. We introduce Verification Transport, a reliability test that measures judgment stability under abstraction-induced changes in execution observability. We construct matched native, abstracted, and restored views of the same frozen executions while holding the task, realized trajectory, outcome, ground truth, evaluation criterion, and verifier fixed. Across four agent-evaluation benchmarks, seven verifier backbones, four verification protocols, and three abstraction boundaries, we find substantial transport failure, reaching about 31% under macro abstraction and delegation. Verification protocols exhibit distinct failure modes: direct verification more often produces incorrect verdicts, whereas evidence-grounded and deliberative protocols tend to abstain under limited observability. This suggests that lower transport failure rates do not necessarily imply greater reliability. Restoring the corresponding execution provenance recovers 85.5% of transport failures, while recovery is lower when provenance is lossy or unavailable. These results show that native-view accuracy alone is insufficient to characterize verifier reliability when execution evidence crosses abstraction boundaries.
authors: Disha Sheshanarayana, Sai Linisha Reddy Goli
bullets: Introduces Verification Transport, which measures judgment stability across native, abstracted, and restored views of identical executions.
Evaluates four benchmarks, seven verifier backbones, four protocols, and three abstraction boundaries while holding task, trajectory, outcome, ground truth, criterion, and verifier fixed.
Finds transport failures of about 31% under macro abstraction and delegation.
Direct verification more often gives incorrect verdicts, while evidence-grounded and deliberative protocols more often abstain when observability is limited.
Restoring execution provenance recovers 85.5% of transport failures, but recovery is lower when provenance is lossy or unavailable.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces 'Verification Transport' to measure the reliability of LLM verifiers when execution evidence is abstracted or compressed, relevant to agent evaluation at inference time.
papers.title: Do Verifier Judgments Survive Abstraction? Measuring Verification Transport for LLM Agent Evaluation
papers.tldr: LLM verifier judgments can change substantially when the same agent execution is viewed through abstraction boundaries, so native-view accuracy alone is insufficient for evaluating reliability.

papers.abstract: Agent sessions may involve frequent context edits, which effectively invalidate cached KV state and force requests to wait for re-prefill before decoding. We present Callo, a disaggregated serving system that leverages invalidated KV for speculative drafts to reduce this latency, while verifying drafts against the exact KV after prefill before committing tokens. Callo makes effective use of decode resources by scheduling speculations during periods of underutilization and preempting speculations when drafts are likely to not be accepted. We evaluated Callo on a two-GPU testbed using SWE-agent sessions across three model families, observing all-request speedups of 1.05-1.19x over vLLM at moderate load. We demonstrate that these gains are also realized at scale through cluster-level simulations driven by real-world traces.
bullets: Targets agent sessions where context edits invalidate cached KV and delay decoding.
Uses invalidated KV to generate speculative drafts, then verifies them against the correct post-prefill KV before committing tokens.
Schedules speculation during underutilized decode capacity and preempts low-value speculation.
On a two-GPU testbed across three model families, achieved 1.05–1.19× all-request speedups over vLLM at moderate load.
Cluster-level simulations using real-world traces indicate the gains can extend to larger-scale deployments.

papers.selection_reason: LLM serving optimization that reuses invalidated KV cache for speculative decoding; fits KV-cache and inference-efficiency interests.
papers.title: Callo: Serving Cache-Miss Requests with Speculative Decoding on Invalidated KV under Prefill-Decode Disaggregation
papers.tldr: Callo reduces cache-miss latency in disaggregated LLM serving by speculatively decoding with invalidated KV states and verifying drafts after exact prefill.

papers.abstract: Clinical world models expose language-model agents to predicted patient responses, but simulations can be unreliable for poorly supported treatments or unfamiliar hospitals. We introduce Support-Gated World-Model decision support, a lightweight extension of a propose--simulate--refine agent. A recurrent dynamics ensemble predicts short-horizon physiological responses to documented norepinephrine dose categories, while a behavior model estimates observational action support. The interface withholds predictions with insufficient support or excessive ensemble disagreement and abstains when no candidate qualifies. Evaluation on eICU-CRD includes 70 hospitals and 30,700 decision transitions, with 14 hospitals held out for testing. At 62.0% factual-transition coverage, joint gating yields a MAP mean absolute error of 7.3 mmHg, compared with 9.2 mmHg for random selection at the same coverage. The gated agent achieves 60.0% agreement with recorded actions at 81.0% decision coverage, compared with 55.0% agreement and 99.5% coverage for an ungated ensemble agent. Component ablations show lower factual risk with joint gating than with either gate alone.These results characterize a reliability--coverage trade-off in selective clinical simulation; they do not identify individualized treatment effects or establish improved patient outcomes.

papers.abstract: Reliable use of large language models (LLMs) requires uncertainty estimates that separate ambiguity intrinsic to a prompt from genuine knowledge gaps. Bayesian and deep-ensemble methods deliver this aleatoric/epistemic decomposition in principle, but are computationally prohibitive at LLM scale and require white-box access. Existing black-box methods, in contrast, summarize to a single scalar that cannot make the distinction. We introduce a two-level ensemble that bridges this gap. Stochastic decoding of a fixed prompt forms the inner ensemble; meaning-preserving semantic perturbations of the prompt form the outer ensemble. Variability is measured in a continuous embedding space, and the law of total covariance gives an exact within-/between-perturbation decomposition to estimate aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty (AU/EU); it requires only black-box sampling access. On top of this estimator, we contribute three theoretical results that ground the framework: (i) a finite-sample bias identity for nested Monte Carlo with a closed-form bias-corrected epistemic estimator; (ii) a Bayesian bridge bounding the gap between perturbation-population AU/EU and Bayesian targets; and (iii) a separation result identifying a class of failure modes that any consistency-only black-box method provably misses while perturbation-based EU detects. Across five short QA benchmarks and four instruction-tuned LLMs spanning two families and two scales, our estimator is competitive with strong white-box baselines, and at a matched generation budget it matches leading black-box methods on error ranking while decomposing AU and EU; controlled paired interventions show that AU and EU respond selectively to distinct, actionable sources of failure: prompt ambiguity and model knowledge gaps; and a long-form pilot on the NQ long-answer split shows the framework extends to claim-level factuality without retraining.
authors: Wang Ma, Debarun Bhattacharjya, Junkyu Lee, Nhan H Pham, Harsha Kokel, Qiang Ji
bullets: Addresses the inability of existing black-box uncertainty methods to distinguish aleatoric uncertainty (prompt ambiguity) from epistemic uncertainty (knowledge gaps).
Uses stochastic decoding as an inner ensemble and meaning-preserving prompt perturbations as an outer ensemble, measuring variability in embedding space.
Applies the law of total covariance to decompose uncertainty, with a bias-corrected epistemic estimator for finite nested samples.
Provides theoretical guarantees covering estimator bias, links to Bayesian uncertainty targets, and failure modes missed by consistency-only methods.

Across five QA benchmarks and four instruction-tuned LLMs, matches leading black-box error ranking at matched generation budgets while also decomposing uncertainty; a pilot extends the approach to claim-level factuality without retraining.

papers.abstract: AR-Classroom uses physical models and virtual overlays to help learners explore spatial transformations. To align these overlays on a standalone headset, we developed a markerless six-degree-of-freedom(6DoF) tracker for a LEGO airplane on the Meta Quest 3. A compact YOLO model trained on synthetic Unity renders predicts 20 keypoints from dynamic RGB crops resized to 128 by 128 pixels. A perspective-n-point solver estimates the airplane's pose from these predictions and the corresponding 3D landmarks. In a paired evaluation on 1,000 synthetic validation images, cropping guided by ground-truth boxes increased the detection rate on annotated images from 32.5 to 46.2 percent. Mean keypoint F1 increased from 42.9 to 44.6 percent, with lower keypoint precision in the cropped view. In preliminary headset tests, 2 Hz was the highest tested tracking target at which the application maintained approximately 72 frames per second. A headset demonstration illustrates virtual overlay alignment with the physical airplane before and after a manual rotation. Quantitative 6DoF pose accuracy on real headset footage will be measured in future work.
authors: Guangxi Feng, Philip Yasskin, Wei Yan
bullets: Motivation: AR-Classroom requires robust alignment between virtual overlays and a physical manipulative during spatial-learning activities.
Method: A compact YOLO model predicts 20 airplane keypoints from 128×128 RGB crops, and a perspective-n-point solver estimates 6DoF pose from corresponding 3D landmarks.
Synthetic evaluation: Ground-truth-guided cropping improved detection on annotated images from 32.5% to 46.2% and mean keypoint F1 from 42.9% to 44.6%, while reducing keypoint precision.
On-device demonstration: The application sustained approximately 72 FPS with a tested tracking target of 2 Hz and showed overlay alignment before and after manual rotation.
Scope/limitation: Results are preliminary; quantitative 6DoF pose accuracy on real headset footage remains future work.

papers.abstract: Linear-attention language models replace a growing key-value cache with a recurrent state of fixed size. On an edge FPGA, this state can exceed the on-chip memory and must be paged to external memory. This paper asks whether such paging dominates the cost of decoding (generating tokens). We built a hardware tile that computes one complete layer of a custom 369-million-parameter hybrid Gated DeltaNet model on an Agilex 5 FPGA and pages its recurrent state. The model state needs 6.2 MiB, whereas the device has 0.87 MiB of block memory. Paging adds 26.0 MB of memory traffic per decoded token, at most 11.2 percent of the calculated total. On the board at 75 MHz, with synthetic weights, one token takes 11.15 ms in this layer. The matrix-vector products with the weights take about 62 percent of this time and the state phase, including the paging, 13 percent. The tile is one node of a multicast mesh of tri-mode processing elements. We measure the error of the fixed-point arithmetic against floating point and check that the hardware agrees bit for bit with a fixed-point reference. In simulation, the state logic agrees with the reference on all 18 recurrent layers. On the board, six builds pass all 30 runs of 64 tokens and two runs of 1,024 tokens. For this model and memory interface, the delivery of the weights limits the decoding performance, and the recurrent state does not. State paging is therefore practical for such a model on an edge FPGA.
bullets: The 6.2 MiB recurrent state exceeds the FPGA’s 0.87 MiB on-chip memory, requiring external-memory paging.
Paging adds 26.0 MB of traffic per token, but accounts for at most 11.2% of calculated total cost; the state phase takes 13% of measured layer time.
The tile computes a complete layer of a 369-million-parameter hybrid Gated DeltaNet model at 75 MHz, with one token taking 11.15 ms using synthetic weights.
Fixed-point hardware matches a fixed-point reference bit for bit; state logic also agrees across all 18 recurrent layers in simulation and all reported board tests.
The conclusion is scoped to this model and memory interface: weight delivery remains the decoding bottleneck.

papers.abstract: Humans know that airplanes are fast, that this extends to red airplanes, but that it does not hold for broken airplanes. How do LLMs acquire category knowledge that humans learn and apply effortlessly? We introduce LeCat, a two-part framework to analyze LLM's Learning of Category knowledge. First, we use LeCat to evaluate models on their ability to learn category knowledge, distinguishing between three cases: memorization of in-domain category knowledge, generalization to unseen instances, and ability to flexibly use knowledge in appropriate contexts. Then, we use LeCat to trace how this knowledge can be learned in pretraining from text that may encode category knowledge in various ways, such as verbatim repetition or exceptions, which we refer to as forms of "knowledge expression". We first assess open-source pretrained models using 199 curated category-feature pairs and analyze their training data. Our findings suggest that strengthening context and category-feature co-occurrence likelihood (PMI) improve learning for larger models and verbatim rule-like statements diminish flexible category learning. To systematically isolate these effects, we then train a 68M model from scratch with precise control over the categorical information each sees in their training data, confirming that verbatim repetition reduces flexible learning but mixture of diverse knowledge expressions lead to more robust category learning. Together, our findings highlight that while contextual flexibility is persistently difficult for models, how category knowledge is expressed in pretraining greatly impacts models' acquisition of robust category knowledge.
authors: Jimin Mun, Maarten Sap, Yanai Elazar
bullets: Evaluates category learning through memorization, generalization to unseen instances, and context-appropriate use.
Traces how different pretraining knowledge expressions—such as repetition, rules, and exceptions—shape learning.
Stronger context and category–feature co-occurrence improve learning, especially in larger models.
Verbatim rule-like repetition reduces flexible category learning, while diverse expressions produce more robust knowledge.
Contextual flexibility remains persistently difficult for LLMs.

papers.title: LECAT: Measuring LLM Category Learning from Pretraining Data

papers.abstract: Multimodal continual instruction tuning requires multimodal large language models to sequentially acquire new capabilities without catastrophic forgetting. Mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures offer a promising way to mitigate task interference through expert specialization and combination. However, while existing MoE-based methods avoid overwriting shared parameters by allocating separate experts for each task, this progressive expansion incurs severe cross-task redundancy and linear parameter growth. Specifically, experts across tasks often learn overlapping functions alongside task-specific capabilities. For instance, ScienceQA and TextVQA both locate relevant image regions. To curb parameter redundancy without inducing forgetting, we propose Consolidating and Preserving MoE (CoPre-MoE). For each incoming task, CoPre-MoE first learns task-specific MoE to capture specialized capabilities. To eliminate redundancy and reduce parameter growth across tasks, we design a shared-and-private expert architecture. Specifically, we first evaluate functional overlap to selectively consolidate overlapping experts across tasks into a fixed-capacity generic expert pool. We then factorize the remaining task-specific experts into shared projection bases and compact task-specific cores within a private expert pool. To mitigate forgetting, we construct the router by pairing each expert with learnable retrieval keys, where historical keys remain frozen during continual updates while newly added keys are regularized with an orthogonality penalty. At inference, input-dependent routing dynamically combines both pools without test-time task labels. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CoPre-MoE achieves superior performance while substantially reducing parameter overhead.
authors: Tao Hu, Ling-Xiang Zhang, Da-Wei Zhou
bullets: Addresses catastrophic forgetting and linear parameter growth in task-specific MoE expansion.
Consolidates functionally overlapping experts into a fixed-capacity generic pool.
Factorizes remaining task-specific experts into shared projection bases and compact private cores.
Uses frozen historical retrieval keys and orthogonally regularized new keys to stabilize routing.
Dynamically routes inputs across shared and private pools without requiring task labels at inference; experiments report superior performance with substantially lower parameter overhead.

papers.abstract: We introduce Gamer, a generalist agent framework built for long-horizon tasks in complex interactive environments. Its end-to-end architecture combines perception, memory management, and multi-step reasoning. A shared training and deployment pipeline supports interaction with both conventional 2D graphical interfaces and complex 3D simulated worlds. We first continue pre-training on a dataset constructed from tens of thousands of hours of device-level keyboard and mouse interaction. These trajectories span simulated games and embodied environments, allowing the model to learn environmental dynamics across both physical and virtual domains. Sparse-thinking instruction tuning then substantially reduces redundant computation while preserving the reasoning needed for complex decisions. We train the policy for long-horizon interaction with a stable multi-turn reinforcement learning method that addresses finite context windows, accumulated rollout errors, and sparse rewards. For real-time interaction, a cloud-edge inference engine serves numerous simulated game environments concurrently, supports unbounded-context execution, and keeps online inference latency low. Across multiple challenging 3D open-world games, Gamer demonstrates solid generalization and operational efficiency comparable to skilled players. It also achieves competitive results on a range of conventional 2D game benchmarks. These results suggest that even repetitive keyboard and mouse trajectories can support substantial gains from scaling data and learning algorithms. Training on these trajectories helps Gamer learn complex skills more steadily in environments with both physical and digital properties. This approach offers a path toward generalist agents that can interact across digital and physical worlds.
authors: Run Luo, Kuan Zhang, Qi Deng, Yukun Chen, Zhihao Yang, Yufei Zhang, Renrong Hu, Yi Zhang, Guiyu Ma, Tianyu Fan, Longze Chen, Hao Sun, Jiaming Li, Jiaming Yang, Xiaohao Liu, Tao Tan, Minzheng Wang, Hangtian Jia, Shuai Yuan, Lvdi Wang, Xiao Liu, Chao Ma, Yuting Zou, Yinhe Zheng, Xiaobo Xia, Dawei Jiang, Shaoqing Ren
bullets: Targets complex, long-horizon tasks in both conventional graphical interfaces and 3D simulated worlds.
Continues pre-training on tens of thousands of hours of keyboard-and-mouse interaction trajectories from games and embodied environments.
Uses sparse-thinking instruction tuning and multi-turn reinforcement learning to reduce redundant computation and address finite context, rollout errors, and sparse rewards.
Employs a cloud-edge inference engine for concurrent environment interaction, unbounded-context execution, and low online latency.
Shows solid generalization and operational efficiency across challenging 3D open-world games, with competitive performance on 2D game benchmarks.

At each step, the agent uses the current screen, task context, recent interaction history, long-term memory, and reasoning to generate native keyboard and mouse actions in real time. papers.selection_reason: Introduces 'Gamer', a generalist Vision-Language-Action foundation model for long-horizon tasks in complex 2D and 3D environments, combining perception, memory, and reasoning.
papers.title: Gamer: A Generalist Vision-Language-Action Foundation Model for Long-Horizon Real-Time Game Agent
papers.tldr: Gamer is a generalist vision-language-action agent that combines perception, memory, reasoning, and efficient real-time control for long-horizon interaction across 2D and 3D environments.

papers.abstract: Interactive LLM services must meet latency service-level objectives (SLOs) for the time to first token (TTFT) and the time between tokens (TBT), as streaming and soft real-time applications require predictable token delivery. We identify decode jitters in both aggregated and disaggregated serving. A jitter delays every request in the batch, and long responses span hundreds of steps, so even rare overruns cause many SLO violations. In aggregated serving, SLO-aware schedulers set each step's prefill budget until its predicted latency just meets the TBT target, leaving no room for mispredictions or host stalls. Disaggregation meets average TBT targets at a cost in capacity, yet the steps that admit new requests still run late. We present \sysname, a scheduler that calibrates how much prefill work each decode step carries using the measured tail of its own iteration latency. The SLO determines how rare a late step must be, and \sysname leaves enough headroom in each iteration to prevent overruns and meet the target decode latency. This headroom slows prefill, so \sysname serves the shortest waiting prompt first. When TTFT deadlines grow with prompt length, the long prompts it delays have the most time to spare. Under disaggregation, it spaces admissions so that no request waits on more slow admission steps than its P99 target allows. On three attention families and varying workloads, \sysname sustains 2.4--2.9$\times$ the SLO goodput of the strongest baseline on Qwen3-8B and DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and at least 4.4$\times$ on DeepSeek-V2-Lite. With prefill and decode disaggregated on eight GPUs, \sysname meets the SLO for more than twice as many requests as state-of-the-art baselines.
authors: Ishaan Datta, Alind Khare, Koushik Kumar Dey, Ratnesh Jamidar, Anand Kumar Singh
bullets: Decode jitters can delay every request in a batch, causing repeated SLO violations across long responses.
VelServe uses measured tail iteration latency to reserve headroom for each decode step, with the SLO setting the acceptable rarity of late steps.
It serves the shortest waiting prompt first to offset the prefill slowdown caused by added headroom.
For disaggregated serving, it spaces admissions so requests encounter no more slow admission steps than their P99 target permits.

Across tested attention families and workloads, it achieves 2.4–2.9× baseline SLO goodput on Qwen3-8B and DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and at least 4.4× on DeepSeek-V2-Lite; on eight GPUs, it meets SLOs for more than twice as many requests as state-of-the-art baselines.

papers.abstract: We present contraction-certified sampling-based model predictive control (CS-MPC) for tracking and safety of nonlinear robotic systems under parametric uncertainty, disturbances, and safety constraints that are revealed online. CS-MPC uses a contraction-certified tracking feedback inside every sampled rollout, which concentrates the rollouts around the reference, and an execution layer that verifies the applied input using a quantile-tightened discrete-time control barrier function condition. We derive a verification procedure for nonlinear contraction of the feedback-closed dynamics, and we prove a finite-sample stochastic stability bound and a mission-level probabilistic safety guarantee. We validate CS-MPC in simulation on a rover, a quadrotor, and an asteroid landing. When compared with standard model predictive path integral (MPPI) control, CS-MPC attains the same tracking error with 7 to 20 times fewer rollouts for the rover, and a 2 to 4 times lower tracking error for the quadrotor, with no safety violations in 200 Monte Carlo missions.
bullets: Targets tracking and safety for nonlinear robotic systems with uncertainty, disturbances, and online-revealed constraints.
Uses contraction-certified tracking feedback within each sampled rollout to concentrate trajectories near the reference.
Applies a quantile-tightened discrete-time control barrier condition to verify executed inputs.
Provides finite-sample stochastic stability and mission-level probabilistic safety guarantees.
In simulations, matches MPPI tracking with 7–20× fewer rover rollouts, reduces quadrotor error by 2–4×, and reports no violations across 200 missions.

The system is affected by a mission parameter ϑ drawn once per run, process noise, actuator quantization, and constraints revealed during the mission.

papers.title: CS-MPC: Contraction-Certified Sampling-Based MPC for Nonlinear Systems Under Uncertainty
papers.tldr: CS-MPC combines contraction-certified sampling with barrier-based input verification to enable efficient, probabilistically safe nonlinear control under uncertainty.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models adapt web-pretrained vision-language models to output robot actions, so that web knowledge carries over to physical control. In under 4 years the field has moved from RT-2, the first VLA, to open models that fine-tune on a single consumer GPU and to proprietary generalists that clean unseen homes. This survey reviews 88 works from December 2022 to October 2026, mainly on manipulation and navigation, plus humanoid control, world-action models and evaluation. We follow a VLA through its life cycle, from model design to training and deployment, along seven axes. Model design covers (a) inputs and memory, what the model observes; (b) architecture, how its pipeline is built; (c) action output, how it produces motor commands; and (d) intermediate predictions, what else it predicts, from reasoning steps to future observations. Training covers (e) pretraining data, the mix of robot, web, human and simulated data, and (f) post-training, adaptation to the target robot. Deployment covers (g) real-time execution, keeping pace with the robot. We analyse 22 models on these axes and report their training data, model size, inference speed and hardware. Three trends emerge: (i) training data has broadened, from about 10,000 hours of teleoperated robot data ($\pi_0$) to 23,000 community-collected episodes (SmolVLA) and 20,000 hours of egocentric human video (GR00T N1.7); (ii) model sizes have split: most recent models have 3-7 billion parameters, while a new group under one billion runs on consumer GPUs; and (iii) generalist VLAs are emerging that handle both manipulation and navigation, such as UniVLA and Qwen-VLA. We also compare VLAs with world-action models, which predict future observations as well as actions. We review evidence that some VLAs with near-perfect benchmark scores fail when objects or the camera move slightly, and open up further research questions.
authors: Suvarna Kadam (Witsense AI), Soran Parsa (University of Huddersfield)
bullets: Reviews 88 works from December 2022 to October 2026, focusing mainly on robotic manipulation and navigation, with coverage of humanoid control, world-action models, and evaluation.

Analyzes 22 models, including their training data, parameter scale, inference speed, and hardware requirements.
Identifies trends toward broader training data, a split between 3–7B-parameter models and sub-billion consumer-GPU models, and generalists handling both manipulation and navigation.
Notes that strong benchmark performance may not translate to robustness under slight object or camera movement.

papers.abstract: Automation of heavy machinery offers the opportunity to improve productivity in mechanized industries such as construction, mining, and material handling. Yet, automation of such machines is challenged by their complex dynamics, in part because of hydraulic actuation that involves fluids, flexible elements, and nonlinear delays. A concomitant challenge is the size and weight of these machines, which can make experiments on the physical systems exceedingly dangerous. Here, we show that \ac{RL} in simulation, followed by transfer of the learned policies from simulation to reality, can successfully automate acrobatic maneuvers that push a heavy construction machine to the limits of its actuation and have only previously been accomplished by a small number of elite human operators in official world-record performances. We trained policies that perform autonomous acrobatic maneuvers on a John Deere 332G, an operational 5-tonne skid-steer loader. The policies can autonomously swing the machine up onto two wheels and, while balancing on two wheels, drive over rough terrain, trace out specified trajectories, spin around, and swing the bucket back and forth before landing it safely back onto four wheels. This work demonstrates that \ac{RL} and sim-to-real transfer enable dynamic autonomous control of heavy machinery, directly contributing to greater automation in heavy equipment sectors. Videos: https://sites.google.com/leggedrobotics.com/heavy-metal-acrobatics This is the author's version of the work. It is posted here by permission of the AAAS for personal use, not for redistribution. The definitive version was published in Science Robotics on 11 November 2026, DOI: https://doi.org/10.1126/scirobotics.aef0894
authors: Pierre-Jean Lorentz, Pascal Egli, Edo Jelavic, Cliff Li, Ramitha Sundar, Harikrishnan Suresh, Paul Montgomery, Lee Redden, Matthias M\"uller, Ozan Sener, Vladlen Koltun, Marco Hutter
bullets: Heavy machinery is difficult to automate because of complex hydraulic dynamics, nonlinear delays, and the risks of physical experimentation.
The approach trains reinforcement-learning policies in simulation and transfers them to a John Deere 332G skid-steer loader.
The loader autonomously performs two-wheel balancing, rough-terrain driving, trajectory tracing, spinning, bucket swinging, and safe four-wheel landings.
The work demonstrates sim-to-real reinforcement learning for dynamic control of heavy construction equipment.
The demonstrated scope focuses on specific high-dynamic acrobatic maneuvers and does not establish general-purpose autonomy.

(Bi) The operator is navigating the SMB accurately along the path by providing high-level commands consisting of linear and angular velocity. Figure 4. Robustness analysis. For all panels, the corresponding snapshot times are indicated in the plot with roman numerals. (A) Robustness to arm movements of the RL controller and the MPC baseline. The arm is moved around its nominal position. Between (I) and (V), the arm moves downward; between (V) and (IX), the arm moves upward. (B) Robustness to spinning at different wheel speeds of the RL policy and the MPC. Spinning is achieved by overlaying a machine rotation command on the policies’ actions. (C) Traversing rough terrain. The SSL successfully navigates the 75 cm bumps, driving forward and backward. The image sequence shows the SSL driving backward over the bumps. The green curve shows the MPC not being able to traverse the first bump, even when increasing the target velocity.

Figure 3. Hardware deployment. (A) Image sequence of the swing-up maneuver. (B) Swing-up in simulation and reality. First, the swing-up controller is executed. When the machine’s pitch reaches −30◦ (dashed lines), the stabilize-and-balance controller is activated. The roman numerals refer to the corresponding images of (A). (C) Soft-landing sequence in simulation and on the real SSL compared with zero command. In the beginning, the balancing controller is active. The landing controller is triggered at t = 1 s and is active after that. When the pitch, pitch rate, and wheel speed are close to zero, the commands are set to zero. If the soft-landing controller is inactive and the action is set to zero immediately after balancing, the SSL falls onto four wheels. However, the front wheels rebound, causing the machine to rock back and forth. (D) Image sequence of the soft-landing maneuver with the roman numerals corresponding to the time stamps in (C). (E) Balancing in place with RL in simulation and on the real machine, with the MPC baseline. (F) Velocity tracking with RL and MPC. The target wheel velocity is increased/decreased gradually up to the maximal/minimal velocity that each controller can successfully track without touching the ground with the bucket or the rear underside. Positive target velocity tracking starts with the swing-up maneuver. Negative target velocity tracking starts with the transient behavior of switching from a positive target to a zero-velocity target.

Figure 6. RL. (A) Initial state distribution at episode start (sampled on 1000 environments). (B) Visualization of different SSL pitch angles. (C) Rewards as a function of the pitch angle for swing-up and soft-landing controllers for different values of c0,1. (D) Swing-up learning: Average reward per time step and curriculum progression on c0 to increasingly penalize touching the ground with the rear underside. (E) Distribution of the pitch angle at the end of an episode. All 1000 trials achieved a pitch angle smaller than −30◦, which is required for successful swing-up. (F) Stabilize and balance learning: The termination probability drops from 1 to 0, corresponding to the transition from failing all of the time to successful balancing without touching the ground. The rewards for the command and the command derivative increase over the course of training as the controller learns how to perform the task using small and smooth actions. (There is no curriculum for this task.) (G) Soft landing learning: The probability of terminating by landing on the bucket or tipping over backward drops to 0. The average reward per time step increases. (There is no curriculum for this task.) (H) Balance and track velocities learning: The probability of falling when balancing and tracking velocities drops from 1 to 0. The tracking reward decreases because of the curriculum on c3.

papers.abstract: The release of GPT-6 Astra marks the emergence of a new paradigm in robotics: agentic robotics. Within weeks, frontier models with agentic harnesses matched or exceeded task-specific policies on many embodied benchmarks. Instead of training a dedicated policy for each family of tasks, an agentic robotic system applies a foundation model to open-world embodied tasks. It operates in a closed loop: observing the environment, interpreting user intent, reasoning about the task, invoking skills and tools, verifying outcomes, and adapting its strategy. Despite these advances, the community has yet to converge on a shared definition, a reliable evaluation framework, or a research roadmap. We argue that Embodied System 2, realized by a foundation model together with an embodied harness, forms the decision-making core of agentic robotics. Its central challenge is to translate general-purpose reasoning into effective and verifiable actions under physical constraints such as limited reaction time, mechanical limits, unpredictable environment changes, and irreversible consequences. Motivated by this perspective, we propose an evaluation framework that measures both model capabilities and closed-loop system performance. Furthermore, we identify the principles that carry over from digital to physical agents and the challenges that must be addressed to achieve reliable physical autonomy. On top of the Embodied System 2 and the evaluation framework, we envision a research roadmap toward sustained autonomy: the ability to perform work safely and reliably with progressively broader responsibility, from executing individual primitives to fulfilling standing roles.
authors: Grid Robotics, :, Qingfeng Lan, Duo Li, Siyao Li, Yiheng Lyu, Shijian Lu, Zhenghao Qi, Shizun Wang, Xinchao Wang, Ming Yang, Zhiqin Yang, Zuhao Yang, Tao Yu
bullets: Frames agentic robots as open-world systems that observe, interpret intent, reason, use skills and tools, verify outcomes, and adapt.
Defines “Embodied System 2” as a foundation model plus an embodied harness for physical decision-making.
Highlights the challenge of converting general reasoning into safe actions under time, mechanical, environmental, and irreversibility constraints.
Proposes evaluating both foundation-model capabilities and end-to-end closed-loop robotic performance.
Outlines a roadmap from executing individual primitives toward safely fulfilling sustained roles with broader responsibility.

figures.caption: Figure 3 | A reference framework for agentic robotics. An Embodied S2 consists of a foundation model and an embodied harness, whose five core parts manage context, tools, planning, memory, and verification. S2 runs on demand or in response to events, whereas S1 and S0 execute at their own rates. A real-time event monitor outside the three systems watches the user, the robot body, and the physical world at a high rate. It interrupts S2 when an event may change the task and, under predefined safety rules, triggers an immediate reaction in S0 without waiting for S2. S2 may call S0 directly through the tool interface; S0 keeps its own real-time loop.

Figure 2 | Two paradigms. (a) An action policy maps the task instruction and observation to action targets. It might include reasoning, subtask prediction, or in-context adaptation. (b) S2 combines a foundation model with an embodied harness. Together, they interpret intent, orchestrate skills and tools, verify outcomes, and adapt subsequent decisions. S1 provides callable skills and tools. S0 performs body control. The S1 path is illustrative; S2 may also call S0 or external tools.

Figure 4 | Three typical execution paths. One system may use all three paths within a single task. For simplicity, the robot body is omitted. (a) Layered orchestration: S2 invokes S1 skills and tools, which produce control targets that S0 executes. (b) Direct control: S2 controls S0 directly through an action interface; S0 still runs its own real-time control loop. (c) Code as policy: S2 writes code that a runtime interpreter executes in the role of S1.

Figure 6 | Core abilities of Embodied S2. These abilities are necessary for Embodied S2 to perform successfully and reliably in the physical world; some reside in the foundation model, while others emerge from its integration with the embodied harness.

Figure 8 | How long each layer takes per decision or control update. All values are given as times, with the equivalent rate in parentheses (time = 1/rate). The S0 and S1 bands are indicative ranges. The S1 band covers control skills only, since the perception and planning modules of S1 are invoked on demand and have no fixed rate. S2 is event-driven rather than periodic, so we plot time per decision; the S2 band is a target for dynamic manipulation, not a requirement for every task. Helix’s “System 2” is a vendor label: its output is a latent representation, so our criterion does not classify it as S2 (Section 3.1); we include it as the fastest upper-level module plotted. The Astra measurements come from different tasks and settings and are not directly comparable with one another.

Figure 11 | What physical agents must rebuild. Foundations replace the four enabling conditions of Figure 10; runtime constraints, which follow from time, irreversibility, and a changing body, govern how the system operates; and evaluation in the running world validates its claims.

Figure 5 | The agentic loop. Top: one cycle comprises six steps. S2 interprets intent, reasons about goals and constraints to decide how to proceed, and invokes an S1 skill, an S0 interface, or an external tool as needed. The invoked capability executes under its contract. S2 then observes and verifies the outcome by answering four questions (whether the request was accepted, whether execution terminated, whether the physical effect holds, and whether the user’s intent is satisfied). Based on the verification, it continues, recovers, asks, or reports. The real-time event monitor, which watches the user, the body, and the scene, can interrupt S2 at any point. Bottom: the same steps on a schematic time axis, labeled with their step numbers and colors. S2 deliberates on demand, S1 runs while a tool executes, and S0 runs continuously; after an interruption, S2 cancels the running tool call and replans while S0 keeps the body stable; the hatched segment marks the canceled execution.

Figure 1 | A vision for agentic robotics: from executing tasks to fulfilling roles. A home breakfast scenario illustrates progressively broader responsibility entrusted to robots: from executing a primitive (L1), completing a task (L2), coordinating a workflow (L3), to fulfilling a standing role (L4).

Figure 9 | The S2 evaluation recipe at a glance: the 9 dimensions (inner ring) and their 53 sub-dimensions (outer ring). Darker cells mark the 29 embodiment-related sub-dimensions: those specific to embodiment or strongly dependent on it; standard evaluations of general language models rarely cover these sub-dimensions.

Figure 7 | Capped scaling. Frontier models scale monotonically: greater capability comes with longer latency. Embodied S2 must instead become more capable within a fixed decision deadline. A decision that arrives after the deadline is usually too late, even if it is correct: the situation has already changed, so acting on it could fail the task or create a hazard. Note that the curves are schematic: they illustrate the qualitative relationship, not measured data.

Figure 10 | The four enabling conditions of digital agents, and how far each domain satisfies them. The domains illustrate how the conditions vary across task settings rather than forming a strict progression of capability or difficulty.
Figure 13 | Spatial scope of delegated work, from a workcell within the robot’s reach to a site with several buildings and outdoor routes. The illustration is conceptual.

Figure 12 | Ladder of delegable work. Progress is measured by the responsibility that a robot can be trusted to carry alone. Each of the four levels includes those below it; typical durations are illustrative.

papers.selection_reason: Roadmap and evaluation framework for foundation-model-driven agentic robotics, directly relevant to embodied AI and vision-language-action systems.

papers.abstract: Accessible mobility is user-conditioned rather than scene-intrinsic, as walkable paths for one embodiment are inaccessible to another. Yet, existing benchmarks evaluate traversability under a fixed and limited embodiment. We present Vision-Language Accessible Navigation (VLAN), containing 1,000 scenes, 20K navigation trajectories, and 160K keyframes across diverse lighting, environmental conditions, scene semantics, and path geometries. For each trajectory, VLAN provides embodiment-specific actions and accessibility features for legged and wheeled agents, including humanoid and quadruped robots and people with visual or mobility impairments, while everyday obstacles and accessibility labels are categorized as Passable, Bypass, HighRisk, and Blocked. Unlike goal-only evaluation, our benchmark measures physical safety and alignment with user-specific constraints via goal-reaching, collision-aware, and accessibility-aligned metrics. We benchmark modern vision-language models and find they often fail to consistently adapt obstacle relevance, path selection, and safety criteria across user profiles, suggesting accessibility-aware navigation requires dedicated datasets, tasks, and metrics beyond conventional embodied navigation evaluation. All data and code open-source at https://github.com/InSAI-Lab/VLAN.
authors: Jie Hu, Yu Zheng, Wenzhi Wu, Weixing Feng, Cunlei Cheng, Jiaming Zhang

Evaluates goal reaching, collision avoidance, and alignment with user-specific accessibility constraints.
Modern vision-language models often fail to consistently adapt obstacle relevance, route selection, and safety criteria across user profiles.

papers.abstract: Weakly Supervised Video Semantic Segmentation (WS-VSS) aims to learn temporally consistent semantic object masks in videos using only video-level labels. While fully supervised models successfully learn temporal relationships by means of cross-attention, training these temporal weights under weak supervision is unstable and even pushes the model below its single-frame baseline. Therefore, existing WS-VSS methods exploit temporal consistency by relying on external priors, such as optical flow. Unfortunately these cues are non-semantic, computationally expensive and noisy, degrading the supervisory signal. Instead of supervising attention weights directly or using external priors, we propose MemCAM, a WS-VSS transformer framework that learns temporal cross-attention directly through feature-space self-supervision. MemCAM introduces a CAM Propagation Algorithm that synthesizes a supervisory signal by propagating past CAMs according to patch-level feature similarities in the latent space. Specifically, we constrain their induced CAMs through a consistency objective between predicted and propagated maps, stabilizing temporal attention learning. Experiments on the YouTube-Objects v2.2 and WS$^2$ datasets demonstrate that MemCAM consistently outperforms the temporal localization and segmentation performance of WS-VSS alternatives, showing that cross-attention can be effectively trained in label-scarce video settings through internal self-supervision.
authors: Andrea Marelli, Alessandro Ardenghi, Giacomo Boracchi, Luca Magri
bullets: Targets temporally consistent object masks from only video-level labels.
Propagates past CAMs using patch-level feature similarities in latent space to create self-supervision.
Trains temporal attention with a consistency objective between predicted and propagated CAMs.
Experiments on YouTube-Objects v2.2 and WS² show improved temporal localization and segmentation over existing WS-VSS methods.
The approach is evaluated in label-scarce settings and avoids reliance on computationally expensive, noisy optical flow.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of MemCAM architecture. Inputs (left) are encoded by the multi-class transformer backbone into class tokens V t cls (a1) and patch tokens V t p (b1). The memory-refined patch embeddings V t p ′ (b2) are reshaped (b3) and passed through the Patch-Level Supervision branch (PLS) to produce per-patch activations V t M and the patch-level loss Lp. Class-aware CAMs V t M ′ are obtained after attention-based refinement and stored in the CAM queue QM of the Memory Bank (d). (b) We convert S into a Probability Matrix P, by keeping only the top K entries per row (and so per current patch) and then applying a per-row softmax. In this way, we can see P as a matching likelihood between current and past patches. (c) The final propagated CAM M̂ t is computed as a weighted aggregation of past CAMs (from QM ), using the probabilities from matrix P to weight the activation values. papers.abstract: Web platforms record user and item activity in relational databases whose schemas differ from platform to platform, which makes it difficult to transfer predictive models between them. Relational foundation models address this through cross-database pretraining, yet recent improvements have relied on increasingly large pretraining corpora. We ask whether a better architecture, together with features specific to the target database, can deliver comparable gains from far less pretraining data. We introduce MoREGT, a mixture-of-relational-experts graph transformer that represents both rows and cells as tokens, adds the log-ages of rows and the names of foreign-key relationships to attention, and routes cells and rows to experts by column metadata rather than by values. A label-blind LLM agent complements the model: it reads the target database's schema and column statistics and adds validated single-row derived columns, without access to labels or model scores. On 21 RelBench tasks with leave-one-database-out pretraining on six databases, the MoREGT backbone improves on the Relational Transformer pretrained on the same databases by 2.25 points of mean AUROC and 5.83 points of mean nMAE. The agent's columns raise mean AUROC from 78.45 to 79.63 and lower mean nMAE from 27.91 to 26.98, the highest means on both metrics among the compared methods, including RT-J, which pretrains on about 400 times as many databases.
authors: Hiren Madhu, Sukanta Ganguly, Kiran Srinivasan, Smita Krishnaswamy, Rex Ying
bullets: Targets transfer across platforms whose relational database schemas differ.
Represents rows and cells as graph-transformer tokens, incorporating row ages and foreign-key names into attention.
Routes rows and cells to experts using column metadata rather than values.
A label-blind LLM agent adds validated single-row derived columns from schema and column statistics.
Across 21 RelBench tasks, the approach achieved the highest reported mean AUROC and nMAE among compared methods, including one pretrained on far more databases.
