papers.abstract: Vision-based perceptive locomotion has enabled legged robots to achieve agile and terrain-aware locomotion across complex environments. However, the reliability of such systems heavily depends on visual observations, which are inherently susceptible to occlusion, reflective surfaces, and illumination variations, often resulting in catastrophic locomotion failures under degraded perception conditions. In this paper, we present PROOF (Perceptive Robustness via Out-of-Distribution Fallback for Legged Locomotion), a perceptive locomotion framework that enables robust locomotion under severe visual disturbances. Our method adopts a two-stage teacher-student learning paradigm that explicitly models perception reliability: the teacher learns both perception-driven and proprioceptive fallback behaviors, while the student predicts exteroceptive features with uncertainty and suppresses them under out-of-distribution inputs. We evaluate our method on a Unitree Go2 quadruped equipped with a RealSense D435 depth camera in real-world settings. Under normal visual conditions, our method enables the robot to successfully perform high-dynamic parkour maneuvers, including traversing large gaps, elevated platforms, and narrow beam terrains. Under severe visual degradation, such as heavy occlusion and strong illumination changes, the robot continues to maintain stable and robust locomotion performance.
authors: Siyuan Wang, Dongjie Zhu, Jinxuan Lu, Wenjun Xu, Jiankun Wang
bullets: Addresses catastrophic failures caused by occlusion, reflective surfaces, and illumination changes in vision-based locomotion.
Uses two-stage teacher–student learning to combine perception-driven behavior with proprioceptive fallback behavior.
Predicts uncertainty in exteroceptive features and suppresses unreliable features for out-of-distribution visual inputs.
Demonstrated on a Unitree Go2 in real-world settings, including dynamic parkour over gaps, platforms, and narrow beams.
Maintained stable locomotion under heavy occlusion and strong illumination changes.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have shown strong semantic and spatial reasoning capabilities in 3D environments. Recently, connecting VLMs with model-predictive controllers (MPC) has emerged as a paradigm for combining strong semantic reasoning with physics-based planning. However, connecting these two for contact-rich robotic manipulation requires a task representation that bridges the two and captures how physical interactions can be reasoned by VLMs. In this work, we introduce Objectives as Policies (OaP), a framework that connects a pretrained VLM to a shared sampling-based MPC through an editable objective program. Each program specifies a sequence of stages for completing a task, combining running and terminal costs from a cost library with stage completion conditions. Given a natural-language task instruction and scene observation, we build a simulation-based digital twin through real-to-sim, and the VLM generates an objective program that is executed by the MPC in the simulation. The program is iteratively updated by the VLM based on MPC rollouts, before being deployed in the real world. We evaluate our framework in both simulation and the real world on four tabletop manipulation tasks, and show that it outperforms strong baselines. Additional videos and examples are available on the project website: https://zihaolu001.github.io/oap-project/
authors: Zihao Lu, Trong Gia Hung Nguyen, Fuquan Wang, Yifan Zhu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of representing physical interactions in a form that VLMs can reason about and MPC can execute.
Uses stage-based objective programs combining running and terminal costs with completion conditions.
Builds a real-to-sim digital twin; the VLM generates and iteratively revises programs using MPC rollouts before real-world deployment.
Evaluated in simulation and on four real-world tabletop manipulation tasks, outperforming strong baselines.
Scope is demonstrated on tabletop manipulation tasks and relies on simulation-based planning with iterative VLM updates.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Method Overview. Given the task specification in the form of a scene observation and a language description, we generate a digital twin through real-to-sim. VLM then generates objective programs given the task specification, the digital twin, and a predefined cost library. The objective program describes the running and terminal objective terms for the MPC, on a potentially multi-stage task, along with completion conditions for every stage. The VLM iteratively improves the objective programs based on the rollouts in the digital twin, with an MPC that optimizes controls based on the objective program. A stage verifier decides when to advance to the next stage when all completion conditions are met. Finally, the object program is deployed in the real world with the same MPC while the digital twin is synced to the real world execution.

Fig. 1. Our method combines the semantic understanding of modern vision-language models and physics-based model-predictive control that encodes physical understanding. papers.abstract: Implicit and explicit representations of geometry are central in computer graphics applications and come with their pros and cons. With surface sampling being faster on explicit representations and spatial queries being faster on implicit representations, finding efficient conversions between them is a highly desirable property. We present TetraCoder, a single resolution hash-free adaptive tetrahedral encoding that links an explicit tetrahedral spatial encoder with an underlying implicit signed distance field (SDF). The resulting hybrid implicit-explicit space is continuous piecewise affine (CPWA) by design, allowing to obtain an exact correspondence between the implicit SDF and the explicit analytic mesh. TetraCoder's design comes with additional perks, in particular: (a) it scales better than multi-resolution encoding methods due to its single resolution optimizable grid, (b) unlike hash-based methods, it is not affected by collisions, (c) it enables fast tetrahedral ray-tracing, geometry and appearance editing, directly through its adaptive tetrahedral scaffold. We demonstrate the versatility of TetraCoder by showing an improvement over state-of-the-art methods on multiple tasks: 2D/3D fitting from images and point clouds, 3D novel view synthesis, 3D reconstruction, and geometry/appearance editing.
authors: Daniele Della Pietra, Antonella Rech, Nicola Conci, Nicola Garau
bullets: Uses a single-resolution adaptive tetrahedral grid to connect an explicit tetrahedral encoder with an implicit signed distance field.
Produces a continuous piecewise-affine representation with exact correspondence between the SDF and analytic mesh.
Avoids hash-grid collisions and is designed to scale better than multi-resolution encodings.
Enables fast tetrahedral ray tracing plus direct geometry and appearance editing.
Improves over prior methods across image and point-cloud fitting, novel view synthesis, reconstruction, and editing tasks.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. We present TetraCoder, an adaptive tetrahedral encoding for neural fields. Multiresolution hash encoding (left) interpolates features on fixed spatial grids at multiple resolutions. Its trilinear interpolation does not produce a piecewise-affine encoding, making analytic mesh extraction impractical. To address that tetrahedral multiresolution hash encoding (center) subdivides these grids into fixed tetrahedra and uses barycentric interpolation to obtain a piecewise-affine encoding. TetraCoder (right) instead uses a single-level, hash-free encoding defined on an adaptive tetrahedral volumetric mesh. Combined with a piecewise-affine decoder, this representation enables fast analytic mesh retrieval. Unlike other encodings, TetraCoder supports novel view synthesis, scene reconstruction, 3D appearance and geometry editing within a unified framework.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) generate text one token at a time, yet how a particular generation relates to the geometry learned in pre-training remains unclear. The fundamental explainability of LLMs is elusive. Here, we build a similarity network from the input embeddings of six open LLMs and map generation onto it. The token-embedding network is scale-free while heavy-tailed, as are random embeddings with matched covariance, but far more fragmented. Distillation barely changes this topology because input embeddings are largely inherited. The knowledge space is thus deterministic from pre-training. Consecutive generated tokens are rarely graph neighbours and, in most models, no more often than in shuffled order, so generation is not a walk on the predefined network, although the tokens it visits are concentrated within it. Through the logit lens in a layer- wise manner, tokens settle late in depth in most models, and repetitive models remain confined to small domain-specific sub-graphs. These observables could serve as inference-time monitors of degeneration. We thus provide a fresh perspective on understanding LLM generation in the microscopic way from node or link prediction by graph learning.
bullets: The study maps token generation onto similarity networks built from input embeddings of six open LLMs.
These networks are scale-free and heavy-tailed, yet more fragmented than matched-covariance random embeddings.
Distillation has little effect on network topology, suggesting the knowledge-space structure is largely inherited from pre-training.
Consecutive generated tokens are rarely network neighbors, though generated tokens remain concentrated within the embedding network.
Layer-wise analysis shows tokens settle late in depth, while repetitive models stay within small domain-specific subgraphs; these patterns may monitor degeneration at inference time.

papers.abstract: Efficient sequential recommendation has emerged as a promising paradigm for providing real-time personalized service. To deploy models under resource-constrained environment, model compression becomes a necessity, yet existing methods typically apply uniform compression ratios, overlooking the heterogeneity in user intent complexity. This "one-size-fits-all" approach leads to a fundamental Capacity-Complexity Mismatch, where computational resources are either wasted on simple instances or insufficient for complex ones. To address this, we propose RACE (Ranking-uncertainty Aware Capacity-Adaptive Customization for Efficient Sequential Recommendation), a framework that dynamically adapts both model structures and input sequences with uncertainty-aware compression ratios. To ensure capacity-adaptive inference, RACE captures the model's intrinsic uncertainty of its predictions and transforms it into a proactive resource allocator. Specifically, we derive a list-wise ranking-uncertainty metric from the distributional stability of top-$K$ predictions, which serves as a measurable proxy for instance complexity. A lightweight predictor is then trained via self-supervision to anticipate this uncertainty from early-layer features. Guided by this signal, RACE performs instance-specific slimming in two dimensions: a hypernetwork-style channel sensitivity extractor identifies parameter redundancy, while importance-aware progressive sequence filtering mitigates data redundancy. Extensive experiments on four popular datasets demonstrate that RACE outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on accuracy, efficiency, and adaptability.
authors: Tianqi Liu, Kaipu Sun, Kairui Fu, Wenkai Wang, Sihao Liu, Hui Zang, Ran Chen, Tao Wang, Shengyu Zhang
bullets: Addresses capacity–complexity mismatch caused by uniform compression for users with different intent complexity.
Estimates instance complexity using top-K list-wise ranking uncertainty and predicts it from early-layer features with a lightweight self-supervised model.
Performs adaptive compression through channel slimming and importance-aware progressive sequence filtering.
Experiments on four datasets report gains over state-of-the-art baselines in accuracy, efficiency, and adaptability.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of the RACE framework. Our approach consists of three key components: (a) Ranking-Uncertainty Guided ResourceAllocation: RACEdesigns a list-wise ranking-uncertaintymetric and transforms it into a proactive instance-complexity proxy to guide resource allocation, utilizing a self-supervised threshold predictor to anticipate ratios early in inference. (b) Interest-Compatible Subnets Identification: Using the predicted ratio, a lightweight hypernetwork-style sensitivity extractor generates channel-wise masks to customize each feed-forward layer. (c) Progressive Sequence Filtering: Using the predicted ratio, RACE calculates relative importance scores to retain semantically relevant items while suppressing noise block by block.

Figure 1: Comparison of on-device recommendation paradigms. (a) On-device Finetuning incurs computational overhead due to backpropagation, and often falls short for capturing shifting interests. (b) On-device Pruning applies a unified-sparsity mask and relies on additional extractors, unable to adapt to the complexity of user intents. (c) Our proposed RACE framework introduces a Ranking-Uncertainty Driven mechanism to dynamically adapt model size to instance complexity. In comparison, RACE achieves sequence and structure slimming and customization in an intrinsic feature reuse and retraining-free manner.

papers.abstract: Single-photon LiDAR (SPL) sensors offer exceptional temporal resolution and single-photon sensitivity for depth imaging. However, cost-effective SPL arrays typically suffer from extremely low spatial resolutions (e.g. $8\times 8$ pixels), limiting their real-world utility. In this paper, we propose a novel, one-step super-resolution framework, D2ToF, Distilled Diffusion for Time-of-Flight, that bridges the gap between high-fidelity generative modeling and real-time execution. Our approach uses an amortized variational distillation strategy that allows for a measurement-based data consistency term to be incorporated directly into the one-step training objective. This encourages that the synthesized high-resolution depth maps are consistent with the captured low-resolution Time-of-Flight (ToF) histograms. To overcome the severe ill-posedness of upsampling extremely degraded inputs, we introduce a multimodal guidance strategy. By leveraging a foundational monocular depth model to extract structural priors from a high-resolution reflectivity image, our network is guided by a rich triad of the ToF histogram, reflectivity map, and relative depth estimate. Experimental results outperform evaluated baselines, achieving $16\times$ spatial super-resolution (from $8\times 8 \times 100$ histograms to $128\times 128$ depth maps) at an accelerated inference speed of approximately $83$ milliseconds.
authors: Pallabjyoti Deka, Lewis Wilson, Stephen McLaughlin, Jonathan Leach, Abderrahim Halimi
bullets: Addresses the severe spatial-resolution limitations of cost-effective single-photon LiDAR arrays.
Uses amortized variational diffusion distillation with a measurement-based data-consistency objective.
Combines ToF histograms, reflectivity images, and monocular relative-depth priors to guide reconstruction.
Achieves 16× spatial super-resolution from 8×8×100 histograms to 128×128 depth maps.
Reports approximately 83 ms inference and outperforms the evaluated baselines.

papers.abstract: Natural-language point-cloud localization typically retrieves candidate map cells and then predicts a position inside each candidate, yet the final output is still determined by retrieval order. A retrieval score measures region-description relevance, not whether the coordinates a region yields are accurate: a relevant region may produce a displaced prediction, and a lower-ranked region may contain a successful one. We study the final selection problem after the candidate pool and Fine predictions are fixed---how to choose the coordinate most likely to localize successfully, and under which conditions the gain holds. We propose SCAR (Spatial Consistency-Aware Reranking). SCAR treats each cell--Fine-coordinate pair as a localization hypothesis, interprets directional relations as functions of position, and reads spatial support at the backbone's actual Fine point (Fine-conditioned Evidence Readout). It organizes this readout with center support, semantic presence, retrieval score, and geometric offsets into a 23-D representation, trains a shared scorer with localization-success labels, and at inference reranks existing hypotheses and returns their original coordinates. Experiments cover four public backbones and a corrected Des4Pos reimplementation across five domains. Excluding one protocol-reference configuration, exploratory TEST point estimates on the remaining 24 configurations show Top-1@5\,m above Original on 23 and Cell R@1 above Original on all 24. On development-set VAL, the Fine readout improves Top-1@5\,m by 5.77 percentage points (pp) over a center surrogate on corrected Des4Pos*KITTI, and the complete scoring scheme improves it by 13.98\,pp over FSR on MambaPlace$\times$nuScenesFull; the latter measures the complete scheme, not learned ranking alone.
authors: Shuhan Dong, Tianyi Shang, Zhenyu Li
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between retrieval relevance and coordinate-level localization success.
Represents each cell–coordinate pair with fine-point spatial evidence, center support, semantic presence, retrieval scores, and geometric offsets.
Trains a shared scorer on localization-success labels, then reranks fixed hypotheses and returns their original coordinates.
Across 24 exploratory TEST configurations, Top-1@5 m improves over the original method in 23, while Cell R@1 improves in all 24.
Validation results show gains from fine-point readout and the complete scoring scheme, though the reported gains are protocol- and configuration-dependent.

papers.abstract: Independently pretrained language models and vision-language-action (VLA) policies provide complementary building blocks for embodied agents, but connecting them does not automatically produce coordinated behavior. The VLA may generate actions that diverge from the LLM's intended subtask and, upon regaining control after a correction, undo the promising state restored by the LLM. We introduce ESI (Embodied Self-Improvement), an automated flywheel that uses environmental interaction to align reasoning and action. ESI treats the modular agent as the unit of post-training, repeatedly refining the prompts that guide the LLM, the shared skill interface that expresses its intent, and the VLA parameters that realize that intent, then redeploying these components together. Our key insight is that collaboration itself can supply supervision for improving this interface. The LLM's subtask decisions provide semantic supervision for what the policy should execute, while its effective corrections and subsequent student continuations provide action-level supervision for recovery and handoff. The student also learns from its own effective execution, allowing locally useful experience to contribute even when the overall episode fails. On ten selected RoboDojo tasks, ESI achieves a mean Score of 62.03 and a mean success rate of 49.41% using an LLM-VLA agent without generating task-specific control code. On both metrics, it outperforms the published reference results of all hybrid embodied agents, including the Agent+WAM system GO-3 Nano Preview (47.27 Score and 36.60% success), as well as all compared code-based methods.
authors: Yundi Cai, Zihan Wang, Chenxi Han, Yi Cheng, Houde Liu, Zilei Wang
bullets: Addresses coordination failures where VLA actions diverge from LLM intent or undo recovery progress.
Uses LLM subtask decisions as semantic supervision and corrections plus continuations as action-level supervision.
Treats the modular LLM–VLA agent as the unit of post-training, repeatedly redeploying improved components together.
On ten RoboDojo tasks, reports a mean Score of 62.03 and 49.41% mean success without task-specific control code.

papers.abstract: Affine correspondences (ACs) enable robust and efficient solvers for multiple-view geometry by constraining the local geometry of point correspondences (PCs). Despite their utility in minimal solvers, AC estimation remains understudied. We revisit AC estimation beyond local image patches, extending it to the image and image-pair levels. Rather than estimating the components of the affine transformation separately, we learn the full 4-DoF matrix jointly. Building on this formulation, we introduce ALoMa, an AC estimator using LoMa keypoint descriptions, demonstrating consistent improvements across a wide range of downstream tasks. Code at https://github.com/davnords/loma.
authors: David Nordstr\"om, Georg B\"okman, Viktor Larsson, Fredrik Kahl, Jonathan Ventura
bullets: Affine correspondences can yield efficient, robust minimal solvers but their estimation is relatively understudied.
The approach extends affine-correspondence estimation to image- and image-pair levels, beyond local patches.
It jointly predicts the full 4-DoF affine transformation matrix rather than estimating components separately.
ALoMa builds on LoMa keypoint descriptions and reports consistent improvements across a broad range of downstream tasks.

papers.abstract: Handwritten text recognition (HTR), particularly when applied to historical documents, remains challenging due to the scarcity of annotated data and the substantial domain shifts caused by variations in handwriting styles, document degradation, acquisition conditions, and linguistic characteristics. While large amounts of unlabeled target-domain data are often available, effectively exploiting them requires adaptation strategies tailored to the specific requirements of HTR. We propose DRA-HTR, an unsupervised generative domain adaptation pipeline specifically designed for HTR and built upon the DRANet framework. The proposed approach combines source-domain pretraining, unsupervised adaptation to the visual characteristics of the target domain, relying on the generation of target-style source samples for task-specific training. We further investigate the integration of post-HTR correction to complement visual adaptation with language adaptation, relying on large language models, which we introduce as DRAL-HTR. The proposed framework is evaluated across seven HTR datasets spanning four languages, using a single set of hyperparameters for all source-target combinations. The recognition model achieves state-of-the-art performance on four datasets and competitive results on the remaining three. In addition, the proposed DRA-HTR establishes a new state-of-the-art for domain adaptation across all seven datasets and substantially improves overall robustness and training stability compared to the original DRANet framework: it reduces the Character Error Rate (CER) in average by 13.52 percentage points, and the average standard deviation decreases from 7.23 to 1.11 percentage points. Finally, post-HTR correction further reduces the CER by 2.16 percentage points.
authors: Gayan H. Pathirage, Florent Imbert, Denis Coquenet, Elisa H. Barney Smith
bullets: Addresses scarce annotations and shifts in handwriting, document quality, acquisition conditions, and language.
Uses unsupervised generative adaptation built on DRANet: source pretraining followed by target-style source-sample generation.
Extends visual adaptation with large-language-model post-HTR correction in DRAL-HTR.
Evaluated on seven datasets across four languages with one hyperparameter setting for all source–target pairs.
Achieves state-of-the-art domain adaptation on all seven datasets, reducing average CER by 13.52 percentage points and improving stability; post-correction gives a further 2.16-point CER reduction.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of the proposed DRA-HTR architecture. The overall content–style adaptation principle follows [1], while the architectures of its main components are redesigned in this work for HTR. The encoder (E) extracts visual features from source and target images, which are decomposed by the separator (S) into content and style representations. The generator (G) recombines source content with target style to generate target-style handwritten text lines while preserving their textual content. The generated images are constrained using adversarial, reconstruction, latent-consistency, and perceptual objectives. DA is performed only once during training to adapt the HTR model to the target domain. After adaptation, the model retains its original inference time.

Step (d): post-HTR correction using Qwen to refine the recognized text by leveraging linguistic context, correcting recognition errors, and improving transcription consistency.

papers.abstract: Fast charging of lithium-ion batteries is a multi-objective control problem that requires reducing charging time and sustaining high energy throughput while suppressing accelerated degradation and safety-critical electrochemical reactions. Conventional protocols are easy to implement but have limited ability to adapt to variations in battery chemistry, operating conditions, and aging state. Model-based optimization and conventional data-driven control often require accurate models, costly iterative search, or task-specific policies. We develop a large language model (LLM)-empowered intelligent agent for adaptive battery fast-charging control. In this closed-loop framework, the agent interprets structured battery states, generates executable charging actions, observes the resulting battery response, and continuously adjusts subsequent decisions. We construct a large-scale simulation corpus with PyBaMM across five battery chemistries and 11 parameter sets and convert the resulting state-action-response trajectories into structured process data for agent training. Our two-stage strategy combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). SFT establishes battery-control semantics and feasible decision priors from simulation-derived demonstrations. GRPO aligns the agent with a multi-objective control objective covering energy throughput, degradation mitigation, and operational constraints. Closed-loop simulations show that, under matched energy-throughput requirements, the agent achieves longer cycling life than conventional charging baselines and optimization-based strategies across heterogeneous battery configurations. This study provides a simulation-grounded proof of concept for using LLM agents as sequential decision makers in battery management and takes a step toward language-model-enabled control of physical energy systems.
authors: Joey Chan, Haoyu Pan, Zhen Chen, ErShun Pan
bullets: Addresses the limited adaptability of conventional, model-based, and task-specific charging controllers.
The agent interprets battery states, executes charging actions, observes responses, and updates subsequent decisions.
Training uses PyBaMM simulations spanning five battery chemistries and 11 parameter sets, with supervised fine-tuning followed by GRPO.
The multi-objective policy targets energy throughput, degradation mitigation, and operational constraints.
Simulations show longer cycling life than conventional and optimization-based baselines at matched energy throughput across heterogeneous configurations.

papers.abstract: Semantic exploration methods for object-goal navigation use large language models (LLMs) to score how strongly a target object is associated with a room type or with a nearby object. This paper considers obtaining from the LLM a spatial prior instead: a distribution over the position of the target in a room. We evaluate whether two open-weight LLMs, Qwen3.5-27B and Gemma-4-31B-it, can provide such a prior. Using real room layouts from CubiCasa5K and ScanNet, we measure the likelihood the models assign to real and perturbed layouts, and the layouts they generate. The object frequencies and room sizes of the generated rooms follow the room type, but the proximity of the objects to the walls does not follow the differences between room types found in real rooms. The likelihood distinguishes real layouts from perturbed ones partly through their geometry and partly through the agreement between the coordinates and a field that states the wall each object touches; for the movable furniture of ScanNet, it is higher for layouts with all objects piled near the room center than for the real layouts in most rooms. When an object is given in the prompt, the models place a related object relative to it. When the wall of each object is given, they place most objects against that wall, but do not keep all objects inside a given room rectangle. As a prior for object search, the generated placements reduce the searched area relative to a uniform prior, but by less than a third of the reduction obtained with a prior built from real layouts, and by less than two thirds when both priors are spatially smoothed. These results support the use of LLMs for object-room associations and for writing coordinates under constraints determined by another component, followed by a geometric check, but not as a source of placement priors where real layouts are available.
bullets: The study evaluates Qwen3.5-27B and Gemma-4-31B-it as spatial-prior generators for object-goal navigation.
Using CubiCasa5K and ScanNet layouts, it tests likelihoods on real and perturbed rooms and examines generated layouts.
Generated rooms capture room-type object frequencies and sizes, but not room-specific wall proximity or reliable room containment.
Models use provided object and wall information to place related objects, though generated placements often need geometric validation.
Generated priors reduce search area versus uniform search, but substantially less than priors learned from real layouts, especially after smoothing.

papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation usually trains a compact student from scratch, which needs a large amount of data even though the teacher's weights already encode most of what the student has to learn. In this work, we explore building the student directly from the teacher's weights. We propose Concertina, which folds every group of N adjacent teacher layers into one shared block that is executed N times. Each loop step carries a low-rank correction initialized from the layer it replaces, and a per-token gate mixes these corrections, to let every token recover the behavior of the original layers from a single shared block. We further design a distillation data recipe that balances general, mathematical, academic and targeted multiple-choice data, to recover all capabilities of the teacher together rather than one at the expense of another. On Qwen3-4B, a 2.27B Concertina model distilled on 22B tokens retains about 90% of the teacher on commonsense and mathematical reasoning and 84% on average across eight benchmarks. It outperforms same-size dense and layer-sharing baselines, as well as Qwen3-1.7B, which is trained on over a thousand times more data. These results suggest that a compact model need not be retrained at scale, since folding the teacher into itself and distilling it on the right data recovers most of its capabilities. Code is available at https://github.com/myboker/concertina.
authors: Ziyang Zhang, Yubin Jing, Yuyao Li, Haofan Wang, Yichen Gong
bullets: Addresses the data inefficiency of training compact student models from scratch, despite the teacher already encoding useful knowledge.

On Qwen3-4B, a 2.27B Concertina model retains about 90% of teacher performance on commonsense and mathematical reasoning and 84% on average across eight benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Reaching a goal state in a complex environment often requires a robot to overcome challenging terrain and obstacles. Which routes are accessible depends on the robot's physical design, the control policy it uses, and how it modifies its surroundings. We present a kinodynamic rapidly-exploring random tree (RRT) planner that uses physics simulation to exploit skills encoded in the control policy, which allows it to find a path in the scene with respect to the robot's capabilities. The planner samples states from a reduced state space in 3D around the scene and expands the RRT toward each sample using policy rollouts. We guide sampling with a preplanned path for a simple mass-point model to focus exploration on promising regions leading toward the goal state, reducing planning time by up to 63%. Simulation experiments with quadrupeds, humanoids, and wheeled robots demonstrate that our approach supports drop-in integration of various robots and control policies, exploiting their physical and policy capabilities without modifying the underlying planning algorithm. Predefined environmental modifications, such as placing a plank across a gap to build a bridge, will automatically be picked up by the planner as the robot's reachable space expands.

Demonstrated in simulation with quadruped, humanoid, and wheeled robots using drop-in robot and policy integration.
Automatically accounts for predefined environmental changes, such as placing a plank to create a bridge.

papers.abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) models have made substantial progress in visual realism, aesthetic quality, and instruction following. However, real-world prompts often go beyond explicit visual descriptions and require implicit facts, structured knowledge, and domain-specific commonsense. Existing evaluations mainly focus on explicit prompt-to-image semantic alignment or specific knowledge subdomains, lacking unified evaluation and diagnosis of world-knowledge grounding in T2I models. We introduce KnowVis for dual-view evaluation and diagnosis of world-knowledge grounding in T2I generation. Built on a hierarchical knowledge taxonomy with case-level annotations, KnowVis combines two complementary benchmark views with a structured MLLM-based VQA judge protocol. The Skill-Tree Benchmark supports fine-grained atomic knowledge evaluation, while the Generalized Benchmark examines open-ended knowledge composition and expression. The protocol uses Required VQAs to assess atomic knowledge correctness in the Skill-Tree Benchmark, and combines Required, Optional, and dynamically discovered knowledge expressions with human-judge collaborative evaluation in the Generalized Benchmark. We validate the protocol's reliability on the Skill-Tree validation split, enabling scalable evaluation and diagnostic error attribution. Experiments show that KnowVis reveals notable gaps in world-knowledge grounding across existing T2I models and provides structured diagnostic signals for knowledge-intensive image generation.
authors: Yonghang Yu, Ruoyu Wang, Haoyu Zhang, Lin Qi, Yawei Zhou, Changqian Yu
bullets: Addresses a gap in evaluations focused mainly on explicit prompt–image alignment or narrow knowledge domains.

Experiments reveal substantial world-knowledge grounding gaps in existing T2I models and support structured diagnostic error attribution.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward multi-view transformers such as VGGT recover the cameras and geometry of a video in one pass, but the cost of their cross-frame attention grows quadratically with the frame count, and their accuracy drops on long videos. Most remedies approximate attention over all frames within a budget or select a few keys by their content. We hypothesize that the keys of a long video can be chosen without looking at its content, and our experiments on VGGT and $\pi^3$ support it: a few dozen evenly spread frames can serve as the keys of every frame. We present EcoVGGT, a training-free inference framework whose keys form a Pinned Key Set of 31 such frames. A pin pass stores their tokens in a Scene Cache, and the other frames read it in independent batches that reproduce joint inference with these keys exactly, at a constant cost per frame. An Online Stream updates the pinned frames during recording. Six middle global blocks align the frames and form a reusable VGGT module: the Alignment Score reads their attention to flag failures, and Alignment Refocusing reduces them by fine-tuning only these blocks (3.6 GPU hours). EcoVGGT ($\pi^3$) matches the success rate of $\pi^3$ on 1,000-frame ScanNet videos at 13.8 times its speed. With refocusing, EcoVGGT (VGGT) raises the success rate of VGGT from 70% to 82% at 8.5 times its speed on 500 frames. EcoVGGT reconstructs 4,000 frames on one GPU, and EcoVGGT ($\pi^3$) streams 1,000 frames at 18.6 frames per second with the lowest online absolute trajectory error.

papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) achieve strong multimodal performance, yet they remain prone to object hallucination---generating answers that are linguistically fluent but visually ungrounded. This issue is especially severe in low-resource languages, where weaker cross-modal alignment causes models to rely more on language priors than on image evidence. Existing remedies either require costly multilingual annotations or external translation/reward models, or intervene at inference time in ways that can distort the output language. We propose VEPO(Visual Evidence-guided Preference Optimization), a training-time method that transfers reliable visual grounding from English to other languages without external models. VEPO first localizes key visual evidence using English queries via mid-layer cross-modal attention, then constructs preference pairs that share the same correct answer but differ in evidence sufficiency (full image vs.\ key-region masked image). Direct preference optimization on these pairs encourages low-resource inputs to prefer answers supported by complete visual evidence. Experiments on multilingual POPE and MME with Chinese, French, and Hindi show consistent hallucination reduction and perception gains, with the largest improvements on the lowest-resource language. Analyses further confirm that VEPO sharpens question-relevant attention and that evidence-guided masking outperforms random masking.

Gains are largest for the lowest-resource language; evidence-guided masking outperforms random masking.

papers.abstract: We partially resolve Conjecture 1 of [Karagodin et al., Clustering in Causal Attention Masking (NeurIPS 2024)] and extend it to time-dependent parameter regimes. The conjecture predicts that causal attention dynamics converge to two clusters aligned with the eigenvectors associated with the largest eigenvalue $\lambda_{\max}$ of the value transformation. We prove that this behavior holds when $\lambda_{\max}>0$ and is generally false when $\lambda_{\max}\le0$. The resulting two-cluster regime is common in practice and substantially more challenging than the classical single-cluster setting studied previously. A central contribution of our work is the identification of a rigorous dimension reduction phenomenon: despite evolving in a high-dimensional embedding space, token trajectories collapse onto a two-dimensional structure governed by a small number of dominant directions. Building on this insight, we introduce a new analytical framework--instability within the flow--inspired by instability phenomena in physical systems. This framework enables the analysis of steady-regime behavior in non-monotone, non-autonomous attention dynamics. Our theoretical findings are illustrated through simulations and experimental studies using Group Query Attention (GQA) layers.
authors: Trinh T. Nguyen, Duy-Tung Pham, Hoang-Son Do, Tan Minh Nguyen, Thieu N. Vo

Introduces an “instability within the flow” framework for analyzing non-monotone, non-autonomous attention dynamics.
Illustrates the theory with simulations and experiments involving Group Query Attention layers.

papers.abstract: Direct image-to-video diffusion models entangle pixel synthesis with implicit latent motion, precluding persistent 3D mechanical equilibrium, mid-rollout intervention, and counterfactual force control. Conversely, single-pass programmatic 3D reconstruction from an uncalibrated photograph leaves monocular depth and support clearance underconstrained, causing reconstructed scenes to interpenetrate or collapse under gravity. We present TelePhysica, a closed-loop framework that reconstructs an executable, multi-regime physical world from a single photograph to drive stateful 3D interaction and trajectory-grounded video synthesis. A vision-language coding agent synthesizes separable visual meshes and declarative physical models within a two-stage verification loop that pairs pixel-aligned silhouette critique with a zero-force gravitational equilibrium preflight. The verified world compiles into a unified solver coupling rigid bodies, articulated chains, co-dimensional cloth shells, and 3D tetrahedral elastodynamics, whose simulated rollouts condition pretrained video diffusion models through pixel-aligned structural streams. On a 100-scene single-image benchmark, closed-loop execution raises equilibrium-verified world recovery from $0\%$ in single-pass synthesis to $81\%$. Controlled constitutive ablations show over an order-of-magnitude larger localized corner displacement and out-of-plane pleating in finite-element cloth than in matched rigid-plate proxies. Conditioning video diffusion on simulated trajectories increases dynamic motion-mask overlap by $2{\times}\text{--}5{\times}$ and preserves motion direction under counterfactual force reversals where direct image-to-video models fail.
authors: Ruiqi Shu, Xufeng Zhan, Yuanzhi Liang, Haibin Huang, Chi Zhang, Xuelong Li
bullets: Addresses image-to-video models’ lack of persistent 3D mechanics and single-pass reconstruction failures such as interpenetration or collapse.
Uses a vision-language coding agent with silhouette critique and zero-force gravitational preflight to build verified visual meshes and physical models.
Compiles scenes into a solver supporting rigid bodies, articulated chains, cloth shells, and tetrahedral elastodynamics.
On a 100-scene benchmark, equilibrium-verified recovery improves from 0% with single-pass synthesis to 81% with closed-loop execution.

Simulated trajectory conditioning improves dynamic motion-mask overlap by 2–5× and preserves motion direction under reversed forces; finite-element cloth exhibits stronger deformation than rigid proxies.

papers.abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) achieve strong performance on image recognition tasks, yet their quadratic self-attention complexity over input tokens creates prohibitive computational costs for practical deployment. Token reduction methods offer a practical solution by progressively reducing the token sequence during the forward pass. We propose Saliency-Weighted Asymmetric Merging (SWAM), a training-based token merging framework that extends the Bipartite Soft Matching (BSM) with two saliency-aware mechanisms. We introduce a two-step matching formulation in which cosine similarity decides candidate pairs, while a multiplicative maximum saliency penalty regulates their selection for merging. We then further use asymmetric exponential saliency-weighted aggregation, which allows more salient tokens to contribute more strongly to the merged representation. A lightweight MLP-based saliency prediction module (75k parameters per stage, 1% of backbone parameters) supervised via attention rollout is trained end-to-end jointly with a DeiT-Small backbone using a composite cross-entropy, knowledge-distillation, and saliency-alignment objective. On CIFAR-100, TinyImageNet, and ImageNet-100, under a conservative schedule that reduces tokens from 196 to 100 patch tokens, with the CLS token retained throughout, 27.5% FLOPs reduction and 1.35 times speedup, SWAM matches or exceeds baseline across the reported results. Under an aggressive schedule (196 to 70 tokens with the CLS token kept throughout, 33.8% FLOPs reduction, and 1.46 times speedup), accuracy gains are achieved on ImageNet-100 (+0.23%) with minimal losses on CIFAR-100 and TinyImageNet.
authors: Utkarsh Kumar Singh, Manish Das, Shiv Ram Dubey, Satish Kumar Singh
bullets: Addresses the quadratic self-attention cost of ViTs through progressive token reduction.
Extends Bipartite Soft Matching with saliency-guided pair selection and asymmetric saliency-weighted aggregation.
Uses a lightweight MLP saliency predictor trained jointly with a DeiT-Small backbone and supervised through attention rollout.
With conservative merging, reduces FLOPs by 27.5% and achieves 1.35× speedup while matching or exceeding baselines across reported datasets.
With aggressive merging, reaches 33.8% FLOPs reduction and 1.46× speedup, including a 0.23% ImageNet-100 accuracy gain, with minimal losses elsewhere.

papers.abstract: Hallucination benchmarks for text-to-image generation are predominantly designed around diffusion models, limiting their diagnostic value for visual autoregressive (VAR) models and the development of mitigation methods. We identify two limitations in existing prompt construction paradigms: many prompts are no longer challenging for modern generators, while category-based construction relies on recurring object-attribute-relation templates and rarely tests interactions among multiple visual requirements within a single image. We introduce InfiHall-Bench, a controlled benchmark of 411 prompts constructed by systematically composing five foundational and visually verifiable skills: attribute binding, spatial relation, action relation, part consistency, and scene consistency. Each prompt covers 4.05 annotated skills on average, enabling the evaluation of hallucinations under diverse combinations of visual requirements. Using this benchmark, we find that hallucinations in VAR models exhibit a scale-wise persistence pattern: semantic errors can emerge at different autoregressive scales and are rarely corrected by subsequent fine-scale steps. Motivated by this observation, we propose Confidence-Masked Hallucination Mitigation (CMHM), which estimates the prediction confidence of target visual tokens at each autoregressive scale during teacher-forced fine-tuning. CMHM downweights reliably predicted tokens, allowing optimization to focus on uncertain predictions across scales. Experiments show that InfiHall-Bench distinguishes models that existing compositional benchmarks rate as comparable, while CMHM consistently outperforms uniform LoRA fine-tuning for VAR-based text-to-image generation.
authors: Yuxia Qiao, Xinhao Zhong, Junhao Li, Yi Sun, Jiaxin Hong, Shuoyang Sun, Bin Chen
bullets: Addresses the lack of diagnostic hallucination benchmarks tailored to visual autoregressive (VAR) models.
Introduces 411 prompts combining five verifiable skills: attribute binding, spatial and action relations, part consistency, and scene consistency.
Finds that VAR hallucinations can persist across autoregressive scales and are rarely corrected by later fine-scale steps.
Proposes Confidence-Masked Hallucination Mitigation (CMHM), which downweights confidently predicted tokens during teacher-forced fine-tuning.
Reports that the benchmark separates models judged similarly by prior compositional benchmarks, while CMHM outperforms uniform LoRA fine-tuning for VAR generation.

papers.abstract: Automated lidar feature detection from lidar point clouds can support archaeological surveys, but models trained in one landscape may transfer poorly to another because of differences in terrain, vegetation, acquisition characteristics, and feature morphology. We address this problem for cross-region detection of ancient terraces using transductive unsupervised domain adaptation that exploits an unlabelled target survey. We propose MELD (Multi-level Embedding-space Latent Diffusion), which trains separate diffusion denoisers on target-domain representations at four hierarchical PointNet++ feature levels. These target distribution priors are then used to refine source representations during supervised training and target representations during inference, allowing adaptation to act directly on the multi-scale features consumed by the segmentation decoder. We additionally investigate local geometric descriptors derived from K-nearest-neighbour neighbourhoods, including surface normals, slope, and aspect. MELD is evaluated bidirectionally between the Teyuna and Miraflores lidar surveys in the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, Colombia, against a source-only model and nine configurations of established domain adaptation approaches. MELD raises F1 over the source-only model from 0.397 to 0.459 for Teyuna-to-Miraflores transfer and from 0.557 to 0.594 in the reverse direction, achieving the highest F1 among the evaluated adaptation methods in both directions. Adding local geometry further raises F1 to 0.542 and 0.606, respectively. Multi-level ablation shows that refining all four PointNet++ levels provides the strongest performance in both directions. These results show that explicit modelling of target feature distributions in hierarchical point cloud feature space, complemented by local geometry, provides an effective route to cross-region archaeological mapping without target labels.
authors: Sina Mohammadi, Roderik Lindenbergh, Javier Ruiz-P\'erez, Marco Madella, Sebastian Fajardo
bullets: Addresses poor transfer caused by differences in terrain, vegetation, acquisition, and terrace morphology.
Uses transductive unsupervised adaptation with an unlabelled target survey and diffusion denoisers at four PointNet++ feature levels.
Refines source features during training and target features during inference, with optional local geometry descriptors such as normals, slope, and aspect.
Across bidirectional Teyuna–Miraflores transfer, F1 improves from 0.397 to 0.459 and from 0.557 to 0.594; local geometry raises these to 0.542 and 0.606.
All four hierarchical feature levels perform best in ablation, supporting multi-scale target-distribution modelling.

figures.caption: Figure 2: High-level overview of the MELD framework. During joint training, unlabeled target/test features train the level-specific diffusion denoisers, while labeled source features are refined by the target-trained denoisers and decoded under source ground-truth supervision. The diffusion loss updates the denoisers, whereas the segmentation loss updates PointNet++ through the straight-through refinement path. A held-out source-validation set ranks checkpoints by adapted validation F1. At inference, the top three paired PointNet++ denoiser checkpoints are applied independently to all target/test points using deterministic target-guided DDIM refinement; their terrace-class probabilities are averaged point-wise and thresholded at 0.5 to obtain the final binary prediction. No target labels are used for adaptation or checkpoint selection. Preprocessing and the PointNet++ backbone are detailed in Figure 3, target domain latent diffusion adaptation in Figure 4, and source-feature refinement with the straight-through estimator in Figure 5; adapted inference is described in Section 3.5.

Figure 3: PointNet++ segmentation backbone. Each 20m × 20m point cloud tile is converted by sampling or padding into a fixed 4096-point input patch, which is then normalized. The patch may contain either only xyz coordinates (C = 3) or xyz coordinates augmented with optional KNN-derived geometric features (C = 9), including normals, slope, and sine/cosine of aspect. The encoder comprises four set-abstraction (SA) layers that progressively reduce the number of points while increasing feature dimensionality, producing hierarchical latent features Z1, Z2, Z3, and Z4. The decoder then uses four feature-propagation (FP) stages with interpolation and skip connections to recover pointwise features at the original resolution. A per-point classification head, implemented with 1× 1 convolutions, batch normalization, ReLU, dropout, and log-softmax, produces per-point class log-probabilities; applying exp(·) yields the corresponding per-point class probabilities. The generic Zl notation used in this figure denotes the multi-level encoder features that serve as latent representations in the target-adaptation and source-refinement stages, where they are written explicitly as Zl tar and Zl src in Figures 4 and 5, respectively.

Figure 1: Reference terrace annotations for the two study regions. Left: Teyuna (Ciudad Perdida); right: Miraflores. Reference terrace annotations are shown over the labelled study extents. Mapped terraces cover approximately 6.5% of the labelled Teyuna extent and approximately 1.5% of the Miraflores extent.

Figure 5: Source refinement for supervised segmentation training. A labeled sourcedomain input patch Xsrc is passed through the shared PointNet++ encoder to obtain hierarchical latent features Zl src for l ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4}. At each feature level, the encoder output is tokenized into U l 0,src, partially noised to a shared starting depth tl0, and then refined token-wise through a deterministic DDIM reverse process using the level-specific target-trained denoiser Dl. The refined token matrix Ũ l 0,src is unflattened to Z̃l src and supplied to the decoder through a straight-through estimator (STE), so that the decoder uses the refined features in the forward pass while segmentation gradients flow back to the original encoder features during backpropagation. The decoder output is supervised by the source ground-truth labels using the class-weighted NLL loss Lseg. The figure shows the principal configuration in which all four PointNet++ feature levels are refined. During training, source refinement is stochastic overall because the initial Gaussian perturbation is sampled randomly, whereas the subsequent DDIM reverse trajectory is deterministic conditional on the resulting partially noised token.

Figure 4: target domain latent diffusion adaptation. Unlabeled target domain input patches Xtar are passed through the shared PointNet++ encoder to obtain multi-level latent features Zl tar, l ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4}. At each level, the target features are detached from the backbone and flattened into token matrices U l 0,tar, so the target domain diffusion objective does not propagate gradients into PointNet++. Each token is independently assigned a diffusion timestep tli and perturbed with Gaussian noise according to the forward diffusion process. A level-specific denoiser Dl(·, ·;ϕl), conditioned on the noisy token and its timestep embedding, predicts the added noise. Within each level, the same denoiser is shared across all tokens, while denoiser parameters are not shared between feature levels. The level-wise noise-prediction losses are computed as mean-squared error between the sampled and predicted noise and are combined into the total diffusion loss Ldiff . Consequently, target domain adaptation updates only the denoiser parameters ϕl, allowing the denoisers to learn the latent feature distribution of the unlabeled target domain for subsequent source-feature refinement and adapted inference. The figure shows the principal configuration in which all four PointNet++ feature levels are active; the level-ablation experiments use the corresponding subsets of these levels.15

Figure 6: Precision–recall curves for the three principal configurations, averaged over three random seeds. The left panel shows Teyuna → Miraflores and the right panel Miraflores → Teyuna. Solid lines show the mean across three random seeds, and shaded regions indicate one standard deviation across seeds. The compared configurations are sourceonly PointNet++, MELD, and MELD+geometry.

Table 1: Cross-region terrace detection (point level, all points): F1 as mean ± standard deviation over three random seeds. Single applies adaptation at the deepest level (l = 4); multi at all four levels (l ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4}). Mean is the unweighted average of the two directions. Best result per column in bold. The target-only oracle (italic) is an in-domain supervised reference trained with five-fold cross-validation on the evaluation region of each direction; it is not a competing UDA method and is reported for context only.

papers.title: Multi-level latent-diffusion adaptation for cross-region point cloud segmentation of ancient terraces

papers.abstract: Large language and vision-language models have substantially advanced robotic behavior planning from natural-language instructions and visual observations. However, safe manipulation in tabletop environments remains challenging because the safety constraints required for a task depend on the surrounding scene and may not be explicitly specified in the instruction. We propose a safety-aware behavior planning framework based on an explicit Constraint Space that stores reusable textual safety rules. Rather than retrieving rules solely by semantic similarity, we formulate constraint selection as task- and environment-conditioned applicability learning. A lightweight query-conditioned dual-tower model identifies the constraints applicable to the current context, which are then provided together with the original task and image to a multimodal behavior planner. To handle incorrect constraint selections and previously unseen hazards, we introduce a multimodal Safety Inspector that evaluates generated primitive plans, reconstructs the complete applicable constraint set, and provides corrective planning feedback. Validated inspection feedback is further used for test-time adaptation of constraint applicability and parameter-efficient adaptation of the Safety Inspector through LoRA, while newly identified constraints are incorporated into the Constraint Space. The resulting framework integrates explicit safety knowledge representation,context-aware constraint selection, corrective safety inspection, and test-time knowledge adaptation for safety-aware robotic behavior planning.
authors: Xianxu Wu, Shang-Ching Liu, Zhaocong Liang, Hengxiang Chen, Yujian Ma, Shenwen Deng, Qiang Li, Jianwei Zhang
bullets: Addresses the challenge that tabletop manipulation safety constraints are scene-dependent and often absent from instructions.
Stores reusable textual safety rules in an explicit Constraint Space rather than relying only on semantic retrieval.
Uses a lightweight query-conditioned dual-tower model to select applicable constraints from the task and environment context.
Employs a multimodal Safety Inspector to detect incorrect selections and unseen hazards, then provide corrective planning feedback.
Uses validated feedback for test-time adaptation and adds newly identified constraints to the knowledge base.

papers.title: A Generalizable Approach to Safety-Aware Robotic Behavior Planning with an Explicit Constraint Space

papers.abstract: Diffusion models sometimes memorize and reproduce regions of their training images, raising privacy and copyright concerns. We aim to localize these regions. Existing contrast-based methods use the diagonal of the denoiser Jacobian, which reflects the posterior variance of each pixel. However, a small diagonal entry is ambiguous: it signals either memorization or averaging over many neighboring pixels in smooth or predictable regions. To resolve this ambiguity, these methods subtract a reference map, which requires a second evaluation with a null prompt or an earlier checkpoint. Unconditional models have no null prompt, and earlier checkpoints are unavailable in general. We show that Jacobian row sums (JaRS), unlike the diagonal, separate memorization from local averaging without a reference map. Pairing JaRS with an image-level detection score that uses the same statistic at an early denoising step yields JaRS+. Across Stable Diffusion v1.4 and v2.1, Realistic Vision v5.1, and an unconditional diffusion Transformer (DiT), JaRS+ outperforms contrast-based localization methods.
authors: Saisuchith Mahajan, Aditey Nandan, Rohit Singh, Nishanth Shetty, Chandra Sekhar Seelamantula
bullets: Existing Jacobian-diagonal methods confuse memorization with smooth or predictable regions and require a null prompt or earlier checkpoint.
JaRS uses Jacobian row sums to distinguish memorization from local averaging without a reference map.
JaRS+ combines JaRS localization with an image-level detection score computed at an early denoising step.
Evaluated on multiple conditional and unconditional diffusion models, JaRS+ outperforms contrast-based localization methods.

papers.abstract: V2X collaborative perception improves single-vehicle perception by aggregating multi-view features from collaborative agents. However, existing methods typically rely on simple spatial warping to align the collaborative features, which can cause semantic misalignment during fusion. Meanwhile, these deterministic warping-based methods are highly sensitive to the positional noises. In this paper, we propose a plug-in module called Robust Semantic and Spatial Aligner (RSSA), which performs semantic and probabilistic spatial transformations for robust feature alignment. Specifically, a Semantic Transformation (SemT) block modulates feature channels based on the observed relative pose to correct semantic inconsistencies. Subsequently, a Probabilistic Spatial Transformation (P-SpaT) block performs probabilistic warping by sampling from the Gaussian-modeled relative pose space. A Relative Transformation Augmentation (RT-Aug) strategy is further introduced to augment the relative poses and facilitate the training of the RSSA. Extensive experiments on both simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate that RSSA improves the state-of-the-art methods by a large margin under the configuration of both clean and noisy positions.
authors: Zhihao Yang, Zhiyu Xiang, Peng Xu, Tianyu Pu, Kai Wang, Eryun Liu, Dongping Zhang, Yong Ding
bullets: Addresses semantic misalignment and sensitivity to positional noise in spatial-warping-based collaboration.
Uses a Semantic Transformation block to modulate feature channels from the observed relative pose.
Uses probabilistic spatial warping by sampling relative poses modeled as Gaussian distributions.
Introduces Relative Transformation Augmentation to support RSSA training.
Experiments on simulated and real-world datasets show large gains over existing methods under clean and noisy positions.

papers.abstract: Agent-based image restoration has achieved promising performance by coordinating restoration tools to handle heterogeneous and coupled degradations. However, existing agents often improve their decisions through accumulated successful and failed executions, without explicitly identifying the conditions under which learned restoration strategies remain effective. Consequently, changes in degradation severity, spatial coverage, or interactions may invalidate previous decisions, while providing limited guidance on how these decisions should be revised. In this paper, we propose \textbf{RecurIR}, a recursive self-improvement framework that enables restoration agents to learn when and how to revise their decision rules. Specifically, we introduce a policy-hypothesis discovery mechanism to identify testable, condition-dependent rules through matched tool executions. We then design a rule-falsification-driven task evolution mechanism to generate targeted degradation variations, examine the validity of learned rules, and identify their applicability boundaries. Based on the resulting evidence, we develop a change-conditioned policy revision mechanism that learns how variations in degradation conditions should modify tool selection, execution order, operation strength, and processing regions. We further incorporate independent verification to retain effective revisions and use the resulting feedback to guide subsequent hypothesis discovery and task evolution. Through this recursive process, RecurIR progressively refines its restoration policies as degradation conditions change. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.
authors: Hu Gao, Haoran Zhang, Yulong Chen, Lizhuang Ma
bullets: Targets failures caused by shifts in degradation severity, spatial coverage, and interactions.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning has enabled robust humanoid locomotion, yet training recipes (rewards, architectures, hyperparameters) remain hard to reuse across robots with different native joint coordinates, since policies output native joint angles while action scales, bounds, gains, and penalties are defined in those robot-specific coordinates. Existing transmission models convert native targets into actuator commands but do not standardize the coordinate interface exposed to the policy. We introduce a body-aligned virtual joint space upstream of this mapping: policy actions and observations follow a common anatomical convention, and a deterministic kinematic layer maps virtual targets to native ones, leaving the existing transmission and low-level control stack unchanged. Under a single unmodified recipe on three humanoids with different leg-axis layouts, it is the only interface that tracks accurately, keeps the feet aligned with the travel direction, and trains stably on all three, and on Unitree G1 hardware it reduces heading drift by nearly a factor of six.
authors: Sol Choi, Mingon Kim, Seokin Seo, Jongeun Choi, Donghyeon Kim, Yisoo Lee
bullets: Native joint coordinates make rewards, action bounds, gains, and penalties robot-specific, hindering recipe reuse.
The method exposes policy actions and observations in a common anatomical space.
A deterministic kinematic mapping converts virtual joint targets to each robot’s native coordinates while preserving the existing control stack.
Across three humanoids, it tracked accurately, maintained foot alignment, and trained stably with one unmodified recipe.
On Unitree G1 hardware, it reduced heading drift by nearly sixfold.

papers.abstract: For imbalanced data streams with delayed labels, is it worth adding a streaming oversampler, or does continuous re-evaluation of earlier predictions already recover the cost of the delay? We address this through an extensive experimental comparison of streaming oversampling and continuous re-evaluation under joint class imbalance, concept drift, and label delay. Streaming oversamplers are typically evaluated under the test-then-train assumption of immediate labels; their behaviour under these conditions, assessed through re-evaluation, has not been systematically studied. We close this gap with a decision framework that predicts when oversampling adds value over re-evaluation, organised around three axes: drift density, minority-class learnability, and delay relative to the refinement window, and operationalised as a competition between a recovery channel (re-evaluation) and a minority-coverage channel (oversampling). Evaluating $15$ classifiers on $6$ synthetic and $6$ real streams, we find: re-evaluation recovers delay-induced loss on drift-active streams but is silent on stationary ones; oversampling's marginal contribution over re-evaluation is statistically detectable in only one real-data configuration; and cost--performance Pareto recommendations from synthetic streams do not transfer to real data, where fronts partition by drift regime. Method selection should therefore be conditioned on the stream's profile and re-estimated as it evolves, not inherited from synthetic benchmarks.
bullets: Studies imbalanced data streams with delayed labels and concept drift, comparing streaming oversampling with continuous re-evaluation.
Frames the choice through a recovery channel (re-evaluation) versus a minority-coverage channel (oversampling).
Identifies three decision axes: drift density, minority-class learnability, and delay relative to the refinement window.
Across 15 classifiers, 6 synthetic streams, and 6 real streams, re-evaluation recovers delay-related losses on drift-active streams but has little effect on stationary streams.
Oversampling showed statistically detectable additional benefit in only one real-data configuration; synthetic cost–performance recommendations did not transfer reliably to real streams.

papers.abstract: Chinese Grammatical Error Correction (CGEC) is typically formulated as a text-to-text problem. While suitable for digital texts, this formulation falls short in real-world K-12 education, where AI-assisted corrections are expected directly on essay images, which are primarily handwritten and exhibit many irregularities. To bridge this gap, we introduce Grounded Chinese Grammatical Error Correction (G-CGEC), an image-to-grounded-edit task requiring systems to predict both corrections and their positions on essay images. We propose G-CGEC-Eval, a benchmark comprising real-world images of K-12 Chinese essays with fine-grained annotations. For evaluation, we adapt IoU-based metrics from object detection and propose a more tolerant alternative based on center-distance matching. Using this benchmark, we evaluate open-source and proprietary vision-language models under a direct single-pass setting, as well as settings with auxiliary components (OCR and character grounding) coordinated via pipelining or agentic harnessing. Results show that even top-tier proprietary models perform surprisingly poorly in the single-pass setting, while pipelining and agentic harnessing yield meaningful improvements. Notably, an error-type-based multi-agent workflow achieves the best performance, establishing it as the strongest baseline for future G-CGEC research. Through ablations and fine-grained analysis, we find the task remains far from solved, with linguistic error discovery and character-level grounding as the primary bottlenecks. This underscores the need for models that better integrate visual perception with linguistic reasoning and visual grounding.
authors: Weiru Zhang, Yuzhong Hong, Junwei Bao, Lemao Liu, Dejing Dou

papers.abstract: Arbitrary-scale light field spatial super-resolution reconstructs high-resolution views at any requested scale from low-resolution multi-view observations. Gaussian primitives enable continuous reconstruction, but generating separate primitive sets for each view redundantly encodes shared scene structure across views and causes the primitive count grow linearly with the number of views. To avoid such redundancy, we propose MacroGS, a feed-forward decoder that jointly predicts a single shared Gaussian set per macro pixel rather than generating separate sets for each view. Disparity-dependent replacement and angle-conditioned appearance allow each set to be reused across all output views, keeping the predicted primitive count independent of the number of views at each requested scale. The decoder iteratively predicts per-primitive disparities, retrieves the corresponding multi-view features, and updates the primitive states. Gaussian splatting and residual refinement then reconstruct the output light field. Despite being learned without geometric supervision, the predicted disparities strongly correlate with underlying scene geometry. Experiments across five benchmarks demonstrate that MacroGS integrates effectively with diverse light field encoders, improving reconstruction quality at fixed scales while achieving leading performance across most evaluated arbitrary-scale settings. The decoder also achieves speedups of approximately $2$-$10\times$ over state-of-the-art implicit light field decoders and $10$-$18\times$ over the view-wise Gaussian baseline.
authors: Zeqiang Wei, Angulia Yang, Min Xu
bullets: Targets redundant, view-wise Gaussian representations whose primitive count grows with the number of output views.
Predicts one Gaussian set per macro pixel and reuses it across views through disparity-dependent replacement and angle-conditioned appearance.
Iteratively updates primitive states using predicted disparities and retrieved multi-view features, followed by Gaussian splatting and residual refinement.
Improves reconstruction quality at fixed scales and performs strongly across most arbitrary-scale evaluations on five benchmarks.
Reports roughly 2–10× speedups over implicit light-field decoders and 10–18× over a view-wise Gaussian baseline.

papers.abstract: Deep learning-based hyperspectral unmixing (HSU) has followed a trajectory of increasing architectural complexity, from simple autoencoders to transformers and, most recently, Mamba-based models, each claiming to advance the state of the art. Contrary to this trend, we propose a lightweight CNN-based autoencoder, coined "Not New Autoencoder Unmixing" (nnAEU). It is derived from the backbone of UNMamba (2025) through a pruning study that removes the Mamba component entirely. nnAEU uses less than 10 times fewer parameters than UNMamba, and far fewer than other transformer- and GAN-based methods, while outperforming them in accuracy. We provide a complete, minimal, reproducible code, available at https://gitlab.telecom-paris.fr/ring/nnAEU.git.
authors: Edgard Dabier, Christophe Kervazo, Pietro Gori, Florence Tupin
bullets: Targets the growing complexity of deep-learning architectures for hyperspectral unmixing.
Builds on the UNMamba backbone after pruning away its Mamba component entirely.
Uses fewer than one-tenth as many parameters as UNMamba and fewer than transformer- and GAN-based alternatives.
Reports higher accuracy than the compared methods, according to the abstract.
Provides minimal, reproducible code publicly on GitLab.

papers.abstract: Federated learning (FL) under differential privacy (DP) is typically evaluated on large client cohorts, where subsampling and cross-client averaging amplify privacy and smooth injected noise. Personal biosignal applications such as wearable EEG instead involve small federations of a handful of subjects, a regime whose interaction with formal client-level DP is largely uncharacterized. We study differentially private federated class-incremental learning in this small-cohort regime, combining a public EEG dataset with a custom four-channel MUSE 2 recording set into a K=5-client federation, and give a masked per-class training protocol that avoids degenerate gradients and missing negative supervision under class-incremental streaming. We propose FedEEG, combining Synaptic-Intelligence consolidation with a lagged adaptive FedProx term, and show it reduces catastrophic forgetting relative to FedAvg, FedProx, and a federated Learning-without-Forgetting baseline; on-device balanced-batch replay reduces mean forgetting by a further 56.7%. A class-scoping diagnosis yields $50.5\%\pm3.6\%$ accuracy with 6 seeds and 2.02 times chance. We also introduce head-scoped client-level DP, which protects the classification head and alone reduces the achievable $\varepsilon$ by 200 times at a matched round budget; combined with fewer communication rounds it reaches $\varepsilon\!\approx\!10.4$ with utility not statistically distinguishable from non-private training.
authors: Baran Can G\"ul, Ali G\"ul\"umser, Nasser Jazdi, Michael Weyrich
bullets: Addresses the underexplored interaction between client-level differential privacy and small federations of wearable-EEG subjects.
Uses masked per-class training to prevent degenerate gradients and missing negative supervision during class-incremental learning.
Combines Synaptic Intelligence with a lagged adaptive FedProx term; balanced-batch replay further reduces mean forgetting by 56.7%.
Head-scoped client-level DP reduces the achievable privacy budget by 200× at a matched round budget and reaches ε≈10.4 with utility not statistically distinguishable from non-private training.
A class-scoping diagnosis achieves 50.5% ± 3.6% accuracy across six seeds, or 2.02× chance.

papers.abstract: Attention is essential for modeling spatio-temporal dependencies in video diffusion transformers, but its quadratic cost makes it a major inference bottleneck. Its high sparsity offers an opportunity to accelerate generation by focusing computation on important interactions. However, accuracy and execution favor different granularities: each query attends to its own key tokens, whereas GPU kernels work on tiles. We present Token2Tile, a training-free sparse attention operator that combines per-query scoring and a per-query residual with tile execution. An online low-rank space, computed directly from queries and keys to preserve attention logits, makes clustering, scoring, and residual approximation efficient. Token2Tile unites query-specific selections to allocate exact work across query clusters, then packs the selected keys into GPU tiles. On MiniMax-H3 and Wan2.1-14B, Token2Tile delivers 1.48-1.54x end-to-end speedup over dense FlashAttention-3 with VBench scores within 0.5 points of dense. At comparable speeds on H3, it improves PSNR over SOL and SubBlock by 5.5-6.8 dB; on Wan, it exceeds SOL by 4.6-4.8 dB while running faster.
authors: Xuecheng Wu, Aichen Feng, Jinyan Chen, Qingjie Zhao, Julien Lai
bullets: Targets the quadratic inference cost of spatio-temporal attention in video diffusion transformers.
Uses per-query scoring and residual approximation in an online low-rank space derived from queries and keys.
Clusters query-specific selections and packs selected keys into GPU tiles for efficient execution.
Achieves 1.48–1.54× end-to-end speedup over dense FlashAttention-3, with VBench within 0.5 points of dense.
Outperforms SOL and SubBlock in PSNR at comparable or higher speeds on the evaluated models.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free sparse attention for video diffusion transformers, improves efficiency.
papers.title: Token2Tile: Token-Wise Sparse Attention with Tile Execution through a Low-Rank Space for Video DiTs
