papers.abstract: Adaptation for neural-signal classification is usually transductive: each batch is scored after updating on it, and the gain depends on the adapted model [4]. This paper asks what an aggregate change fails to characterise inside the cohort. Full test-time adaptation (full_ttt) was evaluated in 11 dataset-encoder cells (four each on Siena/EEG and PTB-XL/ECG, three on Sleep-EDF/EEG), with splits and source-model evaluation fixed; the subject was the unit, exact sign tests were Holm-corrected and conditional on the shared stream, and bootstrap intervals accompanied a dependence audit. Two results of different kinds follow. In the binary case balanced accuracy gives a one-class decoder the same value as one reporting both classes at 50%, so the aggregate cannot identify a class that stopped being reported; a class covering a tenth of a subject's samples went unpredicted in 26-47 of 112 subject-cells, against 7-9 for the controls, which is a descriptive count. With cohort, split and update rule fixed, the within-subject class contrast follows the encoder, tested directly rather than inferred from tests against zero: two of six Siena encoder pairs survive the dependence readings at their nominal reference and one at a fold-level reference, while two of ten Sleep-EDF stage pairs pass the run-clustered gate at its nominal reference; aggregate and contrast named different encoders in 10 of 11. The protocol bounds both results, since a stream-interleaving effect reverses sign with state sharing (+3.5 to -2.4 pp). An aggregate score can hide individual harm, as [1] showed, but it cannot distinguish a uniform loss from a deleted class; class-level change should therefore be reported alongside the aggregate and subject-level change alongside it, with both results conditional on the cell, the rule and the stream construction.
bullets: In binary decoding, a one-class decoder can match the balanced accuracy of a decoder scoring 50% on both classes.
A class covering 10% of samples went unpredicted in 26–47 of 112 subject-cells under full test-time adaptation, versus 7–9 in controls.
Within-subject class contrasts depended on the encoder and identified different encoders from aggregate scores in 10 of 11 cells.
Results were conditional on cohort, split, update rule, and stream construction; interleaving could reverse the adaptation effect (+3.5 to −2.4 percentage points).

figures.caption: Figure 1. What a single aggregate score cannot identify under streaming test-time adaptation. (A) Online TTA applies one unsupervised update to each unlabelled batch and scores that same batch with the updated model; the state carries across batches and subjects without a reset, and evaluation often reports one number, balanced accuracy (BA), the unweighted mean of per-class recalls. (B) Four limits of that aggregate: no labels or held-out set are available to foresee a harmful update; a decoder reporting one class and one reporting both classes at 50% receive the same BA; the same mean change is compatible with a broad decline and with a few subjects driven to the floor; and class-level redistribution and the sign of a stream-order effect can reverse with the encoder or with state sharing. (C) The readouts reported here, recomputable from archived per-subject predictions, keep the subject as the only independent unit: the within-subject aggregate change, the between-encoder contrast, the subject-level distribution of changes and the within-subject class-level contrast, accompanied by a terminal-state score and a dependence audit. The analyses group into performance/subject, class-structure and decision/stream evidence families; the requirement is to report class-level change alongside the aggregate, the subject-level distribution alongside the mean, and the encoder as part of the result. Colour encodes per-subject, per-class and aggregate quantities, and the footer marks what remains unresolved. Design specification (§3.2–§3.4): five datasets enter subject-wise cross-validation and each seed defines a new split and refitted source model; four encoders give three datasets × four backbones, minus the memory-limited MedFormer × Sleep-EDF cell, which is omitted rather than scored as zero, with BCI-IV-2a a boundary extension and CHB-MIT a monitoring/low-skill extension. Under full_ttt, all weights are updated with masked-feature reconstruction (mask ratio 0.3; span 16); h0 is held at zero throughout; the streaming score concatenates post-update predictions, and the terminal-state score re-evaluates the final model on the full test set for four cells in S11. Paired orders share the recorded test-subject lists, the source-only evaluation and one cached source model; the adapted weights of the paired-order runs were not hashed. All graphics are schematic, not raw data.

Figure 8. What can be seen without labels, and what cannot. (a) Batch unanimity rate (fraction of batches whose predictions are all one label) against balanced accuracy minus chance, under the original order; the size of each marker is the number of folds. A high unanimity rate means the model emits one label per batch. (b) The same rate under three arrangements — original, fully shuffled, block-shuffled — one row per cell, sorted by the original value; rows are not labelled individually, colour gives the dataset. (c) Number of cells flagged by a single label-free risk indicator, against the number expected under two null rates: the nominal 5% and the empirically measured false-positive rate of this pipeline. Holm-corrected survivors are shown in the panel.

Figure 2. Negative mean changes conceal different subject distributions. Each panel shows one cell and one random split (seed): PTB × CNN (n = 198), Siena × Mamba (n = 13), Sleep-EDF × CNN (n = 20). Upper part: percentage of subjects per 10 pp bin of the per-subject change (adapted − source, same test samples, pp), with bin edges identical in all twelve panels; lower part: one dot per subject, coloured by sign, with a box plot (Q1–Q3, median, whiskers at 1.5 × IQR) and the mean as a white diamond. Splits are shown separately rather than pooled, because a new split re-partitions the same subjects and pooling would inflate n fourfold. Numbers above each panel give n, the count at exactly zero, the mean and the median. The three rows are not the same quantity: in Siena and Sleep-EDF each subject contributes both classes and the value is a change in balanced accuracy, while in PTB every subject contributes a single true class, so balanced accuracy is undefined and the value is the change in the recall of that class; the point mass at zero is a ceiling, not indifference.

Figure 4. How the change unfolds along the stream under full_ttt. (a) Balanced accuracy above chance in each fifth of the stream, one line per dataset × encoder cell; horizontal position is arrival order. Only the three interleaved arrangements are used, because under the natural order the first fifth can contain as few as four subjects, which would confound a temporal reading with subject composition. (b) Share of the total drop already complete within the first fifth; bar length gives the share, the right-hand column the total drop in pp. Cells whose score did not fall are absent from (b) rather than plotted at zero, because a share is undefined when there is no drop to divide. Curves are four-seed means. The last fifth is not a terminal-state score: its earlier batches are scored by less adapted models and it covers only the last fifth of the samples (S11).

Figure 3. Class-associated and within-subject changes across datasets. (a) PTB: each subject contributes one true class, so class stratification forms two subject groups (n = 51 / 147); this is a between-group comparison. Values are changes in recall for each subject’s true class; points show subjects across four backbones, averaged over four splits, with boxplots as in Figure 2. (b) Siena × Mamba: within-subject change in per-class recall, one row per subject (n = 13). (c) Sleep-EDF: mean within-subject change in per-class recall for five sleep stages and three backbones. Panels (b) and (c) use separate symmetric colour scales (±40 and ±80 pp); values are printed in each cell. Subject–class cells with fewer than 20 samples are missing, not zero.

Figure 5. Three quantities that are often conflated, shown side by side for all eleven cells. Rows are datasets × backbones. (a) Sample-level composition of the 2 × 2 outcome table: whether a test sample was correct before and after adaptation, as a percentage of all test samples. (b) Net effect: per-subject balanced accuracy after minus before, in pp, reported under two weightings — subject-equal (filled) and sample-weighted (open); they coincide only when every subject contributes the same number of samples. (c) Correctness-flip rate: percentage of test samples whose prediction changed between correct and incorrect. On the two-class datasets this equals the rate at which the predicted label changed; on the five-class dataset labels change more often than correctness does. (d) Order effect on transitions: churn under the original order minus the mean churn under three shuffled orders, pp; negative values mean shuffling reduced churn. Panels (a) and (c) are sample-level; panel (b) is subject-level. No confidence intervals are drawn: the independent unit is the subject, and two of the three datasets have fewer than 21 of them.

Figure 7. Two block-preserving arrangements against three free permutations, eleven cells. Vertical axis is balanced accuracy minus chance, so that datasets with different chance levels share an axis; each point is the mean over the folds of one cell under one arrangement, seed 1, with the same source weights throughout. Colour gives the dataset and marker the encoder; the thick line is the cell used as the example in the text. The three free permutations are draws from one family rather than three replicates — on PTB-XL with Mamba they read 12.8, 16.9 and 12.8 points above chance, so no single permutation is a reliable estimate for that cell — and on Siena the two block-preserving arrangements differ by at most 1.7 points in every cell, so they act as one control. A cell already at chance has little room to fall, so a small move there is not evidence of stability.

Figure 6. The stream-organisation contrast depends on source headroom. One point per core cell. Horizontal axis: balanced accuracy minus chance under the original arrangement. Vertical axis: δ, the mean over three shuffled arrangements minus the original adapted score, in pp; both values are four-split means. The average can hide a wide range: for PTB-XL × MedFormer, the original score ranges from 13.4 to 30.5 points above chance across splits, and δ from −19.1 to +0.2. The shaded region marks cells within 5 points of chance, where little skill remains to lose. Hollow markers identify cells with shuffled-side SD below half the original-side SD; there δ is partly arithmetic because the shuffled score varies little. The independent unit is the subject, not the split, so the plotted values are descriptive contrasts, not confidence intervals. The three stream arrangements also change adjacency, batch composition and boundaries together.

Figure 9. Cumulative subject shares across deterioration thresholds. Share of subjects whose per-subject change is at or below the value on the horizontal axis, for PTB-XL with CNN, Sleep-EDF with CNN and Siena with Mamba. Thin lines are the four splits, the thick line their mean; subjects are not pooled across splits. The dashed line marks the threshold of §3.5. papers.selection_reason: Analyzes limitations of aggregate metrics in test-time adaptation for neural-signal decoding; relevant to test-time learning.
papers.title: What Balanced Accuracy Cannot Identify in Neural-Signal Decoding under Test-Time Adaptation
papers.tldr: Balanced accuracy can hide a class being entirely unreported during test-time adaptation, so class-level and subject-level changes must accompany aggregate scores.

papers.abstract: Synchronous, colocated RL post-training of large language models (LLMs) today suffers from severe under-utilization due to long-tail rollouts. Inference engines fall idle waiting for long-tail rollouts or decode at low, inefficient batch sizes. To address this, we present TIDE, an RL training system that preserves on-policy training semantics while recovering resource utilization. TIDE does so by two complementary techniques: (1) dynamically repurposing rollout GPUs for training while long-tail rollouts complete and (2) dynamically migrating rollouts between inference engines to boost decoding throughput. TIDE automatically determines the right time to repurpose rollout resources through an adaptive migration policy, obtaining performance improvements that generalize across multiple applications and hardware configurations without requiring bespoke configuration. In our evaluation, TIDE provides end-to-end speedups of up to 1.36x over colocated systems, outperforming all evaluated on-policy baselines and achieving up to 97% of optimal throughput.
authors: Mathew Jacob, Morgan Borjigin-Wang, Kan Zhu, Po Hao Chen, Yi Pan, Andy Ruan, Nayani Modugula, Ethan Lavi, Luis Ceze, Malte Schwarzkopf, Akshay Narayan, Deepti Raghavan, Stephanie Wang
bullets: Addresses under-utilization caused by long-tail rollouts in synchronous, colocated RL training.
Repurposes rollout GPUs for training while delayed rollouts finish.
Migrates rollouts across inference engines to increase decoding throughput.
Uses an adaptive migration policy that generalizes across applications and hardware without bespoke configuration.
Achieves up to 1.36× end-to-end speedup and up to 97% of optimal throughput in evaluation.

papers.abstract: Generative recommendation benefits from long interaction histories, but the cost of processing them directly grows with history length. We propose RecMem, a recurrent memory compression framework guided by three desiderata: space invariance, semantic fidelity, and lifelong evolvability. RecMem compresses historical segments into a fixed set of memory slots using a bifurcated encoder-decoder with shared lower layers and slot-wise forget-gated updates. Recommendation supervision trains the memory to preserve predictive information, while stream-consistency training aligns predictions from sequential and packed processing. By construction, the memory state and decoder context are independent of history length; under contraction and approximate semigroup consistency, we further derive a horizon-independent bound on the state discrepancy between these two processing orders. On MerRec, RecMem uses 16 memory slots and a 216-token decoder context, compared with 1,200 tokens for HSTU-1200, while retaining 87.9% of HSTU-1200's Recall@10 and 97.0% of its Recall@200. It outperforms PHSTU and the evaluated recent-only and retrieval baselines, and analyses of distant history show that archived interactions contribute predictive signal.
authors: Haoyi Hu, Gaoyang Guo, Yunjia Xi, Wen Chen, Weiwen Liu, Jian Wu, Yuning Jiang, Weinan Zhang
bullets: Addresses the growing cost of directly processing long interaction histories in generative recommendation.
Uses bifurcated encoder-decoder compression with slot-wise forget-gated recurrent updates.
Trains memory with recommendation supervision and stream-consistency objectives for sequential-versus-packed processing.
Provides a horizon-independent discrepancy bound under contraction and approximate semigroup consistency.
On MerRec, 16 memory slots plus a 216-token context retain 87.9% of HSTU-1200’s Recall@10 and 97.0% of its Recall@200; archived distant history remains predictive.

papers.abstract: Generating realistic 3D brain MRI volumes from sparse anatomical priors is a highly ill-posed yet clinically valuable problem, with important applications in data augmentation, simulation, and downstream neuroimaging analysis. In this work, we investigate the challenging task of synthesising full 3D brain MRI volumes conditioned solely on vascular label maps. While vascular structures provide strong anatomical and topological cues, they occupy only a small fraction of the brain volume and offer no direct information about surrounding tissue appearance. To address this challenge, we propose Vessel2Brain, an edge-aware multi-scale conditional flow matching framework that explicitly incorporates vascular structure information into the generative process. Our approach formulates vessel-guided brain image synthesis as a conditional continuous flow, enabling stable training and flexible generation while preserving structural correspondence. A multi-scale flow matching strategy is introduced to jointly model global anatomical coherence and fine-grained local details, with auxiliary velocity predictions providing additional supervision across spatial resolutions. Furthermore, we design an edge-aware objective that emphasises vascular boundaries during training, encouraging anatomically faithful tissue synthesis around vessel structures. We evaluate Vessel2Brain on two public 3D brain MRI datasets with paired vascular annotations. Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art generative models in terms of reconstruction accuracy, structural consistency, and distributional realism.
authors: Zhi Chen, Tianyang Zhang, Theodoros N. Arvanitis, Le Zhang
bullets: Addresses the ill-posed task of synthesizing full brain MRI volumes from vascular label maps that provide limited tissue-appearance information.
Uses conditional continuous flow matching to preserve correspondence between generated anatomy and vessel structures.
Combines multi-scale modeling for global anatomical coherence and local detail with auxiliary velocity supervision.
Adds an edge-aware objective to improve tissue synthesis around vascular boundaries.
Evaluated on two public paired 3D brain MRI datasets, with reported gains in reconstruction accuracy, structural consistency, and distributional realism over existing generative models.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the proposed Vessel2Brain framework. Given a 3D vascular label map and a time step t, a UNet-style FlowNet conditioned on timestep and label embeddings learns a velocity field for conditional flow matching. Velocity fields are predicted at multiple spatial resolutions through a main velocity head and an auxiliary velocity head. Edge-aware weighting derived from Sobel operators on the vascular volume emphasises vessel boundaries during training. The predicted velocity fields are integrated to generate the final 3D brain MRI volume, while auxiliary outputs provide additional multi-scale supervision.

Fig. 3. Qualitative comparison on the TopBrain Challenge dataset. The visualization setting and column order are the same as in Fig. 2. Vessel2Brain produces more anatomically coherent brain structures and clearer local details than competing methods under sparse vascular conditioning.

Fig. 2. Qualitative comparison on the CereVessMRA dataset. From left to right: vascular mask, ground-truth brain MRI, 3D Pix2Pix, LDM, 3D VAE, Med-DDPM, and the proposed Vessel2Brain. Results are visualized on representative sagittal, coronal, and axial slices. The highlighted regions and corresponding zoomed-in views illustrate finegrained anatomical details. Compared with baseline methods, Vessel2Brain generates more anatomically consistent brain structures while better preserving vascular-aligned tissue appearance under sparse vessel conditioning.

Vessel2Brain consistently outperforms representative GAN-, VAE-, and diffusion-based baselines across all metrics, highlighting its effectiveness for vesselguided 3D brain MRI generation under sparse conditioning.

papers.abstract: Scaling laws indicate that the generalization error of a large language model (LLM) decreases monotonically with model size once data is sufficient, and the corollary that larger models outperform smaller ones is now widely accepted. We argue that this corollary fails in security: decisions there hinge on anomalous inputs, which are long-tailed (e.g., zero-day attacks) and therefore poorly served by likelihood fitting. Worse still, the capability brought about by scale (e.g., inferring the intended whole from a corrupted part) leads a LLM silently \emph{repair} the anomaly before any downstream security head ever sees it. We formalize this as a tradeoff between two quantities: the cognitive capability $K(W)=I(W;P)$ that a model holds about the world distribution, and the security-information retention $R(W)=\frac{I(Z;S)}{I(A;S)}$ that survives in its intermediate representation. We derive three information-theoretic bounds to connect them: an upper bound on restoration accuracy in terms of $K(W)$, an upper bound on $R(W)$ in terms of the restoration error, and a Fano lower bound on security-task error in terms of $R(W)$. These theorems approximately imply that usable security information is a product of how much security information survives and how well it can be extracted, indicating that optimal usable security information can be achieved at a certain model size. We state this as the \emph{condensing law of security information}: usable security information is unimodal in model size, so security generalization error is U-shaped and is minimized at a finite $N^{\star}$ rather than decreasing without bound. The experiments on various real-world LLMs validate the condensing law, indicating that there is an optimal model size to solve security issues.
authors: Qi Tan, Tianyu Cui, Qi Li, Ke Xu
bullets: Security decisions depend on long-tailed anomalies such as zero-day attacks, which likelihood-based modeling handles poorly.
The paper formalizes a tradeoff between model world knowledge and retention of security information in intermediate representations.
Three information-theoretic bounds link restoration capability, security-information retention, and security-task error.
It proposes a condensing law: usable security information is unimodal with model size, producing U-shaped security error and an optimal finite size.
Experiments on real-world LLMs support the existence of an optimal model size for security problems.

papers.tldr: In security tasks, scaling LLMs can eventually hurt performance because greater world knowledge may silently repair anomalous inputs and discard security-relevant information.

papers.abstract: While current few-shot adaptation strategies for time series forecasting foundation models are predominantly dataset-centric, the necessity of obtaining an additional dataset for the finetuning process poses a significant hurdle for adoption. To address this constraint, we propose Sample-Wise Instance Fine-Tuning (SWIFT), a novel forecasting adaptation framework that achieves fine-grained specialization by leveraging structural priors from the target instance's own history. This shift allows the fine-tuning process to be entirely transparent to the end-user, which significantly enhances the ease of adoption. To implement this framework, SWIFT synergizes Self-Retrieval for historical mining and Frequency-Aware Loss for spectral consistency, while employing Deviation-Aware Dynamic Fusion to balance adaptation with general knowledge preservation. Extensive experiments across four TSFM backbones and three long-history benchmark subsets validate SWIFT, yielding average MASE and WQL reductions of 6.41% and 4.83% across 24 combinations of four backbones and six Chronos Benchmark II datasets. To the best of our knowledge, SWIFT is the first framework to investigate sample-wise instance fine-tuning of time-series foundation models, specializing the model for an individual prediction window using only the corresponding forecasting sample's own observed history.
authors: Yang Chen, Feifan Tian, Cong Wang, Cheng Feng, Wenbin Li, Yang Gao
bullets: Addresses the adoption barrier of dataset-dependent few-shot adaptation for time-series foundation models.
Uses Self-Retrieval to mine historical patterns and Frequency-Aware Loss to preserve spectral consistency.
Applies Deviation-Aware Dynamic Fusion to balance instance-specific adaptation with retained general knowledge.
Validated across four backbones and six Chronos Benchmark II datasets, with average MASE and WQL reductions of 6.41% and 4.83%.
Scope: specializes the model for an individual prediction window using only that sample’s history.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of SWIFT. The framework consists of three stages: (a) Self-Retrieval constructs an intrinsic support set from similar historical and recent subsequences; (b) Frequency-Aware Loss adapts the model with FreAL to emphasize informative spectral discrepancies, together with an anchor regularizer that limits prediction drift; and (c) Deviation-Aware Dynamic Fusion combines adapted and zero-shot predictions to reduce harmful over-adaptation.

Figure 1: Learning from others versus learning from self. The illustrated support-set adaptation learns from a separately supplied support setDsupport of similar sequences, leveraging cross-instance information. In contrast, SWIFT constructs an intrinsic support set Dintr by mining context–target pairs from the target instance’s own history. Both approaches update only LoRA parameters, while SWIFT constructs its support set from the current sample’s own history to specialize the model for its prediction window.

Figure 3: Pairwise win rates across four TSFM backbones and six long-history datasets from Chronos Benchmark II. Each off-diagonal cell reports the percentage and count of comparisons in which the row method achieves a lower error than the column method. Panels (a) and (b) summarize 24 comparisons for MASE and WQL, respectively. Panel (c) pools the two metrics into 48 comparisons, rather than requiring simultaneous improvements in both metrics. Darker colors indicate higher win rates. Diagonal entries are omitted.

Table 2: SWIFT across diverse TSFM backbones. Forecasting performance of zero-shot inference, few-shot fine-tuning, TTA, and SWIFT on the long-history subset of Chronos Benchmark II. The backbone-name rows report zero-shot results, while the remaining rows report the corresponding adaptation methods. Lower values indicate better performance. The best and second-best results within each backbone are marked in bold and underline, respectively.

papers.abstract: Cardiac cine MRI provides time-resolved visualization of cardiac motion and is essential for evaluating ventricular function and anatomy. In routine clinical acquisition, however, cine sequences are frequently temporally sparse or degraded by arrhythmia, motion, and scan-time constraints, which can hinder reliable quantification and downstream analysis. We present CardioTrace, a motion-aware cine synthesis framework that generates a full cardiac cine sequence from limited input while explicitly modeling and tracing cardiac motion. CardioTrace couples two complementary pathways: a pixel-translation branch that directly predicts cine frames in a residual formulation, and a flow-field branch that estimates time-resolved deformation fields from a reference phase to provide interpretable motion correspondences across frames. To further preserve anatomical plausibility, a segmentation branch supervises clinically meaningful cardiac structures at key phases, and a cross-branch consistency objective encourages the synthesized appearance dynamics to follow the explicit motion guidance, mitigating temporal drift and unrealistic shape transitions over long sequences. The framework also supports prompt-style conditioning to incorporate auxiliary patient or acquisition information, improving robustness across heterogeneous multi-center data. Experiments on public cardiac cine MRI datasets demonstrate that CardioTrace improves perceptual quality and temporal coherence over representative GAN- and diffusion-based baselines, while better preserving ventricular morphology throughout the cardiac cycle. \textit{Our codes are available after review}.
bullets: Addresses temporally sparse or degraded cine MRI caused by arrhythmia, motion, and scan-time constraints.
Combines a residual pixel-translation branch with a flow-field branch that estimates interpretable cardiac deformations over time.
Uses segmentation supervision and cross-branch consistency to preserve anatomy and reduce temporal drift or unrealistic shape changes.
Supports prompt-style conditioning with auxiliary patient or acquisition information for heterogeneous multi-center data.
Experiments on public cardiac cine MRI datasets show improved perceptual quality, temporal coherence, and ventricular morphology preservation over representative GAN- and diffusion-based baselines.

papers.abstract: Growing visual data overwhelms storage on resource-constrained edge devices, making compression essential. Traditional codecs offer inadequate rate-distortion performance, motivating the exploration of diffusion codecs. Diffusion codecs face two limitations: (1) At the algorithm level, diffusion decoders preserve perceptual quality under extreme compression, but require substantial computation. (2) At the architecture level, in NPU-centered devices, neural codecs occupy the NPU, interfering with other AI applications. Meanwhile, the complex codec pipeline incurs long I/O paths, leading to additional overhead and energy cost. To address these issues, we propose DiffusionSSD, a cross-level near-data processing framework for extreme visual data compression on edge devices, using an algorithm-architecture co-design method. Specifically, (1) at algorithm level, we present Dual-stage Diffusion, a lightweight solution tailored for diffusion codecs that employs patchification and single-step diffusion, reducing computation cost while preserving perceptual quality; (2) at architecture level, we introduce a Cross-level Near Data Processing architecture that integrates the proposed computational universal flash storage (cUFS) and LPDDR-PIM, enabling codecs to be entirely offloaded to data side while reducing visual-data movement and avoiding SoC redesign; (3) at system level, combining both the algorithm and the underlying architecture, we propose a Patch-Workload co-aware scheduling scheme to enable more efficient system-level execution. Experiments show that Dual-stage Diffusion maintains comparable perceptual quality while reducing computation cost by up to 92.7%. Compared with NPU+DRAM and near-data-processing design such as SmartSSD, cUFS+PIM improves coding throughput by 2.32 times and 2.91 times on average, respectively.
authors: Kuai Yu, Wen Li, Shengwen Liang, Jie Zhang, Ying Wang, Huawei Li, Xin Yao, Renhai Chen, Gong Zhang
bullets: Targets the high computation and system overhead of diffusion codecs on resource-constrained edge devices.
Uses patchification and single-step diffusion to preserve perceptual quality while reducing computation cost by up to 92.7%.

Introduces patch-workload co-aware scheduling for more efficient system-level execution.
Improves coding throughput by 2.32× over NPU+DRAM and 2.91× over SmartSSD on average.

papers.abstract: Many new AI models estimate how far away things are, in metres, from a single photo. To do this they must also work out what camera took the photo. We check whether they really do with a simple test: digital zoom, that is, cropping a photo and enlarging the crop back to full size. Zooming moves nothing in the scene, so a correct model should give the same distance for every point still in the picture. The test is free, exact and needs no labels. Two numbers describe a model's reaction: its depth changes like $s^{-\alpha}$ (ideal $\alpha=0$) and its focal-length estimate like $s^{\beta}$ (ideal $\beta=1$), for zoom factor $s$. On 800 images from KITTI, NYUv2 and DIODE, the widely used Depth Anything V2 has $\alpha=0.95$: it treats a zoomed photo almost as if the camera had moved closer, because it judges distance mainly from how large things look. Models that also predict the camera remove only part of this error ($\alpha\approx0.31$-$0.36$), because their focal estimate grows too little. Given the true camera, Depth Pro and DA3-Nested keep their depth ($\alpha\approx0$), so the error lies in their camera estimate. The reason: a zoomed photo is, pixel for pixel, a normal photo of a scene squashed in depth, so size alone cannot tell the two apart, and a focal estimator trained by regression stays close to the cameras it saw in training. Undoing this needs no labels or training and makes Depth Pro pass the test ($\alpha=0.04$) at almost no cost on normal photos. Controls, including a real optical zoom lens, rule out blur and resizing artefacts. Finally, label-free fine-tuning for self-consistency lowers $\alpha$ to 0.05 on KITTI and 0.07 on NYUv2 once a "blurry means zoomed" shortcut is removed; we report what this costs on normal and unseen photos.
bullets: Digital zoom should not change scene depth, making it a simple, exact, label-free consistency test.
Depth Anything V2 strongly confuses zoom with proximity, while camera-aware models reduce but do not eliminate the error.
With the true camera parameters, Depth Pro and DA3-Nested preserve depth, locating the remaining problem in camera estimation.
A camera-correction procedure makes Depth Pro nearly zoom-consistent at little cost on ordinary images.
Label-free fine-tuning further reduces zoom sensitivity, though the abstract notes trade-offs on normal and unseen photos.

papers.title: Zoom In, Scale Out: Metric Depth Models Mistake Digital Zoom for Moving Closer

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) often exhibit overconfidence, providing firm answers even when visual evidence is insufficient. A prominent case is referential ambiguity in Visual Question Answering (VQA), where multiple entities in an image are plausible referents of a question. Addressing such cases requires recognizing when ambiguity is present: ambiguous questions can be handled by asking for clarification or enumerating plausible referents, while unambiguous questions should receive a direct answer. Current VLMs struggle with this distinction, often defaulting to a single interpretation. To investigate whether activation steering can serve as an inference-time mechanism to elicit such behaviors, we introduce AmbiSteer, a lightweight framework to selectively elicit ambiguity-aware behavior. Across three VLMs, we find that steering alone has limited and model-dependent effects, while prompting is generally more effective. Combining prompting and steering substantially increases clarification and enumeration behaviors, but also elicits them on unambiguous cases. AmbiSteer addresses this using a linear classifier to predict input ambiguity and condition the steering direction accordingly, increasing the proportion of inputs handled appropriately from 59.0% to 77.0% on average across models. Our work sets the ground for lightweight approaches to reduce model overconfidence in uncertain multimodal settings.
authors: Monica Riedler, Samuele Antonelli, Barbara Plank, Raffaella Bernardi
bullets: Targets VLM overconfidence in referentially ambiguous Visual Question Answering.

papers.abstract: Recent open-vocabulary multi-view indoor 3D detection methods typically follow a point-cloud-driven pipeline, where pseudo 3D boxes are generated from reconstructed or estimated geometry and semantic labels are inferred from projected regions. However, such a design makes box generation dependent on the completeness of point clouds and restricts semantic learning to local appearance, causing inferior 3D object localization and open-vocabulary classification. In this paper, we present See and Detect, an image-driven framework that uses multi-view images as the primary evidence for 3D box and semantic label generation. For box generation, we first discover object candidates from individual images, enabling objects missing in point clouds to be recovered from visual evidence. However, single-view predictions are often noisy and redundant. To address this, we propose multi-view consensus box consolidation to fuse spatially consistent predictions across views, and box quality assessment to reduce the impact of boxes with partial object coverage. For semantic label generation, we introduce context-aware semantic learning, where semantic labels are queried from full image context, enabling more accurate semantic prediction. Extensive experiments on ScanNet and ARKitScenes demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art open-vocabulary multi-view 3D detection performance while running over 500$\times$ faster than the previous state-of-the-art method.
authors: Yating Xu, Na Zhao, Chenhan Jiang, Qingwen Zhang, Jiankang Deng, Jifei Song
bullets: Addresses point-cloud incompleteness and limited local appearance in existing open-vocabulary multi-view 3D detectors.
Generates 3D box candidates from individual images, then fuses consistent predictions across views with multi-view consensus box consolidation.
Uses box quality assessment to reduce errors from boxes that only partially cover objects.
Applies context-aware semantic learning by querying labels from full image context.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance on ScanNet and ARKitScenes, with over 500× faster runtime than the previous best method.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models can share experts across layers or computational steps, pooling training information from different contexts. This can reduce local prediction error, but multi-step systems are ultimately evaluated by their final outputs. We study when these local gains survive composition. In specified linear regression models, we derive exact sharing and merging criteria by balancing variance savings against bias from sharing across roles with different target behavior. Under a common fixed linear propagation map, we characterize expected squared final-output risk, retaining error directions and correlations. We construct cases where sharing lowers average local error yet increases final-output error. Within this setting, we also identify when orthogonal full pooling with isotropic noise preserves every local improvement at the final output. For general routed computations, we derive conditional end-to-end error bounds that account for distribution shifts, errors in surrounding components, and changes in expert selection. Separately, we show that correct predictions and route labels alone do not establish that individual experts implement the attributed operations. Controlled experiments realize a strict local-to-final risk reversal. In low-data symbolic settings, trained Transformers exhibit statistically supported teacher-forced one-step gains without statistically resolved free-running final-output gains. Separate intervention tests distinguish successful multi-layer actions from single-expert attribution and generalization to unseen transitions. Together, these results distinguish when sharing improves local estimation, when those gains survive to the final output, and what evidence is needed to attribute reusable operations to individual experts.
authors: Tiantong Wang, Zhiren Gong, Yixin Wang, Tiantong Wu, Wei Yang Bryan Lim
bullets: Derives exact linear-model criteria balancing variance reduction against bias from sharing experts across roles with different targets.
Characterizes final-output risk under shared linear propagation, including error directions and correlations.
Provides end-to-end bounds for routed computations that account for distribution shift, surrounding errors, and changed expert selection.

Shows through constructed cases and controlled experiments that local improvements can reverse at the final output; low-data Transformers show one-step gains without clearly improved free-running outputs.
Finds that correct predictions and routing labels alone do not prove individual experts implement the attributed operations; interventions are needed.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can answer questions about musical scores, but their ability to recognise notation, recover its structure and interpret its musical meaning requires separate evaluation. Existing optical music recognition (OMR) resources establish detection and transcription measurements; a transcription score alone leaves the strengths and bottlenecks of a VLM score reader unresolved. We introduce OmniScore-Bench, an evaluation of OMR capabilities in VLMs through 3,000 questions spanning six aspects and 24 task subtypes. Each question specifies a visible scope, reference annotations and an answer schema, enabling automatic evaluation from symbol localisation to musical consistency and evidence-linked question answering. Our assessment of twelve VLMs reveals operation-specific capability profiles and different transcription leaders across excerpt, single-page and multipage tasks. Controlled analyses examine the roles of score images, auxiliary givens and additional page context. On the tested subset, image removal exposes visual dependence in pitch and repeat interpretation while measuring how much performance remains with public context alone. Separate format and content analyses distinguish answer-format violations from musical errors. OmniScore-Bench supports diagnosing which score-reading operations VLMs perform reliably and which require improvement.
authors: Congren Dai, Zhancheng Guo, Danni Zhao, Wenchu Wang, Xiaobing Li, Maosong Sun
bullets: Introduces 3,000 questions covering six aspects and 24 musical-score reading subtypes.
Evaluates capabilities from symbol localisation and transcription to musical consistency and evidence-linked question answering.
Tests twelve VLMs and finds operation-specific capability profiles, with different transcription leaders by excerpt, single-page, and multipage scope.
Controlled analyses assess dependence on score images, auxiliary information, and additional page context.
Separates formatting violations from musical errors to diagnose reliable operations and remaining weaknesses.

papers.abstract: World-model video encoders such as V-JEPA learn how scenes change (direction, speed, order, state) from video alone. To answer questions, they are joined to a language model trained on captions and question-answer pairs. But each caption or question names only a few attributes of a clip, so the model learns to retrieve those attributes rather than to read the clip, and the dynamics the encoder carries go unused: on the same items, a linear probe reads speed from frozen V-JEPA features at 87% while the VLM answers at chance. We show where dynamics lives in a frozen encoder: in a subspace shared across videos for predictive encoders such as V-JEPA, but not as a shared component of frame-wise, text-aligned encoders such as SigLIP. We then build counterfactual supervision that makes the language model read it: pixel transformations turn public videos into answer-balanced variants whose answers are set by the transformation and differ only in the change. Trained in a single stage on 4.53M public samples with 32 visual tokens per frame, where open video LLMs use several stages, 9M to 172M samples and 64 to 256 tokens per frame on average, the resulting V-JEPA-LM models (1B to 8B, Qwen3 and Llama) lead every size class in average score across eleven video benchmarks; our 4B model scores 72.1, against 61.1 for the best open 4B and 64.8 for the best open 8B model. A controlled encoder x supervision study shows that the encoder decides what can be read and the supervision what is read: at a matched budget, counterfactual supervision adds 4.5 points on average and 38 on the speed questions of natural benchmarks. Code and models: https://github.com/kkt94/Llama-V-JEPA-LM.
authors: Keuntae Kim, Dongjun Kim, Yong Suk Choi
bullets: V-JEPA retains shared representations of dynamics such as direction, speed, order, and state, but standard caption-based training largely leaves them unused.
Counterfactual pixel transformations create answer-balanced video variants whose answers depend specifically on the visual change.
Models are trained in a single stage on 4.53M public samples using 32 visual tokens per frame.
V-JEPA-LM models from 1B to 8B lead their size classes across eleven video benchmarks; the 4B model scores 72.1.
Controlled studies find counterfactual supervision improves average performance by 4.5 points and speed-question performance by 38 points on natural benchmarks.

papers.abstract: With the rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs), an increasing number of users are turning to LLM-powered agents for conversational shopping in e-commerce. However, the user needs continue to change as new product categories, procurement scenarios, and feature requests emerge. At the same time, the product's execution harness-including its tools, skills, and operating procedures-continues to evolve to support increasingly sophisticated interactions. These changes create two practical challenges: 1) Demand drift alters the distribution, intent, and complexity of user requests, causing a model trained once to fall behind; 2) Harness evolution requires the model to use newly introduced capabilities correctly without losing behavior that users already rely on. Periodic manual retraining is too delayed and labor-intensive for this setting. To address these challenges, we present G-CAST, a governed continual self-training system that converts daily production evidence under evolving demand and capability contracts into reward-routed, entropy-prioritized training data and governed reward evolution. Governed checkpoint transition under cumulative evaluation controls each model update, enabling the agent to learn newly introduced behaviors without sacrificing previously accepted capabilities. Experiments on a real production e-commerce agent show that G-CAST achieves stronger adaptation to newly introduced demand while better preserving previously accepted behavior compared with a strong autonomous post-training baseline. Ablations further show that both reward-routed, entropy-prioritized data orchestration and governed reward evolution are important to these gains. G-CAST is now deployed in Yuancai(http://cai.1688.com/), a B2B procurement agent on Alibaba's 1688 platform.
authors: Yuechun Yu, Wenzheng Kong, Xiaofeng Mao, Jin Zhang
bullets: Addresses demand drift and evolving execution harnesses, which make static training and periodic manual retraining inadequate.
Converts daily production evidence into reward-routed, entropy-prioritized training data and evolves rewards under governance.
Uses cumulative evaluation to control checkpoint transitions and prevent regressions in established capabilities.
Real-production experiments show stronger adaptation and better behavior preservation than an autonomous post-training baseline.
Ablations identify data orchestration and governed reward evolution as important; the system is deployed in Alibaba 1688’s Yuancai agent.

figures.caption: Figure 1: G-CAST, a governed continual adaptation loop for deployed e-commerce agents. The main self-evolution loop converts daily production queries into checkpoint updates through multi-rollout generation, reward reliability checking, reward-routed data orchestration, model adaptation, and governed checkpoint transition. When rollout evidence indicates a possible reward error under the current contract, the reward-evolution loop updates the executable reward through contract-grounded annotation, offline reward checks, and trial adaptation before training resumes. Candidate checkpoints are admitted only after cumulative evaluation on both newly introduced and previously retained capabilities, with rejected candidates, regressions, and reward anomalies recorded in the evaluation ledger.

Figure 2: Performance degradation of a fixed checkpoint as the capability contract expands across demand periods. The figure reports the base reward, which excludes auxiliary reward components introduced only in later contract versions, so that performance remains directly comparable across periods. The dark curve shows the cumulative mean over all active evaluation slices, and the colored curves show the period-specific means.

Table 2: Cumulative performance, retention, and adaptation under matched evaluation. The four middle columns report cumulative reward at successive checkpoints. In each of the two rightmost columns, a cell reports the method-specific stage-entry value, the Post-RL value, and their difference. Retained reward is the query-weighted mean over previously introduced 100-query periods, whereas new-period reward is computed on the newly introduced 100-query period. A negative retained delta denotes forgetting. "–" indicates a non-applicable metric or an unreported intermediate result.

Table 3: Routing and prioritization ablation on the cumulative evaluation across Periods 1–4. Reward + Entropy is the full method, Reward + Random removes entropy prioritization, and Random removes both components. Sel. Acc. denotes skillselection accuracy, and Adherence R. denotes skill-adherence reward.

Table 4: Comparison of training-reward designs on the cumulative evaluation over Periods 1–3. All three arms share the same training data and optimization settings, and differ only in reward evolution under the expanded capability contract: Static keeps the original reward unchanged, Ungated introduces a one-time contract-aware reward update without continued gate-controlled evolution, and Gated (ours) admits reward updates only through continued validation gates.

Table 1: Demand contexts sampled from four distinct time periods. Each period defines a frozen snapshot of requests and capability requirements observed during its corresponding time span, rather than a stage of the learning algorithm.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a governed continual self-training system for agents under evolving demand, directly fitting continual/online learning.
papers.title: G-CAST: Governed Continual Self-Training for E-Commerce Agents under Evolving Demands
papers.tldr: G-CAST enables e-commerce agents to continually adapt to changing user demands and tools while preserving previously accepted behavior through governed self-training.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents can coordinate tools and applications to complete complex, multi-step tasks. As their interaction histories grow, effective context management becomes essential for reliable and efficient execution. Existing methods reduce context through summarization, pruning, or history selection. However, shorter contexts do not necessarily support better decisions: summaries can omit exact details needed for later actions, while retaining entire interactions can carry substantial irrelevant information. We propose CarryOn, a lightweight context manager that pairs compact execution state with fine-grained, source-linked evidence. A learned selector and adaptive retention policy keep relevant evidence available without additional LLM calls for context management. We introduce two complementary evaluation metrics: $S_\alpha$ prioritizes task success while accounting for resource use, and normalized cost per success (NCS) measures the resources spent per successful task. Across AppWorld, OfficeBench, and Tau2 Telecom with three LLM Actors, CarryOn achieves 75.7% macro-averaged task success, exceeding the strongest baseline by 6.7 percentage points. It also achieves the best average scores on both metrics.
authors: Lihuan Li, Ruiyi Yang, Jiru Wang, Yifan Duan, Xiachong Lin, Hao Xue, Yang Song, Flora Salim
bullets: Addresses context growth and the trade-off between missing key details and retaining irrelevant history.
Uses a learned evidence selector and adaptive retention policy without extra LLM calls for context management.
Combines compact execution state with fine-grained, source-linked evidence.
Introduces Sα, which balances success and resource use, and normalized cost per success (NCS).
Reaches 75.7% macro-averaged task success across three benchmarks and three LLM Actors, 6.7 points above the strongest baseline; it also leads on both metrics.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon agents increasingly serve as persistent personal assistants across modern web platforms, managing schedules, applications, and multi-step plans over weeks or months. Users often return to an ongoing conversation after a long conversational hiatus, while earlier bookings and preparation notes stay on record. During this hiatus, scheduled dates may pass even though the retained records remain unchanged and event outcomes go unrecorded. Existing evaluations of long-horizon agents focus on fact retention and explicit state updates. Whether agents perceive the passage of time and adapt their advice accordingly therefore remains unknown. We frame this ability as temporal state perception and use, which means perceiving the current time and applying it when interpreting dated records. To study it, we design session-rekindling tasks that keep the earlier conversation fixed and vary only the follow-up date and the way temporal information reaches the agent. Experiments across five model routes and five temporal-information conditions show that agents can obtain the current time but often fail to use it. They reliably query the clock and even note in their reasoning that the scheduled date has passed, yet many still tell users to prepare for the expired event. Supplying explicit temporal context reduces this error, and providing the computed date relation removes it entirely. Keeping up with time therefore depends on turning perceived time into updated plans. Based on these findings, we design a session-rekindling benchmark that provides temporal-awareness guidance for designing long-horizon agents. The code can be found at https://github.com/Adoreu2/session-rekindling-benchmark.
authors: Hongguan Su, Ming Wang, Shun Zhang, Yifan Wang, Rong Yin, Zhiming Ma, Mengzheng Yang, Peng Chen
bullets: Studies temporal state perception: using the current time to interpret dated records.
Evaluates session-rekindling tasks by varying follow-up dates and how temporal information is provided.
Across five model routes and five conditions, agents often recognize that events have passed yet still recommend preparing for them.
Explicit temporal context reduces errors, while supplying the computed date relation eliminates them.
Introduces a session-rekindling benchmark and guidance for designing more time-aware agents.

papers.abstract: Multimodal agentic coding requires robust visual reasoning to analyze observations and evaluate generated artifacts. Current frameworks largely rely on a Thinking-with-Images paradigm, where agents depend on their intrinsic vision to execute visually grounded tasks. However, this architectural coupling introduces a fundamental bottleneck. Agent performance remains strictly bounded by internal perceptual limitations. Furthermore, text-only agents lack native perception. Without specialized tools, they cannot perform visual reasoning. To overcome these constraints, we introduce the Vision-as-a-Tool (VaaT) paradigm. Prior visual tool-use merely manipulates images for an agent's intrinsic vision to read. In contrast, VaaT reframes general-purpose multimodal large language models (MLLMs) as callable external utilities. As a result, text-only agents can completely offload visual reasoning during agentic execution. Meanwhile, vision-capable agents can dynamically augment their native perception on demand. We instantiate this paradigm in VHarness, a unified framework driven by five atomic actions. We comprehensively evaluate VHarness across Image-to-HTML, Image-to-SVG, and Image-to-3D generation tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that VHarness consistently improves visual fidelity and geometric accuracy across both text-only and multimodal coding agents. These findings highlight that modularizing visual reasoning into callable utilities provides a flexible and scalable foundation for future agentic coding systems.
authors: Haolin Yang, Wenshan Wu, Jin Jiang, Yu Cheng, Yan Xia, Ting Song, Yangyu Huang, Zhiliang Peng, Wenhui Wang, Hangbo Bao, Yuzhe Zhang, Wen-Da Wei, Tengchao Lv, Li Dong, Lei Cui, Furu Wei
bullets: Existing agentic coding systems couple visual reasoning to an agent’s built-in perception, limiting performance and excluding text-only agents.
Vision-as-a-Tool (VaaT) treats general-purpose multimodal LLMs as external utilities rather than relying solely on intrinsic vision.
VHarness implements VaaT through five atomic actions in a unified framework.
Across Image-to-HTML, Image-to-SVG, and Image-to-3D tasks, VHarness improves visual fidelity and geometric accuracy for text-only and multimodal agents.
The approach provides a modular, flexible foundation for visual reasoning in agentic coding systems.

papers.abstract: World models that support planning, control, and interpretable reasoning require latent representations that genuinely encode action. Yet the large-scale video data from which such models are learned overwhelmingly lack action annotations. Latent-action models infer action-like variables from observation sequences, enabling action-aware learning from unlabeled videos or trajectories. A fundamental concern, however, remains: a latent that improves future prediction may simply encode the current state, episode progress, task identity, or other predictive shortcuts. Existing evaluation practices---reconstruction loss, rollout fidelity, action recovery, or downstream performance---cannot isolate this distinction. We introduce the Latent Action Support Ratio (LASR), a dimensionless metric that measures, under offline evaluation on held-out data, whether a learned latent provides predictive support for action-related targets beyond the current state and non-action alternatives. LASR provides two complementary summaries: GeoLASR captures typical support, while WorstLASR identifies the weakest case. We instantiate the LASR benchmark with recorded actions and corresponding physical state changes as targets, episode-held-out splits, one predictor type for all comparisons, and positive and negative controls. Experiments on recorded robot manipulation data and a matched multi-task panel demonstrate that LASR detects known action information, rejects representative non-action shortcuts, and enables graded comparisons among imperfect latent representations. We further use LASR to train and audit a lightweight residual adapter, obtaining descriptively better point estimates whose uncertainty is assessed with paired comparisons. LASR thus provides a principled offline protocol for measuring action-related predictive support in world-model latents.
authors: Yu Zhou, Changsong Lei, Yixiang Wei, Kairui Wen, Huankun Sheng, Ming Li, Yeying Fan, Yu-Hui Wen, Yong-Jin Liu
bullets: Addresses the lack of action annotations in large-scale video and the difficulty of validating latent-action representations.
Measures predictive support for action-related targets beyond current state and other non-action alternatives.
Reports typical support with GeoLASR and weakest-case support with WorstLASR.
Uses held-out offline evaluation, recorded actions and physical state changes, episode-held-out splits, common predictors, and positive/negative controls.
On robot manipulation and matched multi-task data, LASR detects action information, rejects shortcuts, compares imperfect latents, and audits a residual adapter.

papers.abstract: Policy gradient methods are widely used to align large language model outputs with human preferences, but the log-likelihoods they require cannot be directly computed in Masked Diffusion Language Models (MDLMs). MDLM post-training therefore relies on a surrogate objective based on the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO), and recent work estimates a blockwise variant of this objective via Monte Carlo methods to support blockwise generation. However, existing estimation schemes randomly sample the block index, so they may evaluate the same block more than once and leave some blocks unevaluated. This introduces variance arising from block selection into the estimates. In this work, we propose a full-block estimator that evaluates every block exactly once and averages the results. We theoretically show that the proposed estimator remains unbiased while eliminating the between-group variance arising from block selection, thereby achieving lower variance than the baseline for the same sample size. In experiments on five benchmarks spanning mathematics, planning, and coding, our method achieves the highest accuracy on four benchmarks and outperforms the random block sampling baseline by an average of 12.79 points.
authors: Yunzhen He, Hiroaki Yamagiwa, Hidetoshi Shimodaira
bullets: MDLMs lack directly computable log-likelihoods, so post-training uses an ELBO-based surrogate objective.
Random block sampling can repeat blocks and omit others, adding variance from block selection.
The proposed estimator evaluates and averages all blocks once per sample.
It is theoretically unbiased and removes between-group variance, yielding lower variance at the same sample size.
Across five math, planning, and coding benchmarks, it had the highest accuracy on four and exceeded random sampling by an average of 12.79 points.

papers.abstract: Running large language models (LLMs) on local devices keeps data private, removes per-token cost, cuts network latency, and keeps working without a connection. Two shifts now strain how such models are served. On one device, several agents share a locally served model with an interactive user. Across devices, a developer or small team often owns several capable machines from different vendors, which sit idle most of the day because every local server serves one runtime on one machine. We present Superfluid, an open-source LLM server built for local inference at both scales. On one device, Superfluid drives llama.cpp, MLX, or BaseRT in isolated worker processes through one scheduler that moves interactive requests ahead of agent work, computes a prompt shared by many requests once, and writes every token to a durable log before it reaches the client. Across devices, one Superfluid server turns a fleet of machines into a single API endpoint. Machines with different hardware serve copies of the same model, receive work according to their measured speed, and can join or fail under load without losing a request. For Qwen3.8-27B on an Apple M5 Pro, a chat sent while eight agents are working receives its first token in 1.5 s, against 291-612 s on llama-server, Ollama, and mlx_lm.server. On six machines from three chip vendors serving 64 simulated users for one hour, Superfluid answers all 5,041 requests while machines join one at a time and one is killed and rejoins; throughput grows from 112 to 534 tok/s and the median first-token time falls from 99 to 12 s. On twelve Mac Studio M3 Ultras it sustains 10,656 tok/s across 38,563 requests from 384 agents without a failure. Superfluid is available under the Apache-2.0 licence at https://github.com/basecompute/superfluid.
authors: Prabod Rathnayaka, Isura Manchanayake, Srikandabala Kogul, Steve Siu, Fabian Waschkowski, Lukas Wesemann
bullets: Addresses local serving for multiple interactive users and agents, plus fleets of heterogeneous devices that would otherwise sit idle.
Uses isolated llama.cpp, MLX, or BaseRT workers with one scheduler, shared prompt computation, and durable token logging.
Distributes model replicas according to measured machine speed, allowing devices to join or fail without losing requests.
In reported tests, it reduced interactive latency under agent load, scaled throughput as machines joined, and completed workloads during machine failure and rejoining.
Released under the Apache-2.0 licence.

papers.abstract: Multi-view visual augmentation often seeks consistency across cameras, but it is unclear which forms of consistency matter for downstream control. We use simulation-state replay to manipulate cross-view coupling while preserving the per-camera perturbation distributions, physical trajectories, and action labels. Across seven LIBERO manipulation tasks, marginal-matched changes in global appearance, ghost injection, and target color have small average costs for a late-fusion Diffusion Policy: point estimates are near zero or negative, and the largest upper endpoint of the 90% posterior credible intervals is 2.55 percentage points. In contrast, geometrically anti-coupled observations reduce success by 3.30 percentage points relative to coupled observations (90% CrI [0.64, 6.28]), with displacement magnitude, direction marginals, and the number of affected views matched. Camera interventions reveal substantial dependence on wrist-view geometry, while feature analysis shows appearance sensitivity patterns associated with the factors randomized during training. ACT shows a higher target-color cost estimate than DP, with uncertainty that includes zero and sensitivity to task composition. Within the tested tasks and policy configurations, these findings motivate selective consistency constraints: appearance coupling can sometimes be relaxed, whereas task-relevant geometry and cross-view spatial correspondence warrant protection.
bullets: The study isolates cross-view coupling effects while preserving per-camera perturbation distributions, trajectories, and action labels.
Global appearance, ghost injection, and target-color changes have small average effects for late-fusion Diffusion Policy.
Geometrically anti-coupled observations reduce success by 3.30 percentage points relative to coupled observations across seven LIBERO tasks.
Wrist-camera geometry strongly influences intervention effects, and ACT shows greater—but uncertain—sensitivity to target color.
The results support relaxing some appearance constraints while preserving task-relevant geometric correspondence.

papers.abstract: Agentic forecasting systems based on large language models (LLMs) are now competitive with expert human forecasters, but these systems still suffer from a critical limitation: the inability to produce forecasts that are logically consistent. For example, forecasts for related events often fail to satisfy the axioms of probability, which in turn implies that related forecasts cannot simultaneously be correct and undermines their utility for decision makers. Enforcing consistency is not trivial -- naive approaches (e.g., projection onto the set of consistent forecasts) can degrade accuracy. We argue that the key to overcoming the apparent tradeoff between consistency and accuracy lies in the reasoning which supports each forecast. We finetune a supervisory language model that leverages this reasoning to jointly reconcile inconsistencies while improving the accuracy of related forecasts. On ForecastBench, our method improves the Brier score of a retrieval-augmented GPT-5.1 forecaster by 9.3% while reducing measures of structural inconsistency by 82-90%. We interrogate our method via a comprehensive series of baselines and ablations, and find that no alternative method matches our gains in consistency and accuracy simultaneously.
authors: Kate Yuan, Rohan Alur, Manish Raghavan, Devavrat Shah
bullets: LLM forecasters can produce mutually inconsistent predictions for related events, limiting their usefulness for decisions.
Naively enforcing probability consistency may reduce forecast accuracy.
The proposed method fine-tunes a supervisory model to use forecast reasoning to jointly reconcile inconsistencies and improve related predictions.
On ForecastBench, it improves the Brier score of a retrieval-augmented GPT-5.1 forecaster by 9.3% and reduces structural inconsistency by 82–90%.
Baselines and ablations indicate that alternative methods do not achieve comparable gains in both consistency and accuracy.

papers.abstract: Depth and 3D foundation models can predict geometry from RGB images, allowing zero-shot object navigation without a depth sensor. However, when predicted depth is mapped as if it came from a sensor, view-dependent errors accumulate in the map, remove exploration goals, and end the search before the agent can observe and correct them. We propose ERA, a training-free object navigation system that replaces the depth sensor with depth predicted from RGB images and poses. ERA follows a paradigm we call Move with Error: movement provides new views that correct map errors, and the corrected map enables further movement. It realizes this paradigm with revisable occupancy and with exploration from reachable viewpoints, which continues the search when no frontier remains, and verifies the target across views before stopping. On three benchmarks, ERA achieves state-of-the-art performance among training-free methods without depth sensors. Its map and exploration components also raise VLFM's success from 10.8% to 61.7% under the same predicted depth. We further deploy ERA on a real robot.
authors: Shunyang Huang, Shuo Wang, Wenyuan Xie, Mingyu Lin, Yue Ding, Hongtao Lu
bullets: Addresses accumulated errors when RGB-predicted depth is treated like sensor depth, which can prematurely end exploration.
Introduces the “Move with Error” paradigm: movement provides views that correct the map and support continued navigation.
Uses revisable occupancy, reachable-viewpoint exploration, and multi-view target verification.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance among training-free, sensor-free methods on three benchmarks.
Improves VLFM success from 10.8% to 61.7% under the same predicted depth and is deployed on a real robot.

papers.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving is predominantly evaluated through ego-vehicle safety and task completion. Its deployment in urban traffic, however, creates sustained interactions among vehicles whose collective effects remain insufficiently evaluated. We introduce Ego2Flow, a closed-loop benchmark for assessing the traffic-system impact of autonomous driving on maps distilled from real-world cities. To construct realistic 3D urban environments for sustained closed-loop traffic simulation, we develop an agent-guided map distillation framework that integrates real-world maps and observations with complementary geographic information. Through an iterative feedback mechanism and a traffic information graph that jointly guide scene generation, the framework preserves lane topology, critical road geometry and decision-relevant visual conditions while simplifying nonessential details and completing unobserved regions. Using our proposed framework, we generate and publicly release six CARLA maps from the Argoverse 2 dataset, covering the corresponding real-world regions and enabling paired comparisons of driving behavior under real and simulated observations. On these maps, Ego2Flow evaluates how autonomous driving policies affect traffic efficiency, safety, stability and energy consumption across diverse road structures. Compared with existing construction methods, our framework achieves the lowest average displacement error between planning outputs from paired real and simulated observations. We further benchmark representative driving policies to characterize their system-level impact on urban traffic. Project Page: https://github.com/Fisher-007/Ego2Flow.
authors: Yu Dong, Weiying Shen, Hangyu Li, Shu Han, Hong Li, Xiangbo Gao, Keshu Wu, Zhengzhong Tu, Soyoung Ahn, Zhiyuan Liu, Xiaopeng Li
bullets: Introduces a closed-loop benchmark measuring traffic efficiency, safety, stability, and energy consumption across diverse urban roads.
Builds realistic 3D environments by distilling real-world maps and observations, completing unseen regions while preserving key road geometry and visual conditions.
Uses iterative feedback and a traffic information graph to guide scene generation and simplify nonessential details.
Releases six CARLA maps derived from Argoverse 2, enabling paired comparisons between real and simulated observations.

The proposed map construction achieves the lowest average displacement error among compared methods for paired planning outputs; representative policies are evaluated for system-level traffic effects.

papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT) systems increasingly combine sensed time series with external text such as expert reports and news, yet how reliably models use text that agrees or conflicts with the sensed history remains unclear. We introduce the first real-world diagnostic benchmark organized by text-history relationship: 1,762 text-window pairs across sensor telemetry (Weather), web-service traffic (Wikipedia), and market data streams (Finance), each labeled Aligned, Conflicting, or Unspecified by whether the text's direction agrees with the historical trend, opposes it, or is not stated. Across ten pretrained models evaluated zero-shot, we investigate text selection and combination under text-history relationships (RQ1) and error diagnosis and horizon-scaled revision control (RQ2). For RQ1, we compare two types of text on paired Weather windows: one directly forecasts temperature changes, while the other describes related weather conditions, such as winds and fronts. Under Aligned, the first type yields the lowest error for most models. Under Conflicting, it increases most models' error above the no-text baseline; we therefore add only its stated magnitude and timing to the second type. Compared with either type alone, this combination lowers mean absolute scaled error (MASE) for six models and raises directional accuracy (DA) for seven. For RQ2, an error decomposition attributes the error increase to oversized revisions, and a training-free rule that limits them outperforms forecasts both with and without text for the four models with this trade-off, lowering MASE by 4.49%-21.98% and raising DA by 2.99%-9.71%. Our dataset is available at https://github.com/Shelton1202/ACU-Bench.
authors: Xintong Wang, Haihan Nan, Ruidong Li
bullets: Introduces a real-world benchmark of 1,762 text–time-series pairs from Weather, Wikipedia traffic, and Finance, labeled Aligned, Conflicting, or Unspecified.
Evaluates ten pretrained models zero-shot on text selection, combination, error diagnosis, and forecast revision control.
Aligned, directly predictive text generally performs best; conflicting text often worsens forecasts relative to using no text.
Combining forecast-oriented text with related-condition text improves MASE for six models and directional accuracy for seven.
A training-free rule limiting oversized revisions improves both metrics for four models, with gains reported in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Contrastive vision-language models such as CLIP are trained to align images and text, not to represent taxonomies. Yet empirical studies show that CLIP embeddings exhibit hierarchical structure aligned with the hierarchy of semantic concepts. A theoretical characterization of why such hierarchy emerges from a non-hierarchical objective remains open. In this paper, we formalize this phenomenon as Hierarchical Angular Separation (HAS), a geometric property whereby each non-leaf concept embedding is more similar to its descendants than to off-branch concepts. Empirically, we show that HAS holds approximately in raw images and randomly initialized CLIP image embeddings, while in text embeddings it holds approximately only after contrastive learning. To theoretically explain this asymmetry, we analyze an unconstrained features model in which the image embeddings are fixed and only the text embeddings are trained. At the global minimizer, the text-side HAS violation percentage at each node is at most the image-side HAS violation and near-violation percentage. The key mechanism is the hierarchical co-occurrence structure of image-text pairs, which biases text embeddings toward root-centered image prototypes. For a linear contrastive loss, we derive a closed-form solution that makes this mechanism explicit. We extend the analysis to the InfoNCE loss and establish analogous guarantees under sufficient regularization. Synthetic experiments validate the theory and show that HAS is transferred even beyond the regimes covered by our analysis.
authors: Nghia Nguyen, Tianjiao Ding, Lachlan Ewen MacDonald, Ren\'e Vidal
bullets: Defines Hierarchical Angular Separation (HAS), where concepts are closer to descendants than to off-branch concepts.
Finds that HAS approximately exists in raw images and randomly initialized image embeddings, but emerges in text embeddings after contrastive learning.
Analyzes a model with fixed image features and trained text features, proving that text-side HAS violations are bounded by image-side violations and near-violations.
Attributes transfer to hierarchical co-occurrence patterns in image–text pairs, which pull text embeddings toward root-centered image prototypes.
Derives a closed-form result for linear contrastive loss, extends guarantees to InfoNCE with sufficient regularization, and validates them on synthetic experiments.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of the HAS transfer results. Under assumptions on the data model, both losses decompose the text embeddings into prototypes plus perturbations. Bounding the perturbations relative to the prototype norms gives a bound on text-side violations in terms of image-side margins.

Figure 1: How contrastive learning transfers hierarchy from image to text embeddings. Top-left: the image prototypes are arranged so that each concept is closer to its descendants than to concepts in other subtrees. The blue and red dotted lines indicate the boundary of the dog and cat subtrees, respectively. Top-right: each image of a labrador is a variation of the labrador prototype, and its caption may pair with any concept on the path from the root to that leaf, so an image can be captioned labrador, dog or animal. Bottom-left: the pairing also means that the caption dog pairs with images of dog or any of its descendants, so the average of these images approaches the mean of the dog subtree. Bottom-right: contrastive learning pulls each text embedding toward the corresponding subtree mean, so the text embeddings inherit the arrangement of the image prototypes.

Figure 2: Distribution of HAS-Viol vs depth on ViT-L/14 CLIP embeddings over non-root and nonleaf nodes. Top: text embeddings show that HAS is acquired through pretraining. Bottom: image embeddings show approximate HAS at random initialization and stronger HAS after pretraining.
