papers.abstract: Autonomous agents now run for hundreds of steps with little or no human supervision. In practice, practitioners use runtime monitors such as turn limits and keyword filters to decide when a run should be stopped, upgraded, or assisted. However, these heuristics may stop runs that would otherwise succeed or allow failing runs to continue. To address this limitation, we introduce LeBet (Learn then Bet), a statistical learning framework that derives its learning objective from sufficient conditions for valid and powerful intervention. In particular, LeBet learns an interpretable OR-of-AND monitor and accumulates evidence through a fixed betting statistic, intervening when the evidence reaches a prescribed threshold. Under finite within-class exchangeability and leave-one-out stability, we derive finite-sample guarantees for false-positive control (validity) and detection power conditional on the training data, using the same trajectories for learning and calibration without assuming independent and identically distributed trajectories. To address the intractable combinatorial optimization problem in our learning formulation, we use stochastic local search that leverages the monitor's Boolean structure to propose rule edits aimed at improving empirical separation. On SWE-bench Lite with Ministral 3 8B, the learned monitor saves $34.46\%$ of input-plus-output tokens and increases output precision from $18.33\%$ to $21.59\%$. The empirical false-positive rate is $13.64\%$. Our results show how to formalize the learning problem over interpretable rule sets with statistical conditions and establish training-conditional guarantees for reliable intervention based on partial histories.
authors: You-Lin Chen, Xinyi Lisa Chen, Pedro Herrero-Vidal, Xiaojing Yu, Bingqing Song, Bin Xu
bullets: Targets the shortcomings of heuristic monitors such as turn limits and keyword filters, which can intervene too early or too late.
Learns an interpretable OR-of-AND monitor and accumulates evidence with a fixed betting statistic until an intervention threshold is reached.
Uses stochastic local search to optimize rule sets and supports learning and calibration on the same trajectories.
Provides finite-sample false-positive control and conditional detection-power guarantees under exchangeability and leave-one-out stability, without assuming i.i.d. trajectories.
On SWE-bench Lite with Ministral 3 8B, saves 34.46% of input-plus-output tokens, raises output precision from 18.33% to 21.59%, and has a 13.64% empirical false-positive rate.

papers.abstract: Imitation policies for robot manipulation are often trained on noisy object positions, and they learn to discount the noisy reading. We show how much they discount it, and why. Because demonstrators steer toward the object, the robot's own state carries information about where the object is. A trained policy combines this proprioceptive anchor with the reading and weights the reading by $\alpha = V/(V + s^2)$, where $s^2$ is the reading noise and $V$ the anchor's error variance. $V$ belongs to the learner and is far smaller than a linear model of the demonstrations implies, which is why classical errors-in-variables (EIV) regression overestimates $\alpha$. Measured once, $V$ predicted ten held-out sensitivities across two robomimic tasks, two learners and four new noise levels, with mean absolute error 0.025 against 0.37 for classical EIV, and a parameter-free bias test rules out the simpler explanation that the policies just overestimate the noise. The discount does not carry over to deployment, where the policy produces its own state: closed-loop sensitivity to a persistent reading offset exceeded $\alpha$ in all 15 policies that passed the registered gates, although the stricter registered prediction, that all would follow the offset fully, held for 8 of them. Post hoc, lower $\alpha$ went with lower success, steeply for diffusion, and a registered prospective test confirmed this for diffusion on Can at two new noise levels: the measured $\alpha$ predicted success before any rollout, within 0.03 (95% intervals $\pm 0.08$), although training noise predicts it equally well. Every test was registered before its data, including the classical benchmark that failed, and all other analyses are labelled post hoc; all results are in simulation with synthetic Gaussian noise.
bullets: Policies weight noisy object observations by α = V/(V + s²), where V is the learned proprioceptive anchor’s error variance.
A single measurement of V predicted 10 held-out sensitivities far better than classical errors-in-variables regression (MAE 0.025 vs. 0.37).
In deployment, persistent observation offsets produced closed-loop sensitivities greater than α in all 15 tested policies; full offset following occurred in 8.
Lower α was associated with lower success, especially for diffusion policies; a prospective test predicted success within 0.03.
All results used simulated manipulation, synthetic Gaussian noise, and preregistered evaluations; some findings were post hoc.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes how imitation policies discount perception noise via a proprioceptive anchor, relevant to robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: Imitation Policies Learn a Proprioceptive Anchor: A Predictive Law for Perception Noise and Its Closed Loop Cost
papers.tldr: Imitation policies learn to combine proprioception with noisy object readings in a predictable way, but this noise discounting does not reliably transfer to closed-loop deployment.

papers.abstract: Before an LLM agent cancels a reservation or deletes a folder for a user, what stops it from acting on a false assumption: what its tools show, or what the user says? In this work, we study this gap with presupposition theory from linguistics: an agent may act only if each claim behind the act (e.g., one reservation fits the name) is seen to hold, answered by the user, or disclosed while the act can be undone. A simple bound shows that when lookups cannot tell one record from two, any agent acts without asking first as often with two records as with one. We then vary whether a search lists, counts, or omits a second match, and whether the user states a claim that a record refutes (e.g., "It is empty"). Under a role-only prompt, a count of a second record leaves most of 36 earlier agents acting on the one they see, whereas listing both stops most. When the user says a record such as a folder is empty, however, a count of its one item stops agents about as often as a listing, and stating the claim mostly cuts acting when it is false. The newest Claude and GPT models always open a counted second record, then never act. When we add a same-name, same-zip customer to a retail benchmark, a lookup returning that customer first led to wrong-account writes in about a quarter of conversations, and one that checks a street the user knows kept completion near the one-customer level. Safe writes therefore need lookups that list or check competing records, and evaluations that vary what tools show.
authors: Yue Zhao, Angela Huyue Zhang, S. Alex Yang, Hua Wei, Xiyang Hu
bullets: The study applies presupposition theory to determine when agents should act, ask the user, or disclose reversible actions.
Listing multiple matching records prevents unsafe actions far more reliably than merely counting them.
User statements such as “the folder is empty” can stop actions when tool evidence contradicts them.
In a retail benchmark, returning a same-name, same-zip customer first caused wrong-account writes in about a quarter of conversations.
Safe writes require lookups that reveal competing records or verify distinguishing details, and evaluations should vary tool visibility.

papers.abstract: Generating an evaluation suite from an agent's specification is diversity-driven search: a generator fills a descriptor space (requirements $\times$ personas $\times$ scenario kinds), and the suite it emits is an archive, then scored like a benchmark by its mean pass rate, which throws away the search's product. We inject 7 controlled defects into a $\tau^2$-bench agent across two domains. Coverage yields a ceiling: if a defect's traced footprint holds $b$ scenarios that pass at baseline, it can itself contribute at most $b/N$ to a suite of $N$. For 4 of 5 traceable defects that ceiling lies at or below the detection threshold $\theta = 0.10$, so no within-footprint effect can move the suite past it; in both domains the tool-removal defect destroys every covered scenario it can (exactly its ceiling) while the suite-level pass rate moves the other way. Defects split into two regimes: trace-aligned ones, where per-cell scoring recovers the tool-removal defect in full and reveals a second as a significant improvement, and trace-orthogonal ones, whose footprint is behavioural: forced escalation is detected in retail at a traced coverage of exactly zero. Diversity along the generator's own axes helps only where it aligns: at fixed suite size a happy-path-only suite detects nothing, while a kind-diverse one detects the orchestration defect in 5 of 20 draws. Evaluation archives should be scored per cell and should publish coverage as a first-class property.
bullets: Suite generation is framed as diversity-driven search over requirements, personas, and scenario kinds, with the generated suite serving as an archive.
Coverage limits detectability: for most traceable defects, the affected scenarios cannot shift the suite score beyond the 0.10 detection threshold.
Suite-level pass rates can move in the wrong direction, including when a tool-removal defect destroys every covered scenario.
Per-cell scoring recovers trace-aligned defects and can expose behavioural, trace-orthogonal defects such as forced escalation.
Generator diversity helps only when aligned with the defect: kind-diverse suites detected an orchestration defect, whereas happy-path-only suites detected none.

papers.title: Generated Evaluation Suites as Diversity-Driven Search for Real Agent Regressions
papers.tldr: Generated evaluation suites can miss real agent regressions when scored only by overall pass rate; per-cell scoring and explicit coverage reveal defects more reliably.

papers.abstract: Visuomotor imitation learning has become a predominant paradigm for real-world robotic manipulation, yet it remains data-inefficient and brittle to task-irrelevant visual shifts. Pre-trained visual representations promise to ease this burden by distilling priors from internet-scale data, but the ``right'' representation for robotics remains unresolved: existing studies span broad but sparse task distributions and reach conclusions that vary and even conflict, pointing to strong task and setting dependence. We examine this question by bringing a magnifying glass to a common contact-rich manipulation task: insertion. We compare representations from widely used vision foundation models against an explicit contact-centric representation on two closely related insertion tasks, perturb each along controlled axes of occlusion and physical tolerance, and test whether conclusions transfer to the real world. Task dependence proves to be more subtle than previous, broadly scoped evaluations revealed: the best representation differs even between our near-identical tasks, and small changes shift trends in unpredictable ways. Despite this variability, results across simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate the distinct value of spatially-grounded, and in particular, contact-centric information for contact-rich policy learning, while underscoring how difficult it is to estimate such cues reliably under realistic visual complexity and sensor noise. We hope these findings motivate further study of representations in contact-rich manipulation, along with advances in contact perception and its integration into visuomotor policy learning.
authors: Leon Kim, Dinesh Jayaraman, Michael Posa
bullets: Evaluates vision foundation-model representations against an explicit contact-centric representation for two closely related insertion tasks.
Tests controlled changes in occlusion and physical tolerance in simulation, then examines transfer to real-world settings.
Finds that small task or condition changes can unpredictably alter which representation performs best.
Across experiments, contact-centric and spatially grounded cues provide distinct benefits for contact-rich manipulation.
Reliable contact estimation remains difficult under realistic visual complexity and sensor noise.

papers.selection_reason: Studies visual representations for contact-rich visuomotor imitation learning in manipulation.
papers.title: On the Utility of Pre-Trained Visual Representations for Policy Learning of Contact-Rich Insertion Tasks
papers.tldr: For contact-rich insertion, the best visual representation is highly task- and condition-dependent, but spatially grounded—especially contact-centric—information is consistently valuable for policy learning.

papers.abstract: Multi-view 3D transformers such as VGGT reconstruct a scene from a set of unposed images in a single forward pass, predicting camera poses, depth and 3D points, but the cost of their global attention grows quadratically with the num- ber of images. Accelerators borrowed from large language models assume that each token attends to only a few oth- ers; on these models they lose accuracy or gain little speed. We study the global attention of three multi-view transform- ers on seven datasets and find that every layer plays one of three roles: it averages over the whole scene, matches points across many images, or anchors on the first image, whose coordinates the outputs use. Building on this anal- ysis, we propose Regime-AWare ATTention Approximation (RAWATTA), a training-free method that runs attention in 8- bit precision and keeps 16-bit precision only in the layers where a worst-case calibration check requires it. Its fast set- ting, RAWATTA-Fast, also approximates attention in a few averaging and anchoring layers, while matching layers and the first image keep all their keys. On a 12 GB GPU at 50 im- ages, RAWATTA runs VGGT faster than the released code, mostly through our CUDA engine, and loses at most about one point of pose accuracy (AUC@3) on any dataset; RAWATTA-Fast is slightly faster and less accurate. Both fit 200 images, where the released code runs out of memory at 100.
authors: Muhammed Izzet Sezer, Sevval Belkis Dikkaya
bullets: Global attention in multi-view 3D transformers is costly because its complexity grows quadratically with the number of images.
The study identifies three layer roles: scene-wide averaging, cross-image point matching, and anchoring to the first image.
RAWATTA uses 8-bit attention by default and retains 16-bit precision when a worst-case calibration check requires it.
RAWATTA-Fast additionally approximates attention in selected averaging and anchoring layers while preserving full keys for matching layers and the first image.
On VGGT, RAWATTA is faster than the released implementation, loses at most about one AUC@3 pose-accuracy point, and supports 200 images on a 12 GB GPU where the baseline runs out of memory at 100.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a training-free attention approximation for multi-view 3D transformers, improving efficiency while preserving accuracy, relevant to efficient AI and 3D foundation models.
papers.title: Training-Free Acceleration of Multi-View 3D Transformers via Regime-Aware Attention Approximation
papers.tldr: RAWATTA accelerates multi-view 3D transformers without retraining by adapting attention precision and approximation to each layer’s functional regime.

papers.abstract: Joint world action models (WAMs) generate future actions and states together, modeling world-action trajectories rather than actions alone. However, trajectory imitation does not ensure that these trajectories are task-effective or consistent with dynamics. We present \textbf{world action trajectory optimization (WATO)}, which optimizes generated actions and future states jointly for control. WATO uses both as references in a dynamics-constrained trajectory optimization problem and differentiates the task loss through the optimized trajectory to train the generator. This makes generated trajectories task-aware and dynamics-consistent while using trajectory optimization only during training. At deployment, WATO directly generates candidate trajectories and ranks them with a world model, without iterative trajectory optimization. Across $7$ visual control environments, WATO improves average success from $79.9\%$ for the imitation joint WAM to $91.7\%$, outperforming strong model-based, goal-conditioned RL, and generative control baselines. Compared with cross-entropy method (CEM), WATO is on average $11.5\times$ faster and uses $600.5\times$ fewer world model evaluations at deployment.
bullets: Joint world-action models generate future actions and states, but imitation alone may yield ineffective or dynamically inconsistent trajectories.
WATO jointly optimizes generated actions and states using task loss and dynamics constraints during training.
Gradients through the optimized trajectory make the generator task-aware and dynamics-consistent.
At deployment, it directly generates candidate trajectories and ranks them with a world model, without iterative optimization.
Across 7 visual control environments, WATO raises average success from 79.9% to 91.7% and is faster and more evaluation-efficient than CEM.

papers.abstract: Kernel optimization is essential for efficient large language model (LLM) training and inference on Ascend NPUs. Existing Ascend kernel benchmarks primarily focus on kernel generation, with less emphasis on the ability of agents to optimize existing implementations under input configurations drawn from real workloads. To address this requirement, we introduce AscendGYM, a benchmark whose initial suite comprises 48 kernels across three difficulty levels. Each kernel is paired with test cases whose data types and tensor shapes are collected from real-world training and inference tasks. Consequently, performance improvements on AscendGYM map directly to the corresponding workloads. In terms of usability, two evaluation modes are supported in AscendGYM: model evaluation and model-harness evaluation. The kernel optimization capabilities of both trained models and custom agents are allowed to be measured. It provides a complete execution environment that closely reproduces how Ascend kernels are invoked in practical pipelines. For model evaluation, it additionally includes a built-in harness equipped with search orchestration and experience accumulation. Finally, we propose a new metric, the Speedup-Token Score (STS), which quantifies performance gains relative to token cost. By jointly considering speedup and cost, STS enables the assessment of practical kernel optimization capability of a model or harness under an acceptable budget. AscendGYM is available at https://github.com/SLAI-AITP/AscendGYM.
authors: AI Training Platform Team, Bingwei Zhang, Jing Li, Amir Abdullin, Sihang Chen, Xin Chen, Liangjun Feng, Yingmeng Gao, Tao Guo, Junjie Huang, Dongfang Li, Zhanglian Lin, Jiajun Liu, Zekun Liu, Zhengxuan Lu, Xiaodong Luo, Jian Meng, Ivan Nosov, Linyuan Qiu, Weijian Sun, Wanrui Yan, Binfan Zheng, Zhicheng Zhou, Baotian Hu, Min Zhang, Haizhou Li, Zhiquan Luo

Supports evaluation of both trained models and custom optimization agents through model and model-harness modes.
Reproduces practical Ascend kernel execution pipelines and includes search orchestration with experience accumulation for model evaluation.
Introduces Speedup-Token Score (STS), combining performance gains and token cost under a budget.
Scope: the initial benchmark targets Ascend NPUs and kernel optimization rather than kernel generation.

papers.abstract: High-level behaviors such as sycophancy and hallucination correspond to directions in a model's activation space (Chen et al., 2025). These directions, known as persona vectors, can suppress undesirable traits either at inference time, subtracting the vector during generation, or through preventative steering, adding the vector during fine-tuning, so the optimizer never needs to encode the trait in weights, then removing the vector at evaluation. Chen et al. (2025) recommend preventative steering because it preserves Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) accuracy, but validations of this recommendation have measured capability alone. We primarily evaluate results on preventative steering of sycophancy and hallucination vectors on three models, measuring three safety benchmarks alongside trait expression, coherence, and MMLU. Our findings show that preventative steering still changes refusal behavior, but by an amount that depends on the trait and does not establish that preventative persona steering is safety-neutral, and steering methods should be evaluated on several safety benchmarks.
authors: Sabrina Tang, Nikolai Vo, Carson Murillo, Chira Sukumarnpiti, Sarah Wilson
bullets: Audits preventative steering for sycophancy and hallucination across three models.
Measures trait expression, coherence, MMLU, and three safety benchmarks.
Finds refusal behavior changes, with effects varying by the steered trait.
Concludes that capability preservation alone is insufficient to validate safety.
Recommends evaluating steering methods across multiple safety benchmarks.

papers.selection_reason: Empirically audits the safety side effects of preventative persona steering, a technique for aligning LLMs, relevant to LLM safety and alignment research.

papers.tldr: Preventative persona steering can alter models’ refusal behavior, so preserving capability scores does not guarantee safety neutrality.

papers.abstract: Human demonstrations are becoming the main source of data for dexterous manipulation, and real-to-sim-to-real pipelines multiply each demonstration in simulation. These pipelines rebuild the interaction from vision, which recovers how the hand moves. Which fingers touch, when, and how hard remain unobserved, because a hand pose shows where each finger stops on the surface rather than how far it is driven to close. This gap is a force gap: on held-out recordings, a hand policy that imitates the observed pose grips with 0.31x the recorded force, and a policy trained on physics replays of vision-tracked poses grips with 1.55x. TouchTwin closes the gap with measured human touch. Each selected TouchScale recording, captured with head and wrist RGB-D cameras and an 880-taxel glove, is rebuilt in MuJoCo. Coding agents write the objects as physics-tested programs, and a per-subject tactile hand replays the interaction with the recorded touch setting the contact and the closing force of each finger. In simulation, a policy trained on touch-grounded replays grips at 0.99x the recorded force and succeeds in 20/20 trials on held-out recordings and 35/36 unseen perturbations; a contact predictor trained on them misses 13% of real contact frames, against 32% for vision-based replays. Each replay also seeds perturbed demonstrations with simulated contact and force labels, rendered as realistic video in new views and scenes.
authors: Huiwen Han, Nuo Chen, Ziyao Zeng, Dayou Li, Hao Wang, Amir Hossein Rahmati, Xiaoning Qian, Bangya Liu, Zhiwen Fan
bullets: Vision-based replays miss finger contact timing and force, creating a force gap in simulated demonstrations.
The system combines RGB-D views with an 880-taxel glove and reconstructs interactions in MuJoCo using subject-specific tactile hands.
Recorded touch determines finger contact and closing force during physics-based replay, while coding agents create physics-tested object programs.
Touch-grounded policies reproduced 0.99× recorded force, succeeded on 20/20 held-out recordings and 35/36 unseen perturbations, and reduced contact-frame misses to 13% versus 32% for vision replays.
Replays can seed perturbed demonstrations with simulated contact and force labels, rendered in new views and scenes.

papers.selection_reason: Scales human demonstration data with touch grounding for dexterous manipulation policy learning.
papers.title: TouchTwin: Scaling Human Touch Data via Real-to-Sim-to-Real
papers.tldr: TouchTwin augments real-to-sim-to-real manipulation data with measured human touch, producing simulations that better reproduce contact forces and support robust dexterous policies.

papers.abstract: Behavioral clusters learned over user or item interactions drift as behavior evolves: some fragment into sub-behaviors, some converge, some disappear, and new patterns emerge. Two paradigms dominate the maintenance of evolving clusterings. Threshold triggers fire a pre-specified action when a hardcoded statistic crosses a cutoff; refit-and-track (MONIC-style) re-clusters every window and infers transitions from how the new clusters align with the previous window's. Both hardwire the decision into a threshold or a re-clustering rule. We study an alternative in which a large language model (LLM) makes the lifecycle decision in place. Given a threshold-free, whole-population view of the current cluster set (statistical health, labels, member texts, residual mass), the LLM decides per cluster whether and how to act (split, merge, retire, create, or no-action) without re-clustering. Because the useful signal channel depends on how informative the labels are, we fix a richness-conditioned policy in advance: statistics when label distinctiveness is low, fused statistics+semantics when it is high. On three public datasets spanning label richness (YooChoose 0.17, MOOC 0.50, News-Category 0.70), the policy-selected LLM mode obtains the highest F1 on all three, with far fewer interventions and stronger restraint than tuned threshold heuristics and a MONIC steelman (paired Wilcoxon p <= 0.003, bootstrap 95% CIs excluding zero). The gain is concentrated more in precision than recall. The useful modality shifts from statistics to semantics/fusion as richness rises. Semantics hurt on YooChoose, fusion is roughly neutral on MOOC, and the semantic channel is required on News. One base prompt template and one fixed policy serve all three datasets, whereas the tuned baseline collapses when moved between them. We treat this shift as a practitioner diagnostic observed on three datasets, not a validated law.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes an LLM-guided approach to managing evolving behavioral clusters, addressing the challenge of continual learning and online adaptation in data streams.
papers.title: LLM-Guided Cluster Lifecycle Management: Deciding When and How to Evolve Behavioral Clusters
papers.tldr: An LLM can manage evolving behavioral clusters without re-clustering, selecting restrained split, merge, retire, create, or no-action decisions using signals matched to label richness.

papers.abstract: Evaluations of multi-agent language models often compare communicating architectures against a single greedy pass. This practice confounds coordination with sample multiplicity and inference compute. We synthesize nine primary empirical evaluations comprising 516 unique multi-agent configurations organized along a resource vector R with six dimensions and a baseline ladder with four categories. Against baselines with a single pass (Category A), multi-agent accuracy differences are negative overall and near zero when omitting the largest contributing study. When evaluated against baselines matched on sample count (Category B) or resource budget (Category C), multi-agent systems average -0.042 in accuracy, and multilevel random effects modeling on the log odds scale remains negative across sensitivity checks. Multi-agent accuracy equals or falls below the baseline in 74% of these comparable contrasts, and study means are nonpositive in almost all evaluated studies. Across studies reporting both baselines, moving from a greedy pass to a sampled baseline shifts accuracy differences by -0.038 on average. Because communication adds no information when agents share identical evidence, positive returns require partitioned evidence, external verification, or error diversity across models. We provide a reviewer checklist and accounting utilities.
bullets: The study analyzes 516 multi-agent configurations using a six-dimensional resource vector and four-category baseline ladder.
Against single greedy passes, results are negative overall and near zero when the largest contributing study is excluded.
Against matched-sample or matched-budget baselines, multi-agent accuracy averages -0.042 and is no better in 74% of comparable contrasts.
Switching from a greedy to a sampled baseline reduces the apparent multi-agent advantage by 0.038 on average.
Positive coordination returns may require partitioned evidence, external verification, or model error diversity; the paper provides a reviewer checklist and accounting utilities.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The Baseline Ladder: Single-agent baseline categories and inferential validity. Gray rungs represent comparisons that do not control test-time compute: Category A (Greedy single pass): A single model forward pass (N = 1) without sampling; observed gains are confounded with sample count and token budget. Category B (Sampled baseline): k samples drawn without communication; isolates gains beyond sample multiplicity, though token volume and dollar cost may still diverge. Teal rungs represent comparisons controlling a named compute resource: Category C (Budget-matched baseline): A declared dimension of the resource vector R (such as thinking tokens or iteration steps) is held equal between systems; isolates coordination gains at that matched budget. Category D (Pareto frontier): Sweeps compute budgets to trace the accuracy-versus-cost boundary, establishing whether multi-agent coordination outperforms scaled single-agent reasoning across diverse compute regimes.

papers.selection_reason: Provides a comprehensive empirical analysis of multi-agent LLMs, untangling the effects of coordination, sampling, and test-time compute, directly relevant to LLM agent research.
papers.title: More Agents, More Samples, or More Thinking? Untangling Coordination, Ensembling, and Test-Time Compute in Multi-Agent LLMs
papers.tldr: Across nine evaluations, multi-agent LLMs generally do not outperform single-model baselines when sample count or inference resources are matched, suggesting gains come from compute, evidence diversity, or verification rather than coordination alone.

papers.abstract: A developer running a code assistant on a laptop downloads one model file, and local inference moves the energy of every request onto that machine. A common rule says a larger model at lower precision tends to beat a smaller one at higher precision. We ran 24 GGUF files of Qwen2.5-Coder at four sizes on a fanless MacBook Air M2 and priced each in energy per solved task on 542 EvalPlus tasks. The result is a selection guide indexed by Ollama's listed file size, with an evidence label on each pick. At 1 and 2 GB it picks the q4_K_M files of the 1.5B and 3B models, both on the correctness and energy frontier under every accounting. At 3 GB as listed, the larger-model rule picks 7B-q2_K, the only measured 7B file that fits, and there it does not pay. That file brings no significant gain in solves over the 2 GB pick, 3B-q4_K_M, and the 90% CI limits any 3B-q4_K_M deficit to 2.4 points. Yet 7B-q2_K needs 2.03 times the energy per solved task on CPU, GPU and memory rails, or 1.66 to 1.81 times on whole-system power. On HumanEval+, five alternating session pairs give a ratio of 1.925 against 1.956 in the main grid. At 8 GB, 7B-q6_K buys a significant gain over the 2 GB pick at a higher energy price. From 1.5B up, q4_K_M trails the highest precision measured at its size by less than 3 points (90% CI). We release per-task results, power logs and the analysis script.
bullets: Evaluates 24 GGUF files across four Qwen2.5-Coder sizes on a fanless MacBook Air M2 using 542 EvalPlus tasks.
At 1–2 GB, the 1.5B-q4_K_M and 3B-q4_K_M files lie on the correctness and energy frontiers under all accounting methods.
At 3 GB, 7B-q2_K does not significantly improve solves over 3B-q4_K_M, while using substantially more energy per solved task.
At 8 GB, 7B-q6_K provides a significant accuracy gain over the 2 GB choice, but at a higher energy cost.
For models 1.5B and larger, q4_K_M is within 3 percentage points of the highest measured precision at the same size; results and power logs are released.

papers.selection_reason: Empirical study of quantized code LLMs in terms of energy per solved task and file size, directly addressing efficiency of local LLM inference.
papers.title: Choosing Quantized Code LLMs by File Size and Energy per Solved Task

papers.abstract: Long-horizon navigation from indoors to outdoors remains an open problem for humanoid robots: one instruction covers rooms, doors and roads, and the camera moves with the gait. Worken, AGIBOT's measure of productive robot work, depends on robots that reach their workplaces autonomously. We present X-Nav, to our knowledge the first system to take a bipedal humanoid through a language-instructed long-horizon mission from indoors to outdoors. X-Nav covers a pipeline from data to deployment. Its data engine collects navigation data in open-source scenes, in digital twins of deployment sites and on real robots. Its navigation model, MELIOR, takes only RGB images from the robot's built-in camera and comes in two versions: MELIOR-A predicts actions, and MELIOR-N predicts a navigation goal. Its agentic workflow, X-Navarch, turns a brief human instruction into sub-tasks and deploys MELIOR on the robot with explicit target navigation and obstacle avoidance. On the Lingxi X2, X-Nav completes a mission of about a hundred metres from an office lobby to a store in a neighbouring building; LiDAR and odometry are used for target approach and low-level control. The mission is completed with both versions of MELIOR: the robot follows a change of destination and walks through a door from the lobby to the road, and with X-Navarch it also passes static and dynamic obstacles on the route. During deployment, MELIOR is adapted with data collected in a digital twin of the site; the adaptation raises its closed-loop success rate in the twin, and the adapted model is then deployed on the robot at the real site. In addition, MELIOR achieves competitive results on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks.
authors: Jiaxin Huang, Chengxing Lin, Xiaoyu Luo, Sirui Chen, Jingyu Guo, Aolin Li, Kairui Chen, Rui Zhen, Cheng Wen, Kerui Gu, Shunyao Wang, Zhihui Peng, Shaoli Huang
bullets: Addresses autonomous navigation across rooms, doors, roads, and changing destinations for humanoid robots.
Uses MELIOR, an RGB-only navigation model with action-prediction and goal-prediction variants.
X-Navarch decomposes brief instructions into subtasks and coordinates navigation with explicit target and obstacle avoidance.
Demonstrated on a Lingxi X2 over roughly 100 metres from an office lobby to a neighbouring-building store, including door traversal and static/dynamic obstacle avoidance.
Digital-twin adaptation improved closed-loop success in simulation before deployment; MELIOR also achieved competitive R2R-CE and RxR-CE results.

Figure 4. The generation pipeline of X-Nav-Syn. (1) Goal-pose sampling. We select target instances and sample goal poses that pass reachability, visibility, and clearance checks. (2) Offline planning. We sample start-goal pairs within route quotas, plan paths with A* on the occupancy grid, convert them to action sequences, and check the resulting routes. (3) Replay & annotation. We replay the reference routes to record RGB-D observations and camera poses. A vision–language model generates instructions. We derive action labels from the routes and navigation goal labels from the replayed poses and depth. We combine the observations, instructions, and labels into step samples.

On the robot, the goal adapter converts a navigation goal into a goal pose, and the obstacleavoidance layer passes it to the locomotion controller.

papers.abstract: Reward models are a core component of modern text-to-image systems, serving as the objective for inference-time selection and RL-based post-training. A key prerequisite is visual understanding: to judge prompt adherence and ground aesthetic preferences, a reward model must bind attributes, resolve relations, and count reliably. We find that widely-used reward models perform poorly on targeted visual reasoning evaluations. Even when starting from strong vision-language backbones, preference fine-tuning erodes these capabilities, and continual-learning baselines fail to mitigate a steep tradeoff between visual reasoning and preference accuracy. We propose a data-centric intervention that injects visual reasoning supervision into preference learning by flipping the pairing axis. To complement conventional human preference data (paired images under a shared prompt), we convert existing visual reasoning datasets into preference pairs that share the same image but differ in prompt, and train on the mixture. This yields a Pareto improvement in both visual understanding and preference prediction. Across inference-time best-of-n selection and RL post-training, the resulting reward model improves text-to-image generation on challenging compositional prompts (GenEval) by an average of 4.0% and 5.5% respectively, outperforming HPSv3 which was trained on 6x more preference pairs.

This produces a Pareto improvement in visual reasoning and preference prediction.
Generation improves on compositional GenEval prompts by 4.0% with best-of-n selection and 5.5% with RL post-training, outperforming HPSv3 despite using fewer preference pairs.

papers.abstract: Safety in robotics does not solely depend on geometric constraints, but also on semantics: the given task, environment properties, and interactions between objects in the scene. We present a framework based on vision-language models (VLMs) to infer task- and scene-dependent safety constraints for robot manipulation. We provide the VLM a structured safety tool based on an RGB-D observation and a natural-language task instruction that first decides whether the task should be rejected since its execution may result in a non-recoverable hazardous outcome. Otherwise, it identifies preventable object-pair hazards and specifies the spatial relations that must be avoided. Open-vocabulary segmentation and depth information are then used to ground the detected objects in 3D and construct continuous risk fields that represent the corresponding hazardous regions. These fields are integrated with an obstacle avoidance module that corrects nominal robot motions during execution while accounting for the risk field. We evaluate the framework on preventable hazards, tasks requiring rejection, and safe variants in simulation and the real-world. Project website: https://vlm-hazard-riskfield.github.io
authors: Mariana Sosa Guzm\'an, Yide Song, Amin Abyaneh, Gregory Dudek, Hsiu-Chin Lin

Integrates risk fields into obstacle avoidance to modify nominal robot motions during execution.
Evaluated in simulation and the real world on preventable hazards, rejection-required tasks, and safe task variants.

papers.abstract: Governments are writing rules for artificial intelligence that decide what counts as an automated decision or a harm, often before the people they affect have a chance to question them. We introduce AI-Voyager, a public-interest system for human-AI civic reasoning, in which people and AI work together to understand, contest and shape the rules that govern AI. A resident can find their city's rules on AI in hiring or upload their country's AI strategy, read it as an affected worker would, open the passage behind any answer, and draft a revision. Its architecture turns 3,653 governance documents from city, state, federal and national governments into passages that keep their page and edition, and retrieves evidence through bounded agentic search that verifies each statement. On 360 new questions that require finding the relevant documents, it reached 83.0% macro recall, against 80.5% for the strongest baseline, 73.7% without iterative search and 99.1% on a benchmark with fixed documents. In a study with 24 participants new to two AI bills, most proposed changes asked how provisions would apply. Participants chose lenses for the kind of explanation they wanted, and citations signaled grounding but rarely led them to check the source. By binding AI assistance to the exact text of public documents, this work introduces a grammar of operations and a design space that inform how such systems are designed and evaluated, and how people take part in governing AI.
authors: Snehalkumar `Neil' S. Gaikwad, Dhruv Dixit, Bryen Alvarez, Pratik Patekar, Anika Sharma, Akshara Kolipaka, Paritosh Pandey

(b) Voyager-RAG: For each question, the system identifies which documents are in scope, retrieves and fuses relevant passages, and assembles the evidence used to generate an answer. papers.abstract: A benchmark usually measures a language model alone with a question, and deployment rarely looks like that: answers get contested, and models give up correct ones under counter-reasoning that is itself wrong. We show that what fails there is not a shortfall of accuracy but a capability in its own right -- knowing when to hold a position and when to yield to a better one -- which we call dialectical competence. It stands on first-answer accuracy without following from it: a model can be made materially better at answering and no better at this, and training for accuracy alone can drift against it. Nor can it be bought at inference, by self-reflection or by sampling more. Taking a cue from the dialectical tradition in philosophy, in which productive opposition arises within a position rather than being imposed on it from outside, we hypothesize that this capability can be trained from opposition the model supplies itself. It states a position, generates the strongest case against that position -- its antithesis -- rules on whether the case stands, and is trained on that ruling, with no second model at training or at deployment. We call this learning through Self-Disagreement: reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards throughout, where the same check that scores an answer against its reference scores the ruling too, so no reward model, no preference data and no human annotation enter anywhere. The capability is trained rather than elicited: weak in the base model, it arrives with the reward, is not paid for out of first-answer accuracy, and holds against challengers the model never trained against, including ones stronger than itself. The opposition a model needs in order to improve, it turns out, need not come from outside it.
bullets: Introduces dialectical competence: maintaining a correct position against flawed challenges while yielding to better ones.
Argues this capability is distinct from first-answer accuracy and is not reliably obtained through self-reflection or additional sampling at inference.
Uses reinforcement learning in which the model states a position, generates an antithesis, and rules on whether it succeeds.
Employs verifiable rewards only, requiring no second model, reward model, preference data, or human annotation.
Reports that the capability emerges through training without sacrificing initial-answer accuracy and generalizes to unseen, including stronger, challengers.

papers.abstract: Machine learning in physical hardware promises to reduce training cost by colocating computation, memory and adaptation within device physics. Contrastive local learning networks (CLLNs) offer a compelling route: an electrical circuit relaxes to equilibrium in free and weakly clamped states, and each adaptive element updates from local voltage contrasts rather than backpropagated error signals. Yet whether nonlinear transistor implementations can scale beyond proof-of-concept circuits, and what design principles control that scaling, have remained unknown. Here we show that nonlinear analog circuits trained by contrastive local rules can learn larger machine-learning tasks and remain robust under hardware nonidealities. Using device-level circuit simulations, we systematically explore initialization, operating regime, loss-dependent clamping and training parameters, and scale CLLNs beyond ten thousand adaptive edges. The same local rule trains classifiers that reach the accuracy regime of conventional digital methods on Ionosphere and handwritten-digit benchmarks, and a network that autoregressively generates language over a 122-token vocabulary. These results establish the feasibility of local learning in large nonlinear analog circuits.
authors: Pragyan Pandey, Peter Wu, Deema Alyahya, Eric Y. Ma
bullets: Addresses whether transistor-based contrastive local learning networks can scale beyond small proof-of-concept circuits.
Uses device-level circuit simulations to study initialization, operating regime, clamping, and training parameters.
Shows robustness to hardware nonidealities and scaling beyond 10,000 adaptive edges.
Achieves the accuracy regime of conventional digital methods on Ionosphere and handwritten-digit classification benchmarks.
Demonstrates autoregressive language generation with a 122-token vocabulary.

papers.abstract: Multi-turn conversational human-robot interaction (HRI) continues to be a challenging problem in robotics, as many existing systems rely on rigid, command-driven interfaces that can be unintuitive for users. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) provide a promising direction, given their ability to process natural language, generate structured outputs, and support tool-based reasoning, all of which are relevant for interpreting user intent in robotic settings. However, progress in this area is constrained by the limited availability of datasets and benchmarks that capture the nuances of real-world human communication, such as multi-turn dialogue, ambiguity, and context-dependent requests. In this work, we present a synthetically generated multi-turn dialogue dataset for HRI, annotated with action intents, object references, and task plans across a range of scenarios and user personas. Our primary focus is on evaluating the capability of small, open-weight language models for robotic tasks, particularly in settings where local deployment and efficiency are important. To this end, we frame intent extraction as a tool-calling problem where each predicted action corresponds to a structured function call with arguments grounded in the dialogue and benchmark models ranging from 270M to 8B parameters on their ability to perform intent extraction and action planning without task-specific fine-tuning. Our results show that these models can achieve reasonable performance on the task even at relatively small scales and without any task-specific fine-tuning. This suggests that compact, locally deployable models already provide a useful baseline for conversational robotic systems. We expect that task-specific fine-tuning and more realistic training data will enhance performance further and make such models increasingly suitable for real-world robotic applications.
authors: Deepu Krishnareddy, Mohammad Haziq Khan, Michael Danner, Matthias R\"atsch
bullets: Addresses the limitations of rigid command-based robot interfaces and scarce datasets capturing ambiguity, context, and multi-turn dialogue.
Provides dialogues annotated with action intents, object references, and task plans across varied scenarios and user personas.
Frames intent extraction as structured tool calling, with actions represented as function calls grounded in dialogue context.
Evaluates open-weight models from 270M to 8B parameters for intent extraction and action planning.
Finds that even relatively small models achieve reasonable performance, while noting that fine-tuning and more realistic data may improve real-world suitability.

papers.abstract: Autonomous experimentation systems require characterization models that can interpret heterogeneous measurements and maintain predictive performance as data accumulate. Developing such models involves addressing domain mismatch between data sources, overconfident predictions on unfamiliar inputs, and catastrophic forgetting during sequential updates. In this work, we present a proof-of-concept framework for uncertainty-aware continual interpretation of two-dimensional X-ray diffraction (XRD) data. The framework integrates established components: maximum mean discrepancy-based domain adaptation to reduce simulation-to-experiment discrepancies, a convolutional neural network with a spectral-normalized neural Gaussian process (CNN--SNGP) for predictive uncertainty estimation, and replay with knowledge distillation for sequential model updating. We evaluate the framework using simulated and previously-collected experimental data for crystal structure classification of single-phase body-centered cubic, face-centered cubic, and hexagonal close-packed patterns. Data are organized into predefined sequential blocks to assess adaptation and retention of previously learned knowledge. Within this setting, the results show accurate classification across simulated and experimental data, improved alignment between the two domains, and reduced forgetting compared with na\"ive fine-tuning. Predictive uncertainty is also evaluated on unfamiliar and noisy inputs. The contribution is the integration and evaluation of these capabilities for sequential XRD interpretation. The framework provides a basis for future integration into autonomous experimentation systems, with experimental planning, instrument control, and closed-loop deployment remaining areas for future development.
authors: Zihan Wang, Hyun Sang Park, Ali Rachidi, David Elbert, Todd C. Hufnagel, Wei Chen
bullets: Targets simulation-to-experiment mismatch, overconfident predictions on unfamiliar inputs, and catastrophic forgetting.
Uses MMD-based domain adaptation, a CNN-SNGP for predictive uncertainty, and replay with knowledge distillation for updates.
Evaluated crystal-structure classification for BCC, FCC, and HCP patterns using simulated and previously collected experimental data in sequential blocks.
Reports accurate cross-domain classification, improved domain alignment, reduced forgetting versus naive fine-tuning, and uncertainty evaluation on unfamiliar/noisy inputs.
Scope is proof-of-concept; experimental planning, instrument control, and closed-loop deployment remain future work.

papers.abstract: Image-goal planning with a frozen visual world model depends on how predicted observations are scored against the goal. Mean-squared error (MSE) between embeddings from a pretrained visual encoder can provide a useful signal near a goal, yet favor states across an obstacle that are visually similar to the goal and difficult to reach. We fit a small residual adapter on top of frozen I-JEPA embeddings to improve this latent goal cost. Starting near each goal, a planner collects trajectories from progressively wider regions of initial states. The adapter learns from the order of observations along successful trajectories, with additional comparisons inferred from failed rollouts. No task-specific progress labels are used for fitting, so the procedure can be applied to other goal-reaching tasks. DotWall and PointMaze are used in this work. In paired 50-case evaluations with identical starts, goals, world models, and planner settings, success increases from 54% to 98% in DotWall and from 82% to 96% in PointMaze. On 16 unseen DotWall layout-goal cases, the adapter fitted on one fixed layout improves agreement between latent-cost ordering and shortest legal-path ordering from 71.9% to 85.8%. The results indicate that planning experience can improve a frozen visual representation's goal cost without retraining the encoder or the world model.
bullets: MSE in pretrained visual embeddings can favor visually similar but obstructed states.
A residual adapter is trained on trajectory orderings from progressively broader starts, using failed rollouts for extra comparisons and no task-specific progress labels.
In paired evaluations, success rises from 54% to 98% on DotWall and from 82% to 96% on PointMaze.
On unseen DotWall layout-goal cases, agreement with shortest legal-path ordering improves from 71.9% to 85.8%.
The approach is evaluated on DotWall and PointMaze and depends on planning experience to adapt the goal cost.

papers.abstract: Quantization lets language models run on edge devices, but it sharply increases the number of tensor kernels a library must maintain: every weight format must be paired with every activation format on every instruction set and GPU, with an encoder and a decoder that agree on the stored bytes. In GGML, the tensor library used by llama.cpp, these kernels are written by hand, and only 8 of the 54 weight-activation pairs it runs on our Arm CPU have a tiled matrix-multiplication kernel. We extend Halide's separation of algorithm and schedule to the representation of values. Each approximation is a codec, an encoder paired with a decoder, composed from reusable units: quantizers, integer representations, bit packers and layouts. A new directive, approximate_by, applies a codec to one stage of a program and returns the encoder and decoder as ordinary stages that Halide can schedule, so both decoders fuse into the register tiles of a matrix product. Optional contracts, such as a round-trip law, are checked by property tests; the law exposed an inconsistent block sum in GGML's q8_1. One algorithm and one schedule library generate 347 kernels for 31 of GGML's and KleidiAI's formats on Arm CPUs and Apple GPUs, covering 38 weight-activation pairs for which GGML has no kernel, in 3.7x less code than GGML and KleidiAI. On an Apple M3 Max, our kernels reach at least 95% of the speed of GGML's format-specific kernels in 91.0% of the cases that have one, with a median speedup of 1.13x, and are faster still where GGML falls back to blocked dot products. Counting Apple's BLAS library, which is usually faster for larger f32 products, we still reach that threshold in 86.9% of CPU cases. A port to x86 with Intel's AMX adds 793 lines of code and matches GGML in 83.5% of its cases.
bullets: Quantization creates a combinatorial kernel-maintenance problem across weight formats, activation formats, and hardware targets.
The approach represents approximations as composable encoder–decoder codecs and exposes them to Halide scheduling via `approximate_by`, enabling decoder fusion into matrix-multiplication tiles.
Property-tested contracts can detect format inconsistencies, including an issue in GGML’s `q8_1` block sum.
The system generates 347 kernels for 31 formats, covering 38 Arm CPU and Apple GPU pairs lacking GGML kernels, using 3.7× less code than GGML and KleidiAI.
Performance reaches at least 95% of format-specific GGML kernels in 91.0% of applicable Apple M3 Max cases; an x86/AMX port matches GGML in 83.5% of cases.

papers.abstract: This paper presents a multifidelity (MF) formulation of Operator Inference (OpInf) for learning non-intrusive, physics-based reduced-order models (ROMs) of nonlinear dynamical systems. OpInf learns reduced operators from projections of snapshot data by solving a least squares regression problem. However, generating high-fidelity snapshots can be computationally expensive, limiting parameter coverage and the temporal extent of training trajectories for many aerospace applications, which can lead to inaccurate or unstable ROM predictions. This work proposes MF-OpInf, which combines limited high-fidelity snapshots with more plentiful low-fidelity snapshots through a control-variates-inspired MF least squares formulation to learn a single set of reduced operators across multiple trajectories. Low-fidelity trajectories provide additional parameter coverage and extend beyond the high-fidelity training time horizon. The low-fidelity snapshots are also used to construct an improved reduced basis through weighted proper orthogonal decomposition. We demonstrate MF-OpInf on a nonlinear reaction-diffusion problem with parametrized sinusoidal forcing and a two-dimensional incompressible flow past a cylinder with a parametrized inlet pulse. In these experiments, under an equal training simulation budget, MF-OpInf reduces the mean relative prediction error at unseen parameters by up to $87\%$ for the reaction-diffusion problem and $28\%$ for the cylinder flow problem over the test time regime, which extends beyond the high-fidelity training time horizon. These results demonstrate that MF-OpInf can improve temporal extrapolation and prediction at unseen parameters without increasing the training simulation budget.
authors: Vignesh Sella, Anirban Chaudhuri, Karen Willcox
bullets: Addresses the cost of generating high-fidelity snapshots, which limits parameter coverage and training time horizons.
Uses a control-variates-inspired multifidelity least-squares formulation to learn one set of reduced operators across trajectories.
Incorporates low-fidelity data into a weighted POD basis to improve the reduced representation.
Demonstrated on parametrized reaction-diffusion and cylinder-flow problems, improving unseen-parameter prediction errors by up to 87% and 28%, respectively.
Improves temporal extrapolation beyond the high-fidelity training horizon under an equal training simulation budget.

papers.abstract: Recommendation and Ranking (R&R) models, particularly in digital advertising, require massive inference throughput but exhibit extreme sensitivity to precision loss. Unlike Large Language Models (LLMs) that frequently tolerate quantization-induced accuracy drops of 1% or more, production-grade R&R models enforce a stringent launch bar: model quality must remain within a 0.01% Normalized Entropy (NE) margin relative to the baseline, which commonly uses FP16 or FP32. This tight constraint has historically hindered the adoption of aggressive quantization in this domain. In this paper, we present an empirical evaluation of both MXFP8 and the 6-bit MXFP6 format for industrial-scale R&R inference on the AMD MI350X architecture. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first paper, across R&R and LLM domains, that reports significant speedups from native MXFP6 GEMMs, which quantize both weights and activations and compute directly on 6-bit elements, without sacrificing model quality. We demonstrate that we can selectively apply this 6-bit format to maximize overall QPS gain without breaching the strict NE parity threshold. We further show that MXFP8 is a viable alternative to row-wise FP8: the two formats have nearly the same accuracy on our models, so the faster kernel can be chosen for each GEMM shape. On two production ads ranking models, our implementation shows measured GEMM kernel speedups over FP16 of 1.33--1.55x for MXFP8 and 1.73--1.99x for MXFP6 across all supported linear layers, and up to 2.90x for MXFP6 on individual layers, alongside end-to-end (E2E) inference throughput gains from selective MXFP6 of 1.5--5.3% for Model A and 7.6--14.3% for Model B over their FP8 configurations.
authors: Yavuz Yetim, Bor-Yiing Su, Zhe Wang, Arthur Liu, Pranav Sharma, Ying Wang, Randy Shuai, Luke Pfister, Ruichao Xiao, Bill Zhao, Zihao Liu, Liyuan Li, Jiangyuan Li, Gaoxiang Liu, Nathan Yan, Geonhwa Jeong, Jatin Chhugani, Elias Ellison, Uladzimir Pashkevich
bullets: R&R models need very high throughput but tolerate almost no quantization-induced quality loss: NE must stay within 0.01% of baseline.
The study evaluates MXFP8 and 6-bit MXFP6 on AMD MI350X, including native MXFP6 GEMMs that quantize weights and activations and compute directly on 6-bit elements.
Selective MXFP6 achieves end-to-end throughput gains of 1.5–5.3% on Model A and 7.6–14.3% on Model B relative to FP8 configurations.
Across supported linear layers, MXFP8 GEMMs are 1.33–1.55× faster than FP16, while MXFP6 reaches 1.73–1.99× and up to 2.90× on individual layers.
MXFP8 provides accuracy nearly equivalent to row-wise FP8, allowing the faster format to be selected by GEMM shape.

papers.abstract: Activation steering influences a language model's behaviour by adding a steering vector to its residual stream during generation, but it requires white-box access to modify the hidden states at every generation step. We introduce ActGCG, a modification of Greedy Coordinate Gradient which optimises a suffix to match the target activations obtained by adding a steering vector to the residual stream. We further introduce universal suffixes trained across many prompts at once, a model-translation step that rewrites the suffix into human-readable text midway through optimisation, and a soft-suffix variant to remove the discrete token space constraint. We study two behaviours: steering a model to answer in German, and anti-refusal steering for jailbreaking. For German, a discrete suffix reproduces the steering vector's behaviour almost perfectly and transfers well across prompts and models. For anti-refusal, the equivalence is weaker, succeeding under a phrase-avoidance metric but only partially under the stricter HarmBench classifier. Our results show that a steering vector's behaviour is reachable from the input, with no access to model internals at generation time, up to a loss that depends on the concept being steered.
bullets: Targets behaviors produced by adding steering vectors to a model’s residual stream.
Uses Greedy Coordinate Gradient to optimize discrete suffixes, including universal suffixes across prompts.
Adds model translation for human-readable intermediate suffixes and a soft-suffix variant beyond discrete tokens.

Anti-refusal steering is weaker: it succeeds on phrase avoidance but only partially under HarmBench.

papers.abstract: Ensembles of neural networks have repeatedly been shown to outperform single networks. Ensemble theory attributes this gain to the accuracy of the individual members and the diversity among them. Mixture-of-experts models already combine many experts, but a single router decides how the experts are weighted for each input. Motivated by ensemble theory, we apply ensembling to the routing step: an ensemble of routers, trained jointly with the experts, proposes the expert weights. We systematically evaluate this approach using underparameterized networks on two image-classification and two tabular-regression tasks. We analyse each experiment with a performance-diversity decomposition of the router ensemble, which, to our knowledge, has not previously been developed for routers. We report four findings. First, more routers lower the validation loss. Second, training routers to explicitly maximize expert diversity improves the mean performance on three of the four tasks. Third, explicitly maximizing router diversity has no effect on performance. Fourth, combining router weights with the arithmetic mean works better than combining them with the geometric mean. Routing benefits mildly from ensembling, but this benefit is offset by the computational cost of training additional routers.
bullets: The study replaces a single MoE router with an ensemble of jointly trained routers that proposes expert weights.
Experiments cover two image-classification and two tabular-regression tasks using underparameterized networks.
More routers reduce validation loss, while explicitly maximizing expert diversity improves mean performance on three of four tasks.
Explicitly maximizing router diversity does not improve performance; arithmetic averaging of router weights outperforms geometric averaging.
A performance–diversity decomposition is introduced to analyze router ensembles.

papers.abstract: Diffusion-based generative models have become strong priors over plausible crystal structures, but turning that prior into promising candidates requires steering toward several conflicting properties at once. Fine-tuning is expensive and produces a new model for every new objective, while differentiable guidance is not applicable to many real-world tasks. We instead adapt these generative models at inference time using Diffusion Tree Sampling (DTS), a Monte Carlo tree search procedure over the denoising trajectory. We make two technical contributions on top of DTS that are particularly relevant for AI-for-science applications. First, we show how to use existing property-conditional generative models (e.g., models fine-tuned for classifier-free guidance) as guided proposals inside DTS, without distorting the target distribution. Second, we extend DTS to multi-objective sampling, so that a single search produces samples spanning an entire Pareto front. We instantiate both adaptations on de novo crystal generation: improving the stability of crystals generated by different models, using pretrained conditional models to generate crystals belonging to rare space groups or with high bulk modulus, and generating crystals along a Pareto front of high dielectric constant and high bandgap materials. Across these tasks, DTS-based inference-time adaptation successfully improves model outputs without modifying the models themselves.
authors: Daniel T. Levy, Vineet Jain, Tara Akhound-Sadegh, S\'ekou-Oumar Kaba, Siamak Ravanbakhsh

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the method. (a): DTS treats intermediate states of denoising diffusion as nodes in a tree, and steers sampling towards a reward-tilted distribution. Each node is attached to an estimate of expected reward (denoted here by node size). (b): We may use a different model qc that gives better denoising proposals, but we need to correct its influence by reweighting nodes by the proposal’s ratio with the base model. (c): In the multi-objective setting, we wish to sample from a distribution obtained by integrating reward-tilted distributions over different preferences between objectives. (d): We use a single DTS tree to sample from this multi-objective target, conditioning each pass through the tree on a different preference.

papers.abstract: Current evaluations of Large Language Models (LLMs) report performance at the dataset or task level, revealing what a model achieves but offering little insight into the internal processing associated with its performance. We propose a task-centric framework for characterising the model-internal processing elicited by a benchmark. It combines attention- and activation-based signals with representation-based measures to characterise benchmarks spanning a continuum from retrieval-dominant to reasoning-dominant and to surface failure modes that task-level scores conceal. We evaluate 16 LLMs across 24 diverse benchmarks and conduct targeted internal-state analyses on representative models and tasks, observing systematic differences in processing between knowledge-centric and reasoning-centric tasks. We shift evaluation from asking what score a model achieves toward characterising the processing patterns associated with that score, potentially supporting more targeted benchmark selection and more informed model choice. We open source our code at https://github.com/extraordinarylab/trace-kr.
authors: Yang Wang, Xiao Wang, Yiqi Liu, Chenghao Xiao, Eleni Vasilaki, Goran Nenadic, Chenghua Lin
bullets: Combines attention, activation, and representation-based signals to characterize benchmark-induced processing.
Evaluates 16 LLMs across 24 diverse benchmarks.
Finds systematic processing differences between knowledge-centric and reasoning-centric tasks.
Uses internal-state analyses to reveal patterns and failures beyond task-level performance.

papers.abstract: A rescue robot entering a building with thirty seconds on the clock should sprint toward the single most promising room; given ten minutes, it should instead explore a broader tour. Yet vision-language-navigation (VLN) models are typically evaluated under a fixed episode limit that the policy never observes, even though time-critical missions require behavior to adapt to the available budget. We study budget-conditioned object search: given a target category and an explicit action budget, an agent must find as many distinct target instances as possible before the budget expires. We investigate how to supervise VLNs for this task by comparing a privileged TSP expert, which plans near-optimal routes using the full map and true target locations, with a room-level Bellman expert that maximizes expected return under partial observability using high-level cross-scene semantic priors. Despite the TSP expert achieving substantially higher expert performance, its demonstrations are less effective for learning exploration: on held-out HM3D scenes, the Bellman-supervised VLN consistently outperforms the TSP-supervised VLN, with the advantage becoming more pronounced at longer budgets. At 2000 steps (500m), the Bellman-supervised VLN finds 71.4% of reachable target instances, compared with 65.5% for the TSP-supervised VLN and 44.8% for the pretrained VLN. These results highlight a distinction between optimal routing and optimal exploration: effective exploration supervision should optimize decisions under partial observability rather than imitate routes that are optimal only once the environment is fully known.
authors: Maitree Meher, Siming He, S. Shankar Sastry, Jitendra Malik, Claire Tomlin, Jonas Frey
bullets: Studies object search where agents must find as many distinct targets as possible within an explicit action budget.

At 2,000 steps, Bellman-supervised VLN finds 71.4% of reachable targets versus 65.5% for TSP supervision and 44.8% for pretrained VLN.
The findings distinguish optimal routing in known environments from effective exploration under uncertainty, especially at longer budgets.

papers.abstract: Improving a pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) model requires demonstrations that address its weaknesses and provide effective supervision for learning. Coding agents can autonomously generate demonstrations through environment interaction, yet successful execution alone does not ensure effective supervision for VLA learning. We introduce Agentic-Teacher, an autonomous data engine for failure-driven VLA post-training. Given a VLA checkpoint, a task specification, and configured environment tools, the engine analyzes failed rollouts, selects intervention states, and iteratively develops closed-loop code policies through execution feedback. Validated policies become reusable demonstration generators that collect successful continuations from states where the VLA struggles. To make these demonstrations suitable for learning, Agentic-Teacher introduces temporally correlated action noise to broaden state-action coverage, removes idle frames while preserving gripper transitions, and filters trajectories using the frozen base model's flow-matching loss. The resulting demonstrations are combined with successful VLA rollouts for post-training, yielding an updated policy that operates without coding-agent assistance. Agentic-Teacher thus connects the weaknesses of a target VLA to both the generation and curation of its training data. In simulation, it improves $\pi_0$ success rates from 79.4% to 87.8% on LIBERO-10, from 80.4% to 90.6% on MetaWorld-10, and from 0% to 30.0% across three RoboCasa tasks.

Uses execution-feedback-driven coding agents to develop closed-loop policies that generate successful continuations.

Combines generated demonstrations with successful VLA rollouts, producing an updated policy that no longer requires coding-agent assistance.
In simulation, raises success from 79.4% to 87.8% on LIBERO-10, 80.4% to 90.6% on MetaWorld-10, and 0% to 30.0% across three RoboCasa tasks.

papers.abstract: Large language models are expensive to update through full retraining. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning reduces the cost of adaptation, but repeated adaptation creates a growing pool of task-specific LoRA adapters. This pool complicates adapter selection during inference. Existing routing and encoder-based methods often require retraining when new adapters are added, which limits their use in dynamic settings. This paper treats adapter routing as a representation alignment problem in the adapter-output space. The proposed training-free method selects adapters by matching adapter-conditioned query representations against task prototypes using cosine similarity. Experiments with LLaMA-2-7B and LLaMA-2-13B on a 48-task FLAN-v2 benchmark and on out-of-distribution tasks show that the method outperforms training-free baselines in the cross-task setting and approaches a trained retrieval encoder without learning a router. An ablation confirms the benefit of directional alignment in the adapter-output space.
authors: Inish Melroy D Souza, Tom Jackson, Vitor Castro, Rebecca Higginson, Andrea Soltoggio
bullets: Addresses adapter-selection challenges as pools of task-specific LoRA modules grow dynamically.
Matches adapter-conditioned query representations to task prototypes using cosine similarity.
Avoids retraining when new adapters are added, unlike many routing or encoder-based methods.
Outperforms training-free baselines on cross-task FLAN-v2 evaluations and performs near a trained retrieval encoder, including on out-of-distribution tasks.
Ablation results support the value of directional alignment in adapter-output space.

papers.abstract: LLM memory systems often delete facts classified as stale. We show that this hard-filtering step can reduce downstream accuracy when resolver errors delete query-critical facts. Across three models, a controlled sensitivity intervention moves hard-drop from gains of +0.186 to +0.230 at perfect resolution to losses of -0.176 to -0.181 at the lowest tested reliability. Paired targeted interventions show that false-drop causes significantly greater degradation than false-keep, while a non-deleting baseline can still fail when incorrect labels steer generation. On a frozen 102/102 calibration/test split, a simple deployment-matched gate reaches 0.655 accuracy versus 0.641 for always hard-drop and 0.662 for test-informed oracle selection. Global-accuracy crossovers require gold labels and are model- and task-specific diagnostics, not deployment thresholds. Deletion should instead be treated as cost-sensitive: validate query-critical false-drop risk on matched data, or default to label-free retention when such validation is unavailable.
bullets: Resolver errors can reverse hard-drop’s benefit, turning accuracy gains into losses.
False-dropping critical facts is more damaging than falsely keeping stale ones.
Non-deleting memory can still fail when incorrect labels steer generation.
A deployment-matched gate achieved 0.655 accuracy, below the 0.662 test-informed oracle and above the 0.641 always-drop baseline.
Deletion should be treated as a cost-sensitive decision and validated on matched data.

papers.abstract: Most AI assistants respond only when prompted, remaining silent even when events in the video stream offer meaningful opportunities for conversation. To move beyond purely user-driven interaction, we present AURA 2.0, a streaming video large language model that introduces three core upgrades to AURA. The key advance is Model-Initiated Conversation (MIC), which enables the model to identify topics worth discussing in the evolving visual stream and initiate conversations at appropriate moments without a user query. Stream-Aware Tool Calling (SATC) enables the model to invoke external tools using the current visual and conversational context and incorporate returned information into the ongoing interaction. Interactive Visual Grounding (IVG) supports visual grounding in both user inputs and model outputs. The model can identify objects marked by users on video frames and produce frame-aligned bounding boxes to link its responses to specific objects and regions. To develop these capabilities, we construct a dedicated streaming interaction dataset and adopt a three-stage training scheme to integrate the new behaviors with AURA's existing streaming interaction abilities. We further incorporate Long-Horizon Interaction Memory (LHIM) to maintain contextual continuity over extended video streams. Evaluations on public streaming benchmarks show that AURA 2.0 achieves leading performance among open-source streaming models, while targeted evaluations further validate its new interaction capabilities. We open-source the model weights and inference code.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of assistants that respond only after user prompts.
Introduces Model-Initiated Conversation, Stream-Aware Tool Calling, and Interactive Visual Grounding.
Adds Long-Horizon Interaction Memory for continuity across extended video streams.
Uses a dedicated streaming interaction dataset and three-stage training scheme to integrate these behaviors.
Reports leading performance among open-source streaming models on public benchmarks and releases model weights and inference code.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the AURA 2.0 streaming interaction framework. The model incrementally processes video chunks together with user inputs and interaction history, producing either <|silent|> for silent observation or <|respond|> followed by a text response or tool call. Tool results are incorporated into the context to support subsequent responses. Dashed outlines indicate historical messages beyond the active visual window.

Figure 3. Data construction pipeline for AURA 2.0. The pipeline transforms collected videos into a verified streaming training mixture through three stages: (1) Video collection and preparation standardizes videos into clips and generates clip-level descriptions. (2) Task-specific data synthesis uses the clips and descriptions to construct General QA, MIC, SATC, and IVG trajectories. (3) Streaming assembly and quality assessment aligns the trajectories to video chunks and filters invalid or low-quality samples.

(b) Stage-wise sample and token allocations and silent/response decision proportions. (c) Task-wise sample counts and shares aggregated across stages. Together, these distributions characterize the task coverage and supervision balance of the training mixture.
