papers.abstract: Existing adaptive-reasoning methods shorten the explicit reasoning a model writes, or skip it by switching modes; either way the answer is still written out token by token. \emph{Rather than deciding how much to think}, we explore a different paradigm, \emph{zero-or-$T$ thinking}: a single model either answers from the implicit thinking inside one forward pass, generating no token, or performs full autoregressive reasoning at a cost of $T$ tokens when that is worth paying. We realise it in a \emph{hybrid decision model} (HDM), where one frozen backbone serves both modes and a lightweight \emph{self-routing block} chooses between them. The block estimates the \emph{value of thinking}, the utility the slow mode is expected to add over the fast one, from what that implicit thinking has already produced, and the slow mode runs only where that value exceeds a price $λ$ set per request. Where no per-decision label exists, as in episodic agentic tasks, we introduce \emph{Calibrated Decision Policy Optimisation} (CDPO), a reinforcement-learning recipe that trains the block from episode-level returns. We evaluate HDM on MMLU-Pro, AGIEval, GPQA-Diamond, JevBench, BANKING77 and MiniWoB. Specifically, on JevBench HDM-4B scores $0.857$ against Jev's $0.851$ ($+0.7\%$) at a median $0.179$\,s against $0.652$ ($-72.5\%$). On the agentic venue MiniWoB HDM-27B cuts token cost by $80.1\%$.
bullets: Introduces zero-or-T thinking: each request either uses one-pass implicit reasoning or pays for full token-by-token reasoning.
A lightweight self-routing block estimates the value of additional thinking and compares it with a request-specific price λ.
For episodic agentic tasks without per-decision labels, CDPO trains routing decisions from episode-level returns.
On JevBench, HDM-4B slightly outperforms Jev while reducing median latency by 72.5%.
On MiniWoB, HDM-27B reduces token cost by 80.1%.

papers.abstract: As GPU accelerators grow larger to meet rising compute demands, they exhibit increasingly pronounced non-uniform memory access (NUMA) characteristics that challenge existing LLM frameworks. Chiplet-based architectures provide a practical path to larger GPUs while mitigating manufacturing yield constraints. Modern GPUs such as AMD Instinct MI300X employs such a multi-die design, and further offer GPU partitioning capabilities, partitioning a single physical GPU into multiple logical devices with NUMA-aware memory domains, promising faster kernel launches, and reduced memory access latencies with improved locality. However, current parallelization strategies, designed for homogeneous GPU topologies, when applied under partitioning, extend its unidimensional sharding causing significant performance degradation. Three bottlenecks emerge: (1) memory redundancy; (2) arithmetic intensity collapse; (3) communication overhead from flat collectives. We present Starscream, a rethinking of LLM sharding for the chiplet era. Rather than stretching inter-GPU sharding thinner, Starscream adds intra-GPU sharding along an orthogonal dimension, grounded in three foundational principles: kernel shape preservation, memory redundancy elimination, and communication overhead minimization. These principles form the basis for extending any sharding strategy into the partitioning regime. We demonstrate their effectiveness using tensor parallelism as a case study. On AMD MI300X and MI355X, exploiting partitioning capabilities yields up to 4x speedup for attention and 1.43x for fused GEMMs compared to chiplet-oblivious baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of chiplet-aware designs. Starscream's principles generalize across sharding strategies and future architectures.
bullets: Targets performance losses caused by applying homogeneous-GPU sharding to NUMA-aware GPU partitions.
Addresses memory redundancy, reduced arithmetic intensity, and communication overhead from flat collectives.
Uses orthogonal intra-GPU sharding based on kernel shape preservation, redundancy elimination, and communication minimization.
Demonstrated with tensor parallelism on AMD MI300X and MI355X, achieving up to 4× attention and 1.43× fused-GEMM speedups.
The principles are intended to generalize to other sharding strategies and future chiplet-based architectures.

papers.abstract: Industrial inspection robots must reach work areas and specific equipment. These destinations span spatial scales from regions to objects, so robots must relate each target to its surroundings to interpret the task and determine where to go. Existing methods support multi-scale navigation through rich environment representations, but at substantial computational and storage cost. These costs limit deployment where wireless coverage is incomplete and robots must rely on onboard computation to keep navigating. We introduce EMS-Nav, a biologically inspired multi-scale navigation framework for online, on-device operation. Its core innovation is to organize perception, spatial understanding, and navigation around regions, making local spaces the basic units of both environmental understanding and computation. EMS-Nav groups objects and their relationships into functionally meaningful spaces and builds a hierarchy from local areas to the broader environment. This organization supports efficient map construction alongside the interpretation and execution of language goals at different scales. In multi-scale navigation experiments, EMS-Nav achieves the highest success rates across all four target categories: objects, rooms, regions, and specific instances. It outperforms state-of-the-art open-vocabulary mapping and navigation methods, improving overall first-attempt success by 9.39 percentage points over the strongest baseline while reducing mapping overhead and language-model input size. Local deployment in real indoor environments further demonstrates its applicability to on-device embodied navigation. By establishing regions as the organizing basis for perception, spatial understanding, and language-guided action, EMS-Nav provides a system that combines multi-scale understanding with computational efficiency to support diverse language goals on resource-constrained robots.
bullets: Addresses the computational and storage costs of rich environment representations for industrial inspection robots operating with limited connectivity.
Builds a hierarchical representation from local areas to the broader environment, grouping objects and relationships into meaningful regions.
Supports online map construction and language-guided navigation for objects, rooms, regions, and specific instances.
Achieves the highest success rates across all four target categories and improves first-attempt success by 9.39 percentage points over the strongest baseline.
Real indoor deployments demonstrate applicability to resource-constrained, on-device embodied navigation.

papers.abstract: Imitation policies can perform complex manipulation, yet small execution errors can accumulate and cause failure. Refinement can correct these errors, but existing approaches often require additional on-policy learning or costly online planning. Our key insight is that a pretrained policy already supplies a useful nominal behavior: refinement can focus on predicting how small action corrections change its outcome. We therefore learn this local response in a form that is cheap to optimize. Our \textit{action-affine world model} (A\textsuperscript{2}WM) learns local action sensitivities offline from action-perturbed policy rollouts. Given interaction history and a policy proposal, it predicts task-relevant geometry as a nominal trajectory plus a linear response to corrections. It predicts the full planning horizon directly, avoiding the propagation of intermediate errors through recursive model evaluations. Quadratic penalties on predicted task errors and linear correction constraints then yield a cheap convex quadratic program (QP). Online refinement requires one model evaluation and one QP solve, while both policy and model weights remain frozen. Across four simulated manipulation tasks, our framework achieves the highest success rate among evaluated baselines, adding only 3.8 ms of mean refinement overhead per control step, excluding base-policy sampling.
bullets: Addresses execution errors that accumulate in imitation-based manipulation.
Learns local action sensitivities offline from action-perturbed policy rollouts.
Predicts full-horizon task geometry as nominal behavior plus linear action corrections.
Performs refinement with one model evaluation and one QP solve while keeping policy and model weights frozen.
Achieves the highest success rate among evaluated baselines across four simulated tasks, with 3.8 ms mean overhead per control step excluding policy sampling.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of fast inference-time policy refinement. A frozen base policy generates action proposals every K control steps. At each control step, the action-affine world model uses interaction history and the current proposal to predict a nominal trajectory Z̄ and a causal action-response matrix F , yielding the direct multi-step prediction Ẑ = F∆A+ Z̄. With F and Z̄ fixed, quadratic task costs and linear correction bounds define a convex QP over ∆A. The first optimized correction is applied to the base action, and refinement repeats after the next observation. Both the base policy and world model remain frozen during deployment.

Fig. 1. (a) Success rate comparison across four simulated manipulation tasks. Our method achieves the highest observed success rate on each task among the evaluated refinement methods, tying GPC-OPT on PushT. (b) Success–latency trade-off. Our method achieves the highest taskaveraged success rate with only a modest increase in mean per-control-step inference time over the frozen diffusion policy (DP). Inference time includes both policy sampling and online refinement. GPC-QP is our baseline that linearizes the GPC world model around the action proposal via its Jacobian and solves a quadratic program for refinement.

papers.abstract: Interactive 3D segmentation models such as nnInteractive turn a few spatial prompts (points, scribbles, boxes) into accurate volumetric masks, but a human still does the annotation work: finding each structure, placing prompts, checking the result and correcting it. General-purpose AI agents can now interpret images, call tools and write code. We show that such agents can take over this work without additional training: the user makes a request in plain language, and the agent works out what has to be segmented, locates the targets, prompts nnInteractive, inspects the 3D result, corrects it and responds to feedback. Asked for 'the muscles used for chewing', an agent identifies and segments the masseters and pterygoids; asked to count liver lesions, it writes its own code to find candidates and splits a merged lesion on request. Our open-source nninteractive-agent provides nnInteractive as tools over the Model Context Protocol (MCP), together with a skill that encodes how experienced users prompt it. On a benchmark spanning CT, MRI, PET and micro-CT of humans, a mouse and an ant (14 images; 51 targets from organs and tumours to muscles, foot bones, vessel trees and an insect brain), Claude Code and Codex reach a mean Dice of 0.81 and 0.84 from the request alone; when told where each target is, both reach 0.85 and prompt nearly as effectively as an oracle that places prompts using the reference segmentation. A text-prompted 3D model (VoxTell) is more accurate on most standard radiological targets but less robust: it returns an empty mask for one of them and fails on the leg muscles, the foot bones, the mouse and the ant, where the agents remain accurate. papers.abstract: Physical plausibility is essential for realistic video generation. Existing methods impose physical guidance before synthesis via simulations or refined prompts, but this can limit dynamic diversity, miss errors that emerge only after generation, and require repeated regeneration when inconsistencies remain. We therefore study a generate-diagnose-repair paradigm that preserves the original generation capability and selectively repairs physical inconsistencies afterward, raising two key questions: what to repair and how to repair? To address them, we introduce PhysRepair, an agentic video generation framework that combines causal reasoning over the observed physical failure with prior repair experience to enable localized and adaptive correction. Specifically, Spatiotemporal Causal Constraints identify the first invalid physical state and its causally affected states, producing a repair specification that guides physically plausible local regeneration while preserving unaffected content. Experience-augmented In-context Learning combines the ongoing repair context with relevant experience from previous repairs, allowing the agent to adapt its repair decisions across diverse physical failures and accumulate completed trajectories for future cases. Experiments on Physics-IQ Verified across solid mechanics, fluid dynamics, optics, thermodynamics, and magnetism demonstrate that PhysRepair consistently improves the physical plausibility of generated videos over existing methods. Our project page is available at https://xxkkxxx.github.io/PhysRepair-Website/.
bullets: Addresses failures that emerge after video generation without requiring full regeneration.
Uses Spatiotemporal Causal Constraints to identify the first invalid state and affected downstream states.
Applies localized, adaptive regeneration while preserving unaffected content.
Combines repair context with prior repair experiences through in-context learning.
Improves physical plausibility across solid mechanics, fluid dynamics, optics, thermodynamics, and magnetism on Physics-IQ Verified.

(c) PhysRepair instead follows a generate–diagnose–repair paradigm: it diagnoses physical failures from the generated video (what to repair?) and performs localized, causally constrained repair, while leveraging prior repair experience to adapt the intervention and preserve generated already-valid content (how to repair?).

papers.abstract: In this paper we study the behavior of transformer networks generating text over long periods of time. We show that even a three-token, single-layer attention-only transformer can fail to converge. We then study a rich class of transformers with arbitrary finite depth, layer normalization, MLPs, RoPE encodings, and an arbitrary mix of local and global layers. Every transformer in this class has a softmax temperature threshold above which its empirical cache distribution converges to a unique limit, independent of initial conditions. We show further that, while each transformer has a temperature threshold, the supremum of this set is infinite, so there is no global minimal temperature that forces all transformers to converge.
bullets: Even a three-token, single-layer attention-only transformer can fail to converge.
For a broad class—including finite-depth networks with layer normalization, MLPs, RoPE, and mixed local/global attention—sufficiently high softmax temperature ensures convergence.
Above each model’s threshold, the limiting cache distribution is unique and independent of initialization.
Although every transformer has a threshold, thresholds are unbounded across the class, so no universal temperature guarantees convergence for all models.

figures.caption: Figure 1: A stripped-down model of a transformer with NoPE, no MLPs, and an unbounded context window parameterized by historical distribution Pt.

Figure 2: A two-token example illustrating the temperature transition: x = 2p − 1 and dx/dt = tanh((a/τ)x) − x. For τ > a, the uniform state is the unique globally attracting equilibrium. For τ < a, it becomes unstable and two symmetric stable equilibria appear.

Figure 3: Phase portrait of the three-token example in Section 4, with c = 7. The unique equilibrium P̄ = (1/3, 1/3, 1/3) is a repelling focus. The teal curve is a numerically computed attracting periodic orbit of the limiting ODE. Trajectories starting inside (orange) and outside (gray) the orbit spiral toward it in a counterclockwise direction. The shaded sectors indicate the most probable next token: red for token 1, green for token 2, and blue for token 3. The trajectories represent the limiting deterministic dynamics, not individual stochastic sample paths.

papers.title: Asymptotic Behavior of Transformers
papers.tldr: The paper characterizes when transformers generating text indefinitely converge to a stable empirical cache distribution, and shows the required temperature depends on the architecture.

papers.abstract: An embodied brain, or System 2, must turn an abstract goal into actions while discovering relevant scene conditions and checking whether executed skills achieved their intended effects. Open-loop evaluations cannot test observations shaped by an agent's decisions, while some closed-loop evaluations provide limited evidence during execution or assume idealized skill outcomes. We introduce SCOPER, a suite for studying observation-grounded planning, execution, and recovery. SCOPER-bench combines high-level goals, ongoing visual observations, a shared rule-based System 1 for low-level actions, and controlled execution failures. Its construction and validation pipeline yields 870 tasks across BEHAVIOR and ProcTHOR, complemented by about 3,500 situated questions tied to the evaluated agent's execution. Benchmark results reveal difficulties in retaining scene evidence, monitoring progress, and recovering from unexpected outcomes. To address these difficulties, SCOPER-harness combines Evidence Memory and Progress Verification with a dynamic task agenda and bounded exploration, without additional model training. Across two evaluated open-source backbones and two simulators, the harness improves task success by 11.1-28.6%; a harnessed 9B model outperforms a directly executed 27B model on both simulators. In an offline next-action evaluation using observations from 200 real-robot demonstrations, the harness also improves full-call accuracy by 14.7% and 15.3%. SCOPER provides a setting for diagnosing and improving embodied reasoning throughout a complete task execution cycle.
bullets: Addresses gaps in open-loop and limited closed-loop evaluations that overlook decision-shaped observations and execution failures.
Introduces SCOPER-bench with 870 tasks across BEHAVIOR and ProcTHOR, plus about 3,500 execution-grounded situated questions.
Combines Evidence Memory, Progress Verification, a dynamic task agenda, and bounded exploration in the training-free SCOPER-harness.
The harness improves task success by 11.1–28.6% across two backbones and two simulators, and improves offline next-action accuracy by 14.7% and 15.3%.
Findings highlight persistent challenges in retaining scene evidence, monitoring progress, and recovering from unexpected outcomes.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing reference videos as editable dynamic 3D scenes is an important path toward controllable video generation for filmmaking: these scenes provide modifiable, renderable visual proxies that enable explicit control over scene layout, subject actions, and camera behavior. To evaluate agents' ability to reconstruct editable dynamic 3D scenes from dynamic reference videos, we introduce CineRecon, a benchmark comprising 50 reference videos and 360 annotated evaluation clips. The reference videos span film, real-world footage, and games. Given a complete video, an agent uses tools to construct, animate, render, and refine its reconstruction. We evaluate this task under three representation settings: Proxy, Simplified, and Detailed. These settings increase geometric and appearance requirements while retaining the same requirements for spatial relations, camera behavior, and subject dynamics. This design tests whether agents can reproduce the events in a video when detailed appearance is unnecessary, and how performance changes as representation requirements increase. For evaluation, we construct checklists that associate observable properties and events with specific entities and times. A vision-language judge compares timestamp-aligned reference and rendered frames across 11 categories, grouped into camera, static, and dynamic consistency dimensions. We evaluate 12 models using their corresponding agent harnesses and find failures across all three dimensions. Subject motions and interactions remain difficult to reproduce even under the Proxy setting.
bullets: Introduces a benchmark with 50 reference videos and 360 annotated evaluation clips spanning film, real-world footage, and games.
Tests three reconstruction settings—Proxy, Simplified, and Detailed—with progressively stricter geometry and appearance requirements.
Uses entity- and time-specific checklists plus a vision-language judge comparing aligned reference and rendered frames across 11 categories.
Evaluates 12 models through their agent harnesses and observes failures in camera, static-scene, and dynamic consistency.
Subject motions and interactions remain challenging even when only proxy representations are required.

papers.abstract: Digital cultural heritage collections encode rich relations among objects, places, periods, providers, images, and source institutions, yet users typically access them through keyword search and faceted browsing. We present CULTUREBOT, an interactive framework for natural-language exploration of cultural heritage collections that combines knowledge-graph-guided retrieval, lexical-semantic retrieval, and source-linked generation. CULTUREBOT maps user queries to structured catalogue relations, enriches retrieved records with textual evidence, and generates answers that link back to the underlying repository records. We instantiate the framework on 81,852 SearchCulture records and release an online demonstration. In an expert evaluation involving six cultural-heritage specialists, 55 persona-grounded queries, and 250 evaluations, the graph-guided system was rated significantly higher than two general-purpose assistants and a non-graph ablation, with the largest gains in evidence grounding, diversity, reasoning, and completeness. These results support graph-guided retrieval as a practical way to expose the relational structure of cultural collections through conversational access while preserving links to catalogue evidence.
bullets: Addresses the limits of keyword search and faceted browsing for collections with rich object, place, period, provider, and institution relations.
Maps natural-language queries to catalogue relations, combines graph, lexical, and semantic retrieval, and enriches results with textual evidence.
Generates answers linked to underlying repository records to preserve evidence grounding.

Evaluated on 81,852 SearchCulture records using 55 expert-authored queries and 250 assessments; it outperformed two general-purpose assistants and a non-graph ablation across several quality dimensions.
An online demonstration is released; the evaluation focuses on cultural-heritage specialists and the SearchCulture collection.

papers.abstract: Which context tokens drive a language model's answer? Graph-based tools such as attention rollout and attention flow answer this from a single forward pass, yet their faithfulness in decoder-only models is rarely tested against interventions. We view the layers of a decoder as a causal network whose conductances are attention weights, and read a token's influence on the answer from the resistance between them. We propose RIFT (Resistance-based Information Flow in Transformers), which scores a token by the series resistance of its path of least resistance to the answer, found exactly by a classic shortest-path dynamic program. On synthetic in-context retrieval tasks and extractive question answering over Wikipedia paragraphs, RIFT predicts the effect of replacing a token with a Spearman correlation of 0.52-0.68; predicting a single replacement, it reaches 77-96% of the agreement between two different random replacements. It needs no gradients and no extra forward passes, scoring every token of a prompt in 0.9-3.4 ms on one CPU thread, whereas the replacement experiment needs a forward pass per token. On 576 held-out prompts from four models of two families (Qwen3 and Llama 3.2), it outperforms token distance, attention rollout and attention flow in every pre-specified comparison, by 0.23 to 0.88 in mean Spearman correlation, and it is the best or tied-best of all attention-based scores we test. Aggregates that add up all routes (attention flow, effective resistance and rollout) instead mostly encode token position: as a simple proposition shows, early tokens have many more parallel routes to the answer.
bullets: Frames transformer layers as a causal network, with attention weights acting as conductances.
Scores each token using the series resistance of its path of least resistance, computed exactly via shortest-path dynamic programming.
On synthetic retrieval and extractive QA tasks, its scores correlate with replacement effects at 0.52–0.68 Spearman correlation.
Across 576 prompts from Qwen3 and Llama 3.2 models, RIFT outperforms token distance, attention rollout, and attention flow in all pre-specified comparisons.
Runs in 0.9–3.4 ms per prompt on one CPU thread; aggregate route methods often primarily reflect token position.

papers.selection_reason: Graph-based token influence attribution for decoder-only LLMs; relevant to understanding and improving LLM behavior.
papers.title: RIFT: Token Influence Follows the Path of Least Resistance
papers.tldr: RIFT estimates which prompt tokens influence a decoder-only model’s answer by finding the lowest-resistance information path through its attention graph, without gradients or extra forward passes.

papers.abstract: We consider online binary prediction with paid stochastic features, where the learner can spend resources to obtain better observations of the underlying features. This setting is motivated by applications such as medical testing, where additional cost can provide more precise measurements of patient's features for predicting a binary outcome. At each round, a latent feature is drawn i.i.d., the response is generated through a logistic model, and the learner chooses how much to pay before observing a noisy version of the feature. The goal of learner is to jointly control prediction loss and acquisition cost. In contrast to the former result on the online linear regression with paid features, covariance information alone is no longer sufficient: two noise distributions with the same covariance may induce different optimal logistic losses, and lower variance can even lead to higher loss. Under a structural ordering in which larger payments yield better observations by removing independent noise, we obtain $\widetilde O(\sqrt{T})$ regret when the noise structure is known and $\widetilde O(T^{2/3})$ regret when it is unknown, with matching lower bounds up to logarithmic factors.
bullets: The learner jointly balances binary prediction loss against the cost of obtaining less noisy features.
For logistic loss, equal covariance—or even lower variance—does not determine better performance.
A structural ordering assumes larger payments improve observations by removing independent noise.
Regret is \(\widetilde O(\sqrt{T})\) with known noise structure and \(\widetilde O(T^{2/3})\) when it is unknown.
Matching lower bounds hold up to logarithmic factors.
papers.selection_reason: Online binary prediction with paid noisy features and regret guarantees; fits the online learning subtopic.
papers.title: Beyond Second-Order Information: Paid Logistic Regression with Noisy Features
papers.tldr: Paid feature acquisition enables online logistic prediction with near-optimal regret, but requires information beyond noise covariance.

papers.abstract: Federated vision-language models (FedVLMs) represent one of the emerging frontiers of machine learning, aiming to integrate federated learning within the fine-tuning pipelines of vision-language models (VLMs). In this work, we introduce BLEND, a new framework designed to jointly enhance the personalization and generalization capabilities of FedVLMs. BLEND proposes a selective VLM parameter fine-tuning and aggregation strategy that consists of (i) global vision and text adapters shared across clients, and (ii) a personalized vision projection adapter tailored to each client. BLEND further introduces a novel loss function that blends the outputs of the global and personalized adapters to achieve personalization, while simultaneously promoting generalization through a principled anchor design implemented via the projection heads of the zero-shot VLM. Extensive experiments demonstrate that BLEND consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, highlighting its ability to effectively balance personalization and generalization across diverse system settings. (Code is available at: https://github.com/payamsiabd/BLEND.git)
bullets: Addresses the challenge of improving both client personalization and cross-client generalization in FedVLMs.
Fine-tunes and aggregates global vision and text adapters shared across clients.
Uses a personalized vision projection adapter for each client.
Blends global and personalized adapter outputs, with zero-shot VLM projection heads providing generalization anchors.
Experiments show consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines across diverse system settings.

papers.abstract: In continuous diffusion language models (DLMs), latents generated by the diffusion prior are mapped almost deterministically to tokens, either by a decoder or through a token embedding matrix. Unlike in image generation, where visual details can vary continuously, the diffusion prior must capture fine-grained discrete token choices in continuous space, which can make the joint latent distribution difficult to model. We argue that generative roles should instead be divided: the diffusion prior should generate high-level predictive information, while the decoder should resolve the remaining token-level choices. Based on this view, we introduce Predictive-State Flows (PSF), which partitions a sequence into blocks and associates each block with a predictive state computed solely from the preceding context. A rectified-flow prior generates the sequence of predictive states, after which a block-causal decoder generates all blocks in parallel, autoregressively only within each block. This design reduces diffusion from L token-level states to K << L predictive states and reduces token-level sequential depth to L/K. On unconditional OpenWebText generation, a 197M-parameter model with K=8 achieves a generative perplexity of 22.8 at entropy 5.16 using 0.31 TFLOPs per 1024-token document, versus 24.0 and 7.2 TFLOPs for ELF-B with 32 sampling steps. The corresponding measured operating points yield MAUVE@512 of 0.93 and 0.73, respectively. Controlled comparisons further show that content states, which additionally encode their own blocks, yield 8-16% higher generative perplexity than predictive states, and that replacing sampled predictive-state trajectories with a shared mean lowers MAUVE@512 by 0.11. These results suggest that latent design for continuous DLMs should consider not only how compactly text is represented, but also how generative roles are divided between the prior and the decoder.
bullets: Problem: Token-level diffusion latents must represent fine-grained discrete choices, making their joint distribution difficult to model.

Method: Partition sequences into blocks; a rectified-flow prior generates predictive states from preceding context, and a block-causal decoder generates blocks in parallel while decoding within each block autoregressively.
Contribution: Reduces diffusion from L token-level states to K≪L predictive states and lowers token-level sequential depth to L/K.

Result: On unconditional OpenWebText, a 197M-parameter PSF model with K=8 reaches generative perplexity 22.8 and MAUVE@512 0.93 at 0.31 TFLOPs per document, compared with ELF-B’s 24.0, 0.73, and 7.2 TFLOPs.

Scope: Results support dividing generative responsibilities between the diffusion prior and decoder; predictive states outperform content states and shared mean trajectories in controlled comparisons.

papers.abstract: In this work, we introduce Crazyflow, an accurate, differentiable simulator built on JAX. By leveraging jit compilation via XLA, Crazyflow unifies physics and control into a single differentiable computation graph, enabling massive parallelization on accelerated hardware without sacrificing modeling accuracy. This architecture achieves order-of-magnitude speedups over existing baselines, capable of training deployable reinforcement learning agents in seconds. To highlight its highly modular design, we demonstrate how easily Crazyflow can be extended by integrating a complete, high-fidelity Ultra-Wideband (UWB) and Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) simulation pipeline coupled with a full-state Extended Kalman Filter (EKF). This capability allows for massive parallel controller evaluation under realistic, degraded state feedback with minimal impact on GPU throughput. By combining speed, accuracy, and extensibility, Crazyflow serves as a foundational tool for the next generation of aerial robotics research.
bullets: Unifies physics and control in one XLA-compiled, differentiable computation graph for large-scale parallel simulation.
Supports rapid reinforcement-learning training, with reported order-of-magnitude speedups over existing baselines.
Adds modular, high-fidelity UWB and IMU simulation with a full-state Extended Kalman Filter.
Enables massive controller evaluation under degraded state feedback while preserving GPU throughput.
Demonstrated for aerial robotics; broader performance and applicability depend on the simulator’s modeled sensors and dynamics.

Fig. 3. Simulated tracking of a figure-8 reference with a 10 s cycle time using a geometric controller [18]. With lower sensor quality, the position estimate and the tracking quality degrade.

papers.tldr: Crazyflow is a fast, differentiable JAX simulator for training and evaluating aerial-robot controllers under realistic degraded UWB/IMU feedback.

papers.abstract: Smart factory inspection requires robots to reach connected equipment without a prior map or known target coordinates. Radio frequency (RF) signals from the target can provide directional cues to complement visual observations when occlusion or poor lighting limits target detection. However, multipath propagation can distort these cues, making it difficult to infer the target's true direction from instantaneous RF measurements. To enable navigation research under these conditions, we first construct a Habitat Sionna RT benchmark that uses detailed scene geometry and assigned material properties to generate aligned visual and RF observations in response to robot actions. Building on this benchmark, we propose an uncertainty aware multimodal navigation framework that jointly estimates target direction and its uncertainty from a history of RF, visual, and pose observations. These estimates inform action selection alongside visual context. Experiments in unseen scenes show relative improvements of 18.2% in success rate (SR) and 11.5% in success weighted by path length (SPL) over the strongest evaluated baseline.
bullets: Addresses smart-factory navigation when target coordinates and prior maps are unavailable.
Introduces a Habitat Sionna RT benchmark with detailed geometry and material properties for aligned visual and RF observations.
Jointly estimates target direction and uncertainty from historical RF, visual, and pose data to inform actions.
In unseen scenes, improves success rate by 18.2% and success weighted by path length by 11.5% over the strongest evaluated baseline.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the proposed framework. The uncertainty-aware goal predictor uses the multimodal observation history to predict a von Mises distribution over the source direction. Its goal tokens are stored alongside RGB, depth, and pose tokens in the scene memory transformer. A query formed from the current observation retrieves historical context through cross-attention for actor critic navigation. Ground-truth direction supervision is used only during training.
Fig. 4. Qualitative trajectories of the proposed method. Colored route segments indicate LOS, NLOS, and unavailable RF signals; markers denote the start and goal.

Fig. 2. Habitat–Sionna RT benchmark construction from MP3D scenes. Habitat renders egocentric RGB-D observations, while semantically segmented meshes are assigned electromagnetic material properties using ITU models for RF simulation in Sionna RT.
Fig. 3. (a) Distribution of line-of-sight (LOS), NLOS, and invalid observations along shortest-path oracle trajectories. (b) Mean reward per step during training.

papers.tldr: An uncertainty-aware navigation framework combines RF, visual, and pose histories to guide robots toward targets despite multipath-distorted signals and missing maps.

papers.abstract: Conditional neural fields represent signals continuously, but their effectiveness depends on how the conditional latent representations are inferred from observed data. In meta-learning, this encoding occurs through gradient updates induced by the decoder, tying representation learning directly to decoder design. We formalize this connection by interpreting latent optimization as an optimization encoder, unifying the roles of second-order differentiation, latent parameterization, and task supervision. This concept enables second-order meta-learning for end-to-end training of the encoding procedure alongside the decoder, and clarifies which learning pathway first-order approximations discard. Guided by this view, we introduce Attentive Latent Fields (MetaLF), an equivariant transformer-based neural field that contextualizes a latent pointcloud through self-attention. These interactions shape both field predictions and the updates that construct their representation, allowing local observations to inform coherent non-local structure. Disentangling the inner encoding objective from outer task supervision unifies reconstruction, classification, and segmentation within an end-to-end meta-learning framework, using reconstruction-only latent adaptation at test time. Controlled experiments on polynomial fields link latent coordination to lower effective rank and stronger alignment with the underlying function space. Across image and 3D shape reconstruction, MetaLF improves fidelity within three to five gradient updates, while supporting semantic prediction across images, shapes, and volumes. Together, these findings position the optimization encoder perspective as a unified basis for designing neural fields around how representations are constructed, coordinated, and used.
bullets: Motivation: Neural-field performance depends on how latent representations are inferred, but this process is tightly coupled to decoder design and often simplified by first-order approximations.
Method: Formalizes latent optimization as an optimization encoder and trains the encoding procedure jointly with the decoder using second-order meta-learning.
Model: MetaLF uses an equivariant, self-attentive transformer to coordinate latent pointclouds, enabling local observations to shape coherent non-local structure.

Findings: Controlled polynomial-field experiments associate latent coordination with lower effective rank and better alignment with the underlying function space; image and 3D reconstruction improves within 3–5 updates.
Scope: The framework supports reconstruction, classification, and segmentation, with reconstruction-only latent adaptation at test time.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Second-order meta-learning trains an optimization encoder whose behaviour is shaped by decoder architecture. (a) A conventional encoder maps an observed signal to a latent representation zi, which the decoder evaluates at a query coordinate x. (b) In meta-learned neural fields, an explicit encoder is replaced by K gradient updates on z, forming an optimization encoder. Second-order differentiation propagates the outer objective Lout through these unrolled updates, jointly shaping the finite-step encoding behavior and the decoder fθ. (c) Because the decoder induces the latent updates, its architecture shapes the resulting adaptation trajectory. ENF represents a local fitting model, lacking direct exchange of context among localized latents. MetaLF instead coordinates these latents through attention. This shared context produces coherent updates that quickly capture non-local structure, as illustrated by fitting cardiac signed distance functions.

Figure 5: MetaLF is equivariant under a group action defined by its bi-invariant feature a. Rows show translationequivariant (Rn) and roto-translation-equivariant (SE(n)) MetaLF models on CelebA and ACDC myocardium. Columns show ground truth, reconstruction in the canonical frame, pose-only translation, joint translation of poses and queries, pose-only roto-translation, and the corresponding joint roto-translation. Acting on poses alone transforms the represented field; applying the same group element jointly to poses and queries preserves predicted values at corresponding coordinates when the model respects that symmetry. Accordingly, joint translations match the canonical reconstruction in every row, whereas joint roto-translation does so only for the SE(n) models.

Figure 3: MetaLF as an optimization encoder. (a) K gradient updates encode observations into a spatially grounded, globally contextualized latent representation through SE(n)-equivariant self-attention (SA) layers and cross-attention (CA) with a query coordinate. (b) During meta-training, task-specific outer objectives can shape the decoder through second-order gradients across the adaptation steps. Global contextualization of the latent point set therefore enables flexible meta-training: the same inner-loop encoder can learn representations tailored to diverse downstream objectives.

Figure 1: Example use case of MetaLF meta-learning latent cardiac shape representations [3]. The first three panels illustrate smooth shape recovery as a shared latent pointcloud z is refined over k = 1, . . . , 5 gradient steps. MetaLF learns contextualized latent representations that preserve detail while capturing the underlying function, an ill-posed task for local representation models such as ENF [4].

Figure 6: Training progress on CIFAR10 reconstruction for MAML (blue) and FOMAML (red). (a) MAML develops a higher latent effective rank, while the first-order controls remain at lower ranks. (b) MAML generally has smaller upper response factors, although these fluctuate during training. (c) MAML’s reconstruction error decreases substantially over training epochs, whereas the first-order controls plateau after an initial improvement. (d) Both methods perform best near the three-step training horizon, with reconstruction error gradually increasing under further adaptation.
Figure 10: Uncurated examples generated using latent rectified flow based on the reconstruction meta-learned MetaLF (MetaLF-Diffuser) representation models.

Figure 7: Optimization encoder-side coupling (top) and decoder-side attention routing (bottom) evaluated on the polynomial fields dataset, shown with increasing number of MetaLF self-attention layers (NSA) for N = 25 latent tokens. Additional layers allow information to propagate beyond local latent neighborhoods while retaining the spatial structure of the representation.

Figure 4: A receiving latent j attends to neighbouring source latents j′ using bi-invariant geometric attributes aj′→j . Keys and values combine this geometry with the source content cj′ , and their attention-weighted aggregation produces the updated feature h′ j .

Figure 8: Qualitative example for OMBRIA meta-segmentation, illustrating the 25th percentile, median, and 75th percentile MetaLF test-set performance sample in terms of IoU. In the median case, SpatialFuncta and ENF produce extensive false-positive flood predictions around cloudy regions, whereas MetaLF largely suppresses them. This pattern is consistent with non-local latent interactions using broader spatial context to resolve ambiguous local signals.

papers.abstract: When humans hand each other objects, they incorporate both geometric and semantic information into this process. For example, passing a knife with the handle towards the recipient, rather than the blade, is both more ergonomic and safer. Recent state-of-the-art methods for task-oriented robot-human handovers have progressed from modeling object geometry to incorporating object affordances. However, they often forgo predicting the explicit, task-specific hand poses a human selects to utilize an object. Since many objects support multiple interaction modalities, e.g., a claw hammer used to strike or pull nails, this variability must be modeled to achieve robust task-oriented handovers. To tackle this, we propose a novel approach, GENESIS-Handover (GENErative HypotheSIS), which leverages VLM image generation to produce a variety of task-specific hand-object interaction hypotheses. These hypotheses are matched in real time to the observed human hand pose, enabling inference of the most suitable handover configuration. By leveraging VLMs as priors of plausible hand-object interactions, the method produces task-conditioned handover strategies for previously unseen object-task pairs. We evaluate the standalone interaction proposal module before deploying the full system on a mobile manipulator. In a user study with 12 participants across five task-object pairs, 83.3% perceived our method to have better task understanding than the previous state of the art.
bullets: Addresses the need to model explicit, task-specific human hand poses, especially when objects support multiple uses.
Uses VLM image generation to propose diverse task-conditioned hand-object interaction hypotheses.
Matches generated hypotheses to the observed human hand pose in real time to infer a suitable handover configuration.
Supports previously unseen object-task pairs and is deployed on a mobile manipulator.
In a 12-participant user study covering five task-object pairs, 83.3% perceived better task understanding than the prior state of the art.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of GENESIS-Handover. The system generates task-conditioned hand-object interaction hypotheses (blue), selects the best-matching hypothesis based on the observed human hand (purple), and computes a reactive end-effector target by anchoring the selected relation to the live hand pose (dark green). AFT-Handover provides affordance priors for alignment initialization and object placement in the gripper (white). All inputs to the system are shown in light green.

Figure 3: Overview of the Hand-Object Hypothesis Generation block. From an RGB-D scene observation and task specification, the system generates multiple task-conditioned hand-object hypotheses and maps them into the real object frame: The system first reconstructs the object mesh (I), then generates multiple synthetic hand-object interaction hypothesis images (II), generates depth and hand pose estimates (III and IV), lifts these into metric 3D (V), and expresses each hypothesis as a relative transform between the human hand and the real object (VI).

Figure 4: Example images comparing hand alignment between AFT-Handover and the proposed method for all handovers of one user study participant. GENESIS-Handover more closely matches the human hand configuration, requiring fewer adjustments to grasp the object than AFT-Handover. The initial handover pose is shown in transparent.

Figure 1: Example for the tool-task pair screwdriver, to screw. Initially, GENESIS-Handover generates multiple hand-object interaction hypotheses via a VLM. At handover onset (I), the human hand pose is observed by the onboard camera, and each hypothesis is scored based on joint-level similarity to the observed pose. The closest hypothesis is selected for execution. During execution, the robot continuously adapts its target to the human hand (II and III, hand pose from previous frame blended in). Finally, the handover occurs with the hand configuration matching the selected hypothesis (IV).

papers.abstract: Model merging aims to build a multi-task model cheaply by combining the weights of individual task-specific models. To perform well across multiple tasks, most existing merging methods use an additional dataset to find the coefficients for the best linear combination of task-specific weight updates. However, we identify an implicit regularization in this standard practice: searching over coefficients restricts the candidate models to a subspace spanned by task-specific weight updates. In this work, we investigate whether this regularization is actually useful. Surprisingly, empirical results show that optimizing merged-model weights without this regularization significantly boosts the performance of common merging methods across multiple architectures, domains, and even in an extremely data-limited scenario where only one instance is available per class. Moreover, directly optimizing the pretrained model weights even outperforms some existing merging methods. Analysis shows that better multi-task weights exist outside the subspace and can be found using multiple methods. We study different strategies for using the additional dataset, discussing their practical use and implications for model merging. Overall, this work calls for revisiting the existing model-merging pipeline, motivating a broader exploration of the weight space and a reconsideration of the implicit regularization induced by task arithmetic.
bullets: Existing merging methods often tune coefficients over task-specific weight updates using an additional dataset, implicitly restricting solutions to their spanned subspace.
The study finds that removing this restriction improves common merging methods across architectures and domains, including an extremely data-limited setting.
Direct optimization of pretrained weights can outperform some existing merging approaches.
Analysis indicates that better multi-task weights exist outside the task-update subspace and can be reached through multiple strategies.
The work reassesses how additional data should be used and encourages broader exploration of the weight space.

figures.caption: Figure 1: A new perspective on the model-merging pipeline. The existing model-merging pipeline builds the merged model θmerge by adding a linear combination of task-specific weight updates τi to the pretrained model θ0. Standard practice uses an additional dataset, which we term auxiliary data, to optimize the coefficients λ for multi-task performance. This coefficient optimization regularizes model updates to the subspace spanned by τi. We challenge this pipeline by using the same auxiliary data to optimize the merged-model weights, allowing optimization beyond this subspace. Experimental results show that exploring the broader weight space generally leads to significant performance improvements across merging methods (TA, TIES, DARE, and TSV-M).

Figure 2: Average test accuracy under different uses of auxiliary data. Across vision tasks (top) and language tasks (bottom) with different models, Gradient Descent (GD) from the merged models consistently outperforms both coefficient search and the empirical best performance of its search space (Subspace best) for every merging method (TA, TIES, DARE, and TSV-M).

Figure 7: Positive correlation between Init accuracy of merged models and their afterGD accuracy. Existing model merging methods provide strong initializations for gradient descent, and stronger methods have better afterGD performance.

Figure 6: Computational usage of different ways to use the auxiliary data. Gradient descent on weights (Weight GD) uses slightly more memory than coefficient search. While doing gradient descent requires more compute effort (time/FLOPs), it trades compute for better performance.

Figure 3: Average test accuracy under different sizes and uses of auxiliary data for TA. We downsample the auxiliary data and compare different uses of auxiliary data for TA. We run three random seeds for downsampling, and report error bars as the shaded regions. Figure 5: S-RandOpt sampled weights’ test performance. We sample 64 random weights in language models using S-RandOpt, and compare their test performance with the best point on the task-vector subspace (subspace best). A high proportion of sampled weights from outside the subspace outperforms the best weight on the subspace (Subspace best).

The axes e1, e2, and e3 are the directions of τ1, τ⊥2 , and each run’s update’s orthogonal component to the subspace ∆⊥. papers.title: A Broader Look at Model Merging: Rethinking Implicit Regularization Induced by Task Arithmetic
papers.tldr: Optimizing merged model weights beyond the task-update subspace can substantially improve multi-task model merging, challenging the assumed benefit of task-arithmetic regularization.

papers.abstract: Adversarial training is one of the most reliable defenses against adversarial attacks, but its high computational cost must generally be paid anew for each task. Robust foundation models offer a promising alternative: adversarially pretrain a model once and then transfer its robustness to downstream tasks through lightweight adaptation. However, a fundamental question remains open: can robustness acquired during pretraining transfer to unseen tasks without further adversarial training? In this study, we answer this question affirmatively. A single model adversarially pretrained at scale can achieve optimal robustness on new tasks without additional task-specific training. Specifically, we show that, for a family of Gaussian-mixture classification tasks, a sufficiently deep linear transformer adversarially trained across tasks can asymptotically attain the robust Bayes error on previously unseen tasks through in-context learning from clean demonstrations. By contrast, a standardly trained model cannot. We further analyze convergence under gradient flow, an accuracy--robustness trade-off, and demonstration complexity.
bullets: Studies whether robustness learned during pretraining transfers to new tasks.
Shows this transfer for Gaussian-mixture classification with sufficiently deep linear transformers.
Adversarially trained models asymptotically achieve robust Bayes error on unseen tasks via clean demonstrations.
Standardly trained models do not achieve the same robust performance.
Also analyzes gradient-flow convergence, the accuracy–robustness trade-off, and demonstration complexity.

papers.title: Adversarially Trained Linear Transformers Are Optimal Robust In-Context Learners for Gaussian Mixtures
papers.tldr: Adversarially pretrained deep linear transformers can transfer optimal robustness to unseen Gaussian-mixture classification tasks through clean in-context demonstrations, without task-specific adversarial training.

papers.abstract: We study the implicit bias of Riemannian gradient flow for hyperbolic multiclass classification with fixed class prototypes in hyperbolic space $\mathbb H^n$. Our framework accommodates general permutation invariant relative margin (PERM) losses, a class that includes cross entropy and other standard multiclass losses. Our analysis is based on a decomposition: at large radius, the distance to each prototype splits into a radial term and a direction dependent term described by the Busemann function. This yields two main results. First, we prove a radial dichotomy: the sign of a drift coefficient $μ$ determines whether the radius is pushed toward the ideal boundary or back toward the interior; if the positive drift persists, then $r(t)=\tfrac12\log t+O(1)$, while persistent negative drift returns the trajectory to the large radius threshold in finite time. Second, we show that large-radius directions can approach critical points of the Busemann risk on $\partial\mathbb H^n$, even during radial return. These results provide a rigorous large-radius perspective on two phenomena we refer to as boundary saturation and near-boundary clustering in hyperbolic representation learning.
bullets: Studies Riemannian gradient flow with fixed hyperbolic class prototypes under general permutation-invariant relative-margin losses, including cross entropy.
Decomposes prototype distances at large radius into radial and direction-dependent Busemann terms.
Shows the drift coefficient’s sign determines whether trajectories move toward the ideal boundary or return toward the interior.
Under persistent positive drift, the radius grows as one-half log time plus a bounded term; persistent negative drift causes finite-time return to a large-radius threshold.
Shows directions can approach critical points of the boundary Busemann risk, including during radial return.

The observed nondegenerate attractors have negative drift, illustrating the angular alignment mechanism underlying radial return.

papers.abstract: Accurate bioactivity prediction is a central challenge in early-stage drug discovery, as individual assays often contain too few measurements to train reliable models independently. Meta-learning offers a principled approach to this few-shot setting, but assay heterogeneity may limit its effectiveness. Here, we test this hypothesis and show that meta-learning performance degrades as meta-training tasks become more heterogeneous. To address this, we introduce MetaHeta, a meta-learning framework that accounts for assay heterogeneity by conditioning predictions on auxiliary data from related assays, with relatedness defined flexibly from available assay information. The architecture of MetaHeta combines linear attention over large auxiliary datasets with exact attention over scarce task-specific context, enabling efficient scaling to the former without compromising exact attention over the latter. We demonstrate the benefits of our approach on assays from ChEMBL and BindingDB, improving few-shot bioactivity prediction and downstream compound prioritization in retrospective Bayesian optimization.
bullets: Few-shot assay datasets often lack enough measurements for reliable independent models.
Meta-learning performance declines when meta-training assays are highly heterogeneous.
MetaHeta conditions predictions on auxiliary data from flexibly defined related assays.
It combines linear attention for large auxiliary datasets with exact attention for scarce task-specific context.
Experiments on ChEMBL and BindingDB show improved prediction and retrospective Bayesian-optimization compound prioritization.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Architecture overview of MetaHeta. A shared input MLP embeds context, target, and concatenated auxiliary observations, augmented with task-of-origin indicators, with target activities masked to 0. Encoder layers use exact self-attention for the context and FAVOR+ for auxiliary data, followed by context-to-auxiliary and target-to-context cross-attention. When Daux = ∅, the auxiliary branch is skipped. Finally, an output MLP parameterizes a mean-field Gaussian predictive distribution. Formal definitions of the attention operators are given in Appendix F.

Figure 5: R2 os and inference time of MetaHeta and ICICL-TNP with varying cardinality of Daux. Auxiliary conditioning improves predictive performance with modest incremental cost. Our architecture processes five auxiliary datasets faster than ICICL-TNP processes a single one.
